questions.solution: With 50 votes, the other 51 voters could all choose one other candidate, who would win. With 51 votes, only 50 votes are left, so nobody can match or beat 51. So 51 votes (a majority) guarantees the win.

solve.work: Others hold 101-w votes and could all go to one rival; need w > 101-w, so w >= 51.

questions.stem: Which statement about voting is true?
choices: A candidate with the most first-place votes always beats every other candidate head-to-head
A candidate who wins every head-to-head comparison always has a majority of the first-place votes
A candidate who wins every head-to-head comparison always wins the Borda count
A candidate with a majority of the first-place votes beats every other candidate head-to-head
questions.answer: A candidate with a majority of the first-place votes beats every other candidate head-to-head
questions.solution: If more than half of the voters rank X first, then in any comparison of X with Y those voters all rank X above Y, so X wins every comparison. The other statements fail: a plurality winner can lose head-to-head, and a head-to-head winner may have few first-place votes or lose the Borda count.

solve.answer: A candidate with a majority of the first-place votes beats every other candidate head-to-head
solve.work: A majority winner is ranked above any rival by more than half the voters, so wins every head-to-head. A, C, D are false in general.

questions.stem: Twenty-one voters rank three candidates X, Y and Z. In the head-to-head comparison of Z and X, 12 voters rank Z above X. For Z to be a Condorcet winner, Z must also win the comparison with Y. What is the smallest number of the 21 voters who must rank Z above Y?
questions.solution: Z already beats X (12 votes to 9). To beat Y, Z needs more than half of the 21 voters, which is more than 10.5. The smallest whole number is 11.

solve.work: Winning the Z-Y comparison with no tie among 21 voters needs more than 10.5: 11.

questions.stem: A committee wants to avoid electing a candidate whom many voters rank last. Which method and reason fit that goal best?
choices: The Borda count, because a candidate ranked last by many voters earns few points
Plurality, because a candidate ranked last by many voters cannot have the most first-place votes
Plurality with elimination, because any candidate ranked last by a voter is eliminated first
The Borda count, because it removes any candidate ranked last by even one voter
questions.answer: The Borda count, because a candidate ranked last by many voters earns few points
questions.solution: Borda gives 0 points for each last-place ranking, so many last places drag a total down. Plurality ignores last places entirely (a candidate can win with a third of the votes and be ranked last by everyone else), and the other statements describe rules that do not exist.

solve.answer: The Borda count, because a candidate ranked last by many voters earns few points
solve.work: Borda gives few points to a candidate many rank last. A is false (a plurality winner can be ranked last by many); B and C misdescribe the methods.

questions.stem: A critic of plurality voting points to an election with 120 voters in which the winner received 42 first-place votes. What percent of the voters did not vote for the winner?
questions.solution: $120 - 42 = 78$ voters did not vote for the winner, and $78 \div 120 = 0.65$, or 65 percent. A plurality winner can be opposed by a large majority.

questions.stem: A critic says that pairwise comparison might fail to choose a winner. Which situation is she describing?
choices: One candidate wins every comparison, so the others cannot be ranked
Each of three candidates beats one of the others and loses to another
Two candidates have the same number of first-place votes
Exactly half of the voters rank one candidate last
questions.answer: Each of three candidates beats one of the others and loses to another
questions.solution: When A beats B, B beats C and C beats A (a cycle), every candidate has the same record and no candidate beats all the others. That is the weakness the critic means.

solve.answer: Each of three candidates beats one of the others and loses to another
solve.work: A cycle (Condorcet paradox): each beats one and loses to another, so no candidate wins every comparison.

questions.stem: A town's rule is: "Whenever every voter ranks X above Y, the town's ranking puts Y above X." Which of Arrow's conditions does this rule break?
choices: Non-dictatorship: no single voter's ranking should always decide the result
Independence of irrelevant alternatives: the order of X and Y should depend only on how voters rank X and Y
Unanimity: if every voter ranks X above Y, the group should rank X above Y
Universal domain: every possible set of voter rankings should be allowed
questions.answer: Unanimity: if every voter ranks X above Y, the group should rank X above Y
questions.solution: The rule does the opposite of what the voters unanimously say, which breaks unanimity. It still depends only on how X and Y are ranked, no one voter decides the result, and it accepts any rankings.

solve.answer: Unanimity: if every voter ranks X above Y, the group should rank X above Y
solve.work: The rule reverses a unanimous preference, breaking unanimity.

questions.stem: A voting method ranks X above Y. Then some voters change how they rank a third candidate Z, but no voter changes how they rank X against Y. The method now ranks Y above X. Which of Arrow's conditions does the method break?
choices: Unanimity: if every voter ranks X above Y, the group should rank X above Y
Non-dictatorship: no single voter's ranking should always decide the result
Universal domain: every possible set of voter rankings should be allowed
Independence of irrelevant alternatives: the order of X and Y should depend only on how voters rank X and Y
questions.answer: Independence of irrelevant alternatives: the order of X and Y should depend only on how voters rank X and Y
questions.solution: Z is irrelevant to the order of X and Y, yet moving Z changed that order. That is exactly a violation of independence of irrelevant alternatives.

solve.answer: Independence of irrelevant alternatives: the order of X and Y should depend only on how voters rank X and Y
solve.work: The X-Y order changed though no one changed X vs Y: IIA is broken.

questions.stem: Universal domain says a voting method must accept every possible set of voter rankings. How many different complete rankings (strict orders, no ties) of 4 candidates can a single voter submit?
questions.solution: A voter chooses the first candidate in 4 ways, the second in 3, the third in 2 and the last in 1: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$ rankings.

solve.work: 4! = 24 strict rankings.

questions.stem: Seventeen voters rank four candidates, from first choice to last: 6 voters: A, C, B, D; 5 voters: B, C, D, A; 4 voters: C, D, B, A; 2 voters: D, B, C, A. In a Borda count, each voter gives 3 points to their first choice, 2 to their second, 1 to their third and 0 to their last. How many points does the winner earn?
questions.solution: Candidate C is ranked first by 4 voters ($4 \times 3 = 12$ points), second by 11 voters (the 6 with A, C, B, D and the 5 with B, C, D, A, so $11 \times 2 = 22$ points) and third by 2 voters ($2 \times 1 = 2$ points). C earns $12 + 22 + 2 = 36$ points. The others earn A: 18, B: 29, D: 19, so C is the winner.

questions.stem: In a Borda count of three candidates among 12 voters, the points are 2 for first choice, 1 for second and 0 for last. A club changes the points to 3 for first choice, 2 for second and 1 for last. Which statement is true?
choices: Every total rises by 12, so the winner stays the same
Every total rises by 3, so the winner stays the same
Only last-place candidates gain points, so the winner may change
The totals do not change, so the winner stays the same
questions.answer: Every total rises by 12, so the winner stays the same
questions.solution: Each voter now gives every candidate exactly 1 more point than before, whatever their ranking. With 12 voters, each candidate's total rises by 12. Since every total rises by the same amount, the order of the candidates is unchanged and the winner is the same.

solve.answer: Every total rises by 12, so the winner stays the same
solve.work: Each voter's points for each candidate rise by 1, so each total rises by 12 (number of voters); order unchanged.

questions.stem: Twelve voters rank three candidates, from first choice to last: 4 voters: A, B, C; 4 voters: B, C, A; 4 voters: C, A, B. Which statement about the head-to-head comparisons is true?
choices: A beats both B and C by 8 votes to 4, so A is the winner by pairwise comparison
B beats both A and C by 8 votes to 4, so B is the winner by pairwise comparison
A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, so no candidate beats both of the others
C beats both A and B by 8 votes to 4, so C is the winner by pairwise comparison
questions.answer: A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, so no candidate beats both of the others
questions.solution: A against B: 8 voters rank A higher (the groups A, B, C and C, A, B), 4 rank B higher, so A wins. B against C: 8 rank B higher (the groups A, B, C and B, C, A), 4 rank C higher, so B wins. C against A: 8 rank C higher (the groups B, C, A and C, A, B), 4 rank A higher, so C wins. Each candidate wins one comparison and loses one, so no one beats both of the others.

solve.answer: A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, so no candidate beats both of the others
solve.work: A vs B: A above B in groups 1 and 3 = 8-4. B vs C: groups 1 and 2 = 8-4. C vs A: groups 2 and 3 = 8-4. Cycle, no Condorcet winner.

questions.stem: Twenty-five voters rank four candidates, from first choice to last: 2 voters: A, D, B, C; 8 voters: C, D, B, A; 4 voters: B, D, C, A; 5 voters: A, B, D, C; 6 voters: D, A, C, B. In plurality with elimination, the candidate with the fewest first-place votes is eliminated, and each of that candidate's voters moves to their next choice among the candidates left. This repeats until one candidate has more than half of the votes. How many votes does the winner have at the end?
questions.solution: Round 1 first-place votes: A $2 + 5 = 7$, B 4, C 8, D 6. B has the fewest and is eliminated; B's 4 voters rank D next, so D has 10. Round 2: A 7, C 8, D 10, and no one has more than half of the 25 votes. A is eliminated. The 2 voters with A, D, B, C go to D, and the 5 voters with A, B, D, C go to D too (B is already gone). So D has $10 + 2 + 5 = 17$ votes against C's 8. D wins with 17 votes.

solve.work: First places: A 2+5 = 7, B 4, C 8, D 6. Eliminate B: its 4 (B,D,C,A) go to D: D 10. Now A 7, C 8, D 10; eliminate A: 2 (A,D,..) to D, 5 (A,B,D,C) skip B to D. D 17, C 8. 17 > 12.5. Winner has 17.

questions.stem: In a top-two runoff, the two candidates with the most first-place votes face each other in a second head-to-head vote, and each voter votes for the finalist they rank higher. Twenty-one voters rank four candidates, from first choice to last: 2 voters: C, A, B, D; 6 voters: C, B, D, A; 7 voters: D, A, C, B; 4 voters: B, D, C, A; 2 voters: A, B, D, C. How many voters vote for the winner in the runoff?
questions.solution: First-place votes: A 2, B 4, C $2 + 6 = 8$, D 7. The finalists are C and D. Voters who rank D above C: the 7 voters with D, A, C, B, the 4 voters with B, D, C, A and the 2 voters with A, B, D, C, so $7 + 4 + 2 = 13$. The other 8 rank C higher. D wins the runoff with 13 votes.

solve.work: First places: C 2+6 = 8, D 7, B 4, A 2. Runoff C vs D: C gets 2+6 = 8; D gets 7+4+2 = 13 (B,D,C,A and A,B,D,C rank D above C). D wins with 13.

questions.stem: The monotonicity criterion says that a winner who gains support from voters should not lose because of it. In election 1, the rankings (first choice to last) are 6 voters: A, B, C; 4 voters: B, C, A; 5 voters: C, A, B; 2 voters: B, A, C, and plurality with elimination elects A. In election 2, the 2 voters who ranked B, A, C change their ranking to A, B, C, and nothing else changes. Which statement is true?
choices: A wins election 2, so plurality with elimination satisfies monotonicity here
C wins election 2, so raising A made A lose: plurality with elimination can violate monotonicity
B wins election 2, so raising A made A lose: plurality with elimination can violate monotonicity
C wins election 2, but that does not break monotonicity, because A was not the first choice of a majority
questions.answer: C wins election 2, so raising A made A lose: plurality with elimination can violate monotonicity
questions.solution: Election 1: first-place votes A 6, B $4 + 2 = 6$, C 5. C is eliminated and its 5 voters go to A, so A has 11 of 17 and wins. Election 2: first-place votes A $6 + 2 = 8$, B 4, C 5. Now B is eliminated and its 4 voters (B, C, A) go to C, so C has 9 of 17 and beats A's 8. A gained support and lost, which violates monotonicity. Monotonicity has nothing to do with majorities.

solve.answer: C wins election 2, so raising A made A lose: plurality with elimination can violate monotonicity
solve.work: Election 1: A 6, B 6, C 5; drop C, C,A,B to A: A 11, wins. Election 2: A 8, B 4, C 5; drop B, its 4 (B,C,A) to C: C 9, A 8. C wins (9 > 8.5). A gained support and lost: monotonicity violation.

questions.stem: Fifteen voters rank three candidates, from first choice to last: 2 voters: C, B, A; 6 voters: B, A, C; 7 voters: A, C, B. The Borda count (2 points for first, 1 for second, 0 for last) elects A. Candidate C, who did not win, withdraws. Every voter keeps the same order of the other two candidates, and the Borda count is taken again (1 point for first, 0 for last). Which statement is true?
choices: A wins the second count, so the Borda count satisfies the independence of irrelevant alternatives
B wins the second count, so the Borda count can violate the independence of irrelevant alternatives
B wins the second count, so the Borda count violates the majority criterion in this election
B wins the second count, so the Borda count violates the Condorcet criterion in this election
questions.answer: B wins the second count, so the Borda count can violate the independence of irrelevant alternatives
questions.solution: Original count: A $7 \times 2 + 6 \times 1 = 20$, B $6 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 = 14$, C $7 + 4 = 11$, so A wins. After C withdraws, 7 voters rank A above B, and $6 + 2 = 8$ voters rank B above A. So A has 7 points and B has 8, and B wins. The loser C changed the outcome, which violates the independence of irrelevant alternatives. In the second count B is ranked first by 8 of 15 voters and beats A head-to-head, so there is no majority or Condorcet violation.

solve.answer: B wins the second count, so the Borda count can violate the independence of irrelevant alternatives
solve.work: Borda: A 6x1 + 7x2 = 20; B 2x1 + 6x2 = 14; C 2x2 + 7x1 = 11. A wins. Without C: A above B in 7, B above A in 2+6 = 8. B wins: IIA violation. Pairwise: B beats A 8-7, C beats B 9-6, A beats C 13-2: a cycle, so no Condorcet violation; no majority candidate.

questions.stem: A student says, "Arrow's Impossibility Theorem proves that every voting method is unfair, so elections are pointless." Which is the best reply?
choices: Plurality meets all of the conditions, so a community should always use plurality
It applies only to elections with exactly two candidates, so it says little about most elections
Every ranked method picks the same winner, so which method a community uses does not matter
No ranked method meets every condition at once, so a community must pick which ones matter most
questions.answer: No ranked method meets every condition at once, so a community must pick which ones matter most
questions.solution: Arrow's theorem is about three or more candidates and says that no ranked method satisfies all of its conditions together. It does not say that elections are pointless. A community can decide which conditions matter most to it and pick a method that satisfies those. Plurality fails some of the conditions, and different methods can pick different winners, as the examples in this topic show.

solve.answer: No ranked method meets every condition at once, so a community must pick which ones matter most
solve.work: Theorem says no method meets all conditions at once; choose which conditions matter.

questions.stem: Candidate X wins a plurality election with 40 percent of the first-place votes. All of the other 60 percent of voters rank X last. Which is the strongest objection to calling X the best choice for the group?
choices: X has less than a majority of the votes, and a plurality winner must have a majority
X cannot be the plurality winner, because 60 percent of the voters did not vote for X
Every other candidate beats X head-to-head, so most voters would rather have any of them
The other 60 percent must have voted for one candidate, who should have won instead
questions.answer: Every other candidate beats X head-to-head, so most voters would rather have any of them
questions.solution: For any other candidate Y, the 60 percent who rank X last prefer Y, so Y beats X by 60 percent to 40 percent. So X loses every head-to-head comparison even though X wins by plurality. The other objections are wrong: plurality does not require a majority, a plurality winner may have fewer than half of the votes, and the other voters may have split their first-place votes among several candidates.

solve.answer: Every other candidate beats X head-to-head, so most voters would rather have any of them
solve.work: 60% rank X last, so each other candidate is preferred to X by 60%: X loses every head-to-head.

questions.stem: Twenty-one voters rank three candidates, from first choice to last: 8 voters: A, B, C; 7 voters: B, C, A; 6 voters: C, B, A. Plurality would elect A. The 6 voters who rank C first realize that C cannot win, so they vote for B instead. In the plurality election that follows, how many votes does the winner receive?
questions.solution: The votes become A 8, B $7 + 6 = 13$ and C 0. B wins with 13 votes. (Honest first-place votes would have elected A with 8, so voting insincerely changed the result.)

solve.work: B gets 7 + 6 = 13; A 8. Winner B with 13.

questions.stem: In a plurality election with 100 voters, the first-place votes are Ava 40, Ben 38 and Cal 22. A new candidate, Dee, enters, and 6 of Ava's voters switch to Dee. Which statement is true of the new plurality election?
choices: Ben wins with 38 votes, although Ava won before Dee entered
Ben wins with 44 votes, because Ava's 6 voters moved to Ben
Dee wins with 6 votes, because Dee is the newest candidate
questions.answer: Ben wins with 38 votes, although Ava won before Dee entered
questions.solution: After Dee enters, the votes are Ava $40 - 6 = 34$, Ben 38, Cal 22 and Dee 6. Ben has the most and wins. Dee cannot win but split Ava's support and changed who won (a spoiler effect).

solve.answer: Ben wins with 38 votes, although Ava won before Dee entered
solve.work: Ava 34, Ben 38, Cal 22, Dee 6. Ben wins with 38, a spoiler effect.

questions.stem: In a plurality election with 4 candidates, the winner has 17 first-place votes and there is no tie for first place. Every voter casts exactly one vote. What is the greatest possible total number of voters?
questions.solution: Each of the 3 other candidates can have at most 16 votes (no tie with 17). So the most voters is $17 + 3 \times 16 = 17 + 48 = 65$.

solve.work: Each of the other 3 has at most 16: 17 + 3x16 = 65.

questions.stem: Fifteen voters rank five candidates, from first choice to last: 7 voters: D, E, C, A, B; 3 voters: D, E, C, B, A; 5 voters: E, A, C, D, B. In a Borda count, each voter gives 4 points to their first choice, 3 to their second, 2 to their third, 1 to their fourth and 0 to their last. How many points does the winner earn?
questions.solution: E is second for the first 10 voters ($10 \times 3 = 30$ points) and first for the last 5 voters ($5 \times 4 = 20$ points): 50 points. D earns $10 \times 4 + 5 \times 1 = 45$, C 30, A 22 and B 3. E wins the Borda count even though D has more first-place votes.

questions.stem: In a Borda count with 5 candidates, each voter gives 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 points to their five choices in order. Thirty voters each rank all five candidates. What is the average number of points per candidate?
questions.solution: Each voter gives out $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10$ points, so the 30 voters give $300$ points in all. Spread over 5 candidates, the average is $300 \div 5 = 60$ points.

solve.work: Total 30x10 = 300 points; 300/5 = 60.

questions.stem: In a Borda count (2 points for first, 1 for second, 0 for last), 5 voters honestly rank A, B, C and 4 voters honestly rank B, C, A. Honest voting elects B. The 5 voters who prefer A decide to rank A, C, B instead, to push B down, and the other 4 voters rank B, C, A as before. How many points does the winner now earn?
questions.solution: The new totals are: A earns $5 \times 2 = 10$, B earns $4 \times 2 = 8$, and C earns $5 \times 1 + 4 \times 1 = 9$. A wins with 10 points. (Honestly, B would have won with 13 points to A's 10.)

solve.work: 5 x (A,C,B): A 10, C 5. 4 x (B,C,A): B 8, C 4. A 10, C 9, B 8. A wins with 10.

questions.stem: Nineteen voters rank four candidates, from first choice to last: 3 voters: D, B, C, A; 7 voters: B, C, D, A; 5 voters: D, C, A, B; 4 voters: A, C, B, D. In a Borda count, each voter gives 3 points to their first choice, 2 to their second, 1 to their third and 0 to their last. Which statement is true?
choices: D wins the Borda count, because D has the most first-place votes
C wins the Borda count, even though no voter ranks C first
D and B tie for the Borda win, with 31 points each
A wins the Borda count, because A is never ranked second or third
questions.answer: C wins the Borda count, even though no voter ranks C first
questions.solution: C is second for 7 + 5 + 4 = 16 voters and third for 3 voters: $16 \times 2 + 3 \times 1 = 35$ points. D and B each earn 31 points, and A earns 17. C wins although it has no first-place votes (D has the most, with 8).

solve.answer: C wins the Borda count, even though no voter ranks C first
solve.work: A: 5+12 = 17. B: 6+21+0+4 = 31. C: 3+14+10+8 = 35. D: 9+7+15+0 = 31. Total 114. C wins; no voter ranks C first. B and D tie only for second.

questions.stem: Thirteen voters rank four candidates, from first choice to last: 3 voters: C, B, D, A; 5 voters: A, C, B, D; 2 voters: D, A, C, B; 3 voters: C, D, A, B. In pairwise comparison, each pair of candidates is compared head-to-head, and the candidate ranked higher by more voters wins that comparison. In how many of its 3 head-to-head comparisons does B win?
questions.solution: The six comparisons come out: A beats B, 10 to 3; A beats C, 7 to 6; D beats A, 8 to 5; C beats B, 13 to 0; B beats D, 8 to 5; C beats D, 11 to 2. B wins only the comparison with D, so the answer is 1.

solve.work: B vs A: 3 vs 10, loses. B vs C: 0 vs 13, loses. B vs D: 3+5 = 8 vs 5, wins. One win.

questions.stem: Six candidates are compared head-to-head, each pair once, with no ties. A candidate earns 1 point for each win. Five of the candidates earn 4, 3, 3, 2 and 1 points. How many points does the sixth candidate earn?
questions.solution: There are $6 \times 5 \div 2 = 15$ comparisons, and each gives exactly 1 point to its winner, so 15 points are earned in all. The five known totals add to 13, so the sixth candidate earns $15 - 13 = 2$ points.

questions.stem: Twelve voters rank three candidates, from first choice to last: 5 voters: A, B, C; 4 voters: B, C, A; 3 voters: C, A, B. The winner is decided by a sequence of head-to-head comparisons: first A against C, then the winner of that comparison against B. Who is the final winner?
questions.answer: B
questions.solution: A against C: C is ranked higher by 4 + 3 = 7 voters and A by 5, so C wins. Then C against B: B is ranked higher by 5 + 4 = 9 voters and C by 3, so B wins. (A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, so the winner depends on the order of the comparisons.)

solve.answer: B
solve.work: A vs C: A above C 5, C above A 4+3 = 7: C. C vs B: C above B 3, B above C 9: B. B wins.

questions.stem: Twenty voters take part in a head-to-head comparison of A and B. Fourteen voters rank A above B and 6 rank B above A. What is the smallest number of those 14 voters who would have to change their ranking to B above A for B to win the comparison, with no tie?
questions.solution: If $x$ voters change, A has $14 - x$ and B has $6 + x$. B wins when $6 + x > 14 - x$, so $2x > 8$ and $x > 4$. With 4 changes there is a 10 to 10 tie, so the smallest number is 5.

solve.work: k switch: B 6+k > A 14-k needs k > 4, so 5 (11-9). k = 4 ties 10-10.

questions.stem: Eighteen voters rank three candidates, from first choice to last: 8 voters: A, B, C; 7 voters: C, B, A; 3 voters: B, A, C. Plurality with elimination works like this: eliminate the candidate with the fewest first-place votes, move each of that candidate's voters to their next choice among those still in, and repeat until a candidate holds more than half of all the votes. Which statement is true?
choices: A wins and also beats both others head-to-head, so no criterion is violated
B beats both others head-to-head but is eliminated first, so the election violates the majority criterion
B has the fewest first-place votes, so B cannot beat the others head-to-head
B beats both others head-to-head but is eliminated first, so the election violates the Condorcet criterion
questions.answer: B beats both others head-to-head but is eliminated first, so the election violates the Condorcet criterion
questions.solution: First-place votes: A 8, C 7, B 3, so B is eliminated and B's 3 voters move to A: A has 11 and wins. But B beats A (10 to 8) and beats C (11 to 7), so B is a Condorcet winner who lost: a Condorcet violation. No candidate had a majority of the first-place votes, so the majority criterion is not involved.

solve.answer: B beats both others head-to-head but is eliminated first, so the election violates the Condorcet criterion
solve.work: B vs A: 7+3 = 10 vs 8. B vs C: 8+3 = 11 vs 7. B is the Condorcet winner. First: A 8, C 7, B 3. B out first; its 3 go to A (11): A wins. Condorcet criterion violated.

questions.stem: Twenty-two voters rank five candidates, from first choice to last: 4 voters: C, D, B, E, A; 5 voters: B, C, A, E, D; 3 voters: C, E, B, D, A; 5 voters: D, B, A, C, E; 2 voters: A, D, B, C, E; 3 voters: E, D, A, B, C. In plurality with elimination, the candidate with the fewest first-place votes is eliminated, each of that candidate's voters moves to their next choice among the candidates left, and this repeats until one candidate has more than half of the votes. How many votes does the winner have at the end?
questions.solution: First-place votes: C 7, D 5, B 5, E 3, A 2. A is eliminated and its 2 voters move to D (D has 7). Then E has the fewest (3) and is eliminated; those 3 voters rank D next, so D has 10. Then B has the fewest (5) and is eliminated; B's 5 voters rank C next, so C has 12. C has more than half of the 22 votes (11) and wins with 12.

solve.work: 22 voters, need 12. First: C 7, B 5, D 5, E 3, A 2. A out -> D (7). E out -> D (10). B out: 5 -> C (12). C wins with 12.

questions.stem: Twenty-two voters rank five candidates, from first choice to last: 3 voters: B, C, A, E, D; 5 voters: E, B, A, C, D; 5 voters: C, D, B, E, A; 1 voter: A, D, B, C, E; 3 voters: E, D, B, A, C; 5 voters: D, E, C, A, B. Plurality with elimination works like this: eliminate the candidate with the fewest first-place votes, move each of that candidate's voters to their next choice among those still in, and repeat until a candidate holds more than half of all the votes. How many votes does the runner-up have in the final count?
questions.solution: First-place votes: E 8, B 3, C 5, D 5, A 1. A is eliminated, and A's voter (A, D, B, C, E) moves to D, who has 6. Next B (3) is eliminated and B's voters move to C, who has 8. Now E has 8, C has 8 and D has 6, so D is eliminated: D's 5 original voters rank E next (E has 13), while the voter who came through A ranks C above E, so C has 9. E wins with 13 of 22, and the runner-up C has 9.

solve.work: 22 voters. First: E 8, C 5, D 5, B 3, A 1. A out -> D (6). B out: 3 -> C (8). D out (C 8, E 8, D 6): A voter -> C, 5 D voters -> E. E 13, C 9. Runner-up 9.

questions.stem: Which scenario shows a violation of the monotonicity criterion?
choices: Candidate X wins. Some voters then move X higher on their ballots, nothing else changes, and X no longer wins
Candidate X wins. Some voters then move X lower on their ballots, nothing else changes, and X no longer wins
Candidate X wins. Some voters then move Y higher on their ballots, nothing else changes, and Y wins instead
Candidate X loses. Some voters then move X lower on their ballots, nothing else changes, and X still loses
questions.answer: Candidate X wins. Some voters then move X higher on their ballots, nothing else changes, and X no longer wins
questions.solution: Monotonicity says that extra support must not hurt a winner. The violation is a winner who loses after being moved UP. A winner who loses after being moved down, or a candidate who benefits from more support, is not a violation.

solve.answer: Candidate X wins. Some voters then move X higher on their ballots, nothing else changes, and X no longer wins
solve.work: Monotonicity: raising the winner on ballots should not make them lose.

questions.stem: Five voters rank three candidates, from first choice to last: 3 voters: A, B, C; 2 voters: B, C, A. Candidate A is ranked first by a majority of the voters. In a Borda count (2 points for first, 1 for second, 0 for last), by how many points does the Borda winner beat the candidate in second place?
questions.solution: A earns $3 \times 2 = 6$ points. B earns $3 \times 1 + 2 \times 2 = 7$ points. C earns $2 \times 1 = 2$ points. B wins with 7, and A is second with 6, so B wins by $7 - 6 = 1$ point. (A has a majority of the first-place votes but loses: the Borda count can violate the majority criterion.)

solve.work: A: 3x2 = 6. B: 3x1 + 2x2 = 7. C: 2. Borda winner B by 7 - 6 = 1 (and this violates majority).

questions.stem: In an election with three candidates, head-to-head comparisons show that A beats B, B beats C and C beats A. Which statement is true?
choices: A is a Condorcet winner, because A beats B
No candidate is a Condorcet winner, so the Condorcet criterion does not decide who should win
Any method that elects A violates the Condorcet criterion
The votes must have been counted wrongly, because head-to-head results can never form a cycle
questions.answer: No candidate is a Condorcet winner, so the Condorcet criterion does not decide who should win
questions.solution: A Condorcet winner must beat every other candidate. Here each candidate loses to one of the others, so there is none, and the criterion has nothing to say. Such cycles do occur (this is the Condorcet paradox).

solve.answer: No candidate is a Condorcet winner, so the Condorcet criterion does not decide who should win
solve.work: A cycle: no candidate beats both others, so there is no Condorcet winner and the criterion is silent.

questions.stem: In a plurality election the first-place votes are Ruth 41, Sam 37 and Tia 22, so Ruth wins. Tia then withdraws. Of Tia's 22 voters, 14 vote for Sam and 8 for Ruth, and nobody else changes. In the new plurality election, how many votes does the winner receive?
questions.solution: The new totals are Ruth $41 + 8 = 49$ and Sam $37 + 14 = 51$. Sam wins with 51 votes. Removing Tia, who could not win, changed the winner from Ruth to Sam, which violates the independence of irrelevant alternatives.

solve.work: Ruth 41+8 = 49, Sam 37+14 = 51. Sam wins with 51.

questions.stem: A council wants a method that satisfies both of these: a candidate with a majority of the first-place votes always wins, and a candidate who beats every other candidate head-to-head always wins. Which method meets both?
questions.answer: Pairwise comparison
questions.solution: A candidate with a majority of first-place votes beats every other candidate head-to-head, so pairwise comparison elects them, and it elects any head-to-head winner. Plurality and plurality with elimination can miss a head-to-head winner, and the Borda count can miss a majority winner.

solve.answer: Pairwise comparison
solve.work: A majority winner is a Condorcet winner, and pairwise comparison elects the Condorcet winner, so it meets both. Elimination fails Condorcet; plurality fails Condorcet; Borda fails majority.

questions.stem: Eighteen voters rank four candidates, from first choice to last: 2 voters: B, A, C, D; 4 voters: A, B, C, D; 7 voters: D, C, B, A; 5 voters: C, A, B, D. How many of these four methods elect candidate C? Plurality; the Borda count (3, 2, 1, 0 points); plurality with elimination (fewest first-place votes eliminated, repeated until a candidate has more than half of the votes); pairwise comparison (the candidate who wins every head-to-head comparison).
questions.solution: Plurality: first-place votes are D 7, C 5, A 4, B 2, so D wins. Borda: C earns 35 points, A and B 26 each and D 21, so C wins. Elimination: B is eliminated and its 2 voters move to A (A has 6); then C is eliminated and its 5 voters move to A (A has 11), so A wins. Pairwise: C beats A 12 to 6, B 12 to 6 and D 11 to 7, so C wins. C wins under 2 methods: the Borda count and pairwise comparison.

solve.work: Plurality: D 7. Borda: A 26, B 26, C 35, D 21: C. Elimination: B out -> A (6); C out -> A (11): A. Pairwise: C beats A 12-6, B 12-6, D 11-7: C. C wins 2 methods.

questions.stem: Twenty-one voters rank three candidates, from first choice to last: 9 voters: A, B, C; 7 voters: B, C, A; 5 voters: C, B, A. Plurality elects A, and plurality with elimination elects B. Which defense of elimination does this election support?
choices: B had the most first-place votes at the start, as plurality requires
Elimination removes the candidate with the most first-place votes first
B loses head-to-head comparisons, which shows that elimination is careful
B has more than half of the votes in the last round, but A has under half of the first-place votes
questions.answer: B has more than half of the votes in the last round, but A has under half of the first-place votes
questions.solution: First-place votes: A 9, B 7, C 5. Plurality elects A with 9 of 21 votes (under half). With elimination, C is eliminated and C's 5 voters move to B, who finishes with 12 of 21 (more than half). B also beats A head-to-head, 12 to 9. The other statements are false: B did not lead at the start, the fewest (not the most) first-place votes is eliminated first, and B wins head-to-head.

solve.answer: B has more than half of the votes in the last round, but A has under half of the first-place votes
solve.work: A has 9 of 21 first places (under half). C out: 5 go to B, B 12 > 10.5. D is true; A is false (B beats A 12-9 and C 16-5); B and C false.

questions.stem: A ranked voting method accepts every possible set of voter rankings, never lets a single voter decide every result, and always respects unanimity. By Arrow's Impossibility Theorem (three or more candidates), what must be true of this method?
choices: In some elections it violates independence of irrelevant alternatives
In some elections it violates unanimity
In some elections one voter becomes a dictator
In some elections it refuses to accept some voters' rankings
questions.answer: In some elections it violates independence of irrelevant alternatives
questions.solution: The theorem says no method satisfies all four conditions. This method satisfies universal domain, non-dictatorship and unanimity, so the one it cannot satisfy is independence of irrelevant alternatives.

solve.answer: In some elections it violates independence of irrelevant alternatives
solve.work: Arrow: with 3+ candidates, universal domain, non-dictatorship and unanimity force a failure of IIA in some election.

questions.stem: Why does Arrow's Impossibility Theorem not apply to an election with only two candidates?
choices: With two candidates every election ends in a tie
Majority rule satisfies all of Arrow's conditions when there are only two candidates
With two candidates every voter must rank the candidates the same way
With two candidates a single voter is allowed to be a dictator
questions.answer: Majority rule satisfies all of Arrow's conditions when there are only two candidates
questions.solution: The theorem needs three or more candidates. With two, a simple majority vote is allowed any rankings, respects unanimity, treats voters equally and has no third candidate to be irrelevant.

solve.answer: Majority rule satisfies all of Arrow's conditions when there are only two candidates
solve.work: With two candidates, majority rule meets all of Arrow's conditions; the theorem needs three or more.

questions.stem: In a plurality election, 100 voters give these first-place votes: A 41, B 33 and C 26. Before the result is announced, some voters who ranked A first change their minds and rank B first instead. What is the smallest number of voters who must change so that B has more first-place votes than A and more than C?
questions.solution: If $k$ voters switch, A has $41 - k$ and B has $33 + k$. B needs more than A: $33 + k > 41 - k$, so $2k > 8$ and $k > 4$. With 4 switches the two are tied at 37, so 5 are needed. Check: B has 38, A has 36 and C has 26.

solve.work: x voters switch A->B: A=41-x, B=33+x, C=26. Need 33+x > 41-x, so 2x > 8, x > 4, x = 5: B 38, A 36, C 26. B also beats C.

questions.stem: A weighted voting system has four voters with weights 7, 4, 3 and 2. The quota must be a whole number greater than half of the total weight. What is the smallest quota that works?
questions.solution: The total weight is $7 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 16$. Half of 16 is 8, so the quota must be greater than 8. The smallest whole number greater than 8 is 9.

solve.work: Total weight 7+4+3+2 = 16; half is 8; smallest whole number greater than 8 is 9.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 8, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 5, 3 and 2. A coalition is written as the list of its players. Which coalition has enough weight to win?
questions.solution: A coalition wins when its total weight is at least the quota, 8. $(P_1, P_2)$ has $5 + 3 = 8$, which is enough. $(P_1, P_3)$ has 7, $(P_2, P_3)$ has 5 and $(P_1)$ alone has 5.

solve.work: Weights: P1 = 5; P1+P3 = 7; P2+P3 = 5; P1+P2 = 8 >= 8. Only (P1, P2) wins.

questions.stem: A committee has 4 voters. A coalition is any group of one or more of the voters. How many different coalitions can be formed?
questions.solution: Each voter is either in a group or not, which gives $2^4 = 16$ groups, one of which is the empty group. A coalition needs at least one voter, so there are $16 - 1 = 15$ coalitions.

solve.work: Nonempty subsets of 4 voters: 2^4 - 1 = 15.

questions.stem: In the Shapley-Shubik method the players join a coalition one at a time, in some order. In how many different orders can 4 players join?
questions.solution: There are 4 choices for the first player, 3 for the second, 2 for the third and 1 for the last: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$ orders.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system, what is a critical player in a winning coalition?
choices: a player with the largest weight in the coalition
a player who joined the coalition last
a player whose weight alone is at least the quota
a player whose leaving would make the coalition lose
questions.answer: a player whose leaving would make the coalition lose
questions.solution: A player is critical in a winning coalition if the coalition would no longer reach the quota without that player. Having the largest weight, joining last, or being able to win alone are different ideas.

solve.answer: a player whose leaving would make the coalition lose
solve.work: A critical player is one whose departure turns the winning coalition into a losing one.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 6, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 6, 2 and 1. Which statement is true?
choices: $P_3$ is critical in some winning coalition
questions.answer: $P_1$ is a dictator
questions.solution: A dictator wins alone and decides every vote. $P_1$ has weight 6, equal to the quota, so $P_1$ wins alone, while $P_2$ and $P_3$ together have only 3. Every winning coalition contains $P_1$, and $P_2$ and $P_3$ are never critical, so they have no veto power and are dummies.

solve.answer: $P_1$ is a dictator
solve.work: P1 alone has 6 = quota, so P1 is a dictator. P2, P3 are never critical and have no veto (P1 alone wins).

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 9, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 5, 4 and 3. The coalition of all three players has total weight 12. How many of its players are critical?
questions.solution: A player is critical if the coalition loses without that player. Without $P_1$ the total is $4 + 3 = 7$, below 9, so $P_1$ is critical. Without $P_2$ it is $5 + 3 = 8$, below 9, so $P_2$ is critical. Without $P_3$ it is $5 + 4 = 9$, which still wins, so $P_3$ is not critical. That is 2 critical players.

solve.work: Remove P1: 7 < 9 (critical). Remove P2: 8 < 9 (critical). Remove P3: 9 >= 9 (not). 2 critical.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system, the players $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are critical 6, 4 and 2 times in all the winning coalitions. A player's Banzhaf power index is the number of times the player is critical divided by the total number of times all players are critical. What is the Banzhaf power index of $P_2$?
questions.solution: The total number of critical times is $6 + 4 + 2 = 12$. For $P_2$ the index is $4 \div 12 = 1/3$.

solve.work: Total critical count 6+4+2 = 12. P2: 4/12 = 1/3.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with 4 players, the Shapley-Shubik power index of a player is the fraction of the 24 possible orders in which that player is pivotal. Player $P_3$ is pivotal in 6 of the 24 orders. What is the Shapley-Shubik power index of $P_3$?
questions.solution: The index is the fraction of orders in which $P_3$ is pivotal: $6 \div 24 = 1/4$.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In weighted voting, a player who is never critical in any winning coalition is called
questions.answer: a dummy
questions.solution: A player who can never change a winning coalition into a losing one by leaving, so never matters, is called a dummy. A dictator wins alone, and a player with veto power is needed in every winning coalition.

solve.answer: a dummy
solve.work: A player never critical has no power: a dummy.

questions.stem: A weighted voting system has quota 12, and $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ have weights 7, 5 and 4. The coalition $(P_2, P_3)$ has total weight 9. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is a losing coalition, because 9 is less than the quota 12
It is a winning coalition, because 9 is more than half of the total weight 16
It is a winning coalition, because it has two of the three players
It is a winning coalition, because 9 is more than the largest single weight 7
questions.answer: It is a losing coalition, because 9 is less than the quota 12
questions.solution: A coalition wins only when its total weight reaches the quota. Here 5 + 4 = 9, which is less than 12, so the coalition loses. Having more than half of the total weight (16), having most of the players, or beating one player's weight does not matter.

solve.answer: It is a losing coalition, because 9 is less than the quota 12
solve.work: 9 < quota 12, so losing.

questions.stem: A weighted voting system has quota 13. The coalition made of $P_2$ and $P_3$ has weights 5 and 4. How much more weight would it need to reach the quota?
questions.solution: The coalition has 5 + 4 = 9. It needs 13 - 9 = 4 more.

questions.stem: Five voters, $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $P_4$ and $P_5$, have weights 9, 7, 6, 4 and 2. What is the total weight of the coalition $(P_1, P_3, P_5)$?
questions.solution: The coalition has $P_1$, $P_3$ and $P_5$, with weights 9, 6 and 2. 9 + 6 + 2 = 17.

questions.stem: A committee has 5 voters. How many different coalitions of exactly 2 voters can be formed?
questions.solution: Choose a first voter in 5 ways and a second in 4 ways, which gives 20 ordered pairs. Each pair is counted twice, so there are 20 / 2 = 10 coalitions.

questions.stem: Three voters will each announce their vote, one at a time. In how many different orders can the three voters go?
questions.solution: There are 3 choices for who goes first, then 2 for second, then 1 for last: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.

questions.stem: A group has 4 voters. How many different coalitions of exactly 3 voters can be formed?
questions.solution: Forming a coalition of 3 means choosing the 1 voter who is left out. There are 4 voters to leave out, so there are 4 coalitions.

questions.stem: A voting body has 5 voters. A coalition is any group of one or more of the voters. How many coalitions are there?
questions.solution: Each voter is either in or out of a group, giving 2^5 = 32 groups. One of them is the empty group, which is not a coalition, so there are 32 - 1 = 31.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: Four voters with weights 7, 4, 3 and 2 form a coalition to pass a motion with quota 10. A member is critical if the coalition would lose without that member. How many of the four members are critical?
questions.solution: The coalition has weight 16. Without the member of weight 7 it has 9, which is below 10, so that member is critical. Without 4, 3 or 2 the weights are 12, 13 and 14, all still at least 10. So 1 member is critical.

solve.work: Total 16. Without 7: 9<10 critical. Without 4: 12, 3: 13, 2: 14 all still win. 1 critical.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: A dictator is a player who wins alone while every coalition without that player loses. Each system below is written $[q: w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4]$, with the quota first and then the weights of $P_1$ to $P_4$. Which system has a dictator?
questions.solution: In $[7: 8, 2, 2, 1]$, $P_1$ has weight 8, which is at least 7, and the other three together have only 5, so they cannot win. In each other system no single player reaches the quota.

solve.work: [7:8,2,2,1]: P1 8>=7 alone, others total 5<7, so P1 is dictator. Others: no single weight reaches quota.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 8, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 5, 3, 3 and 1. Which player is a dummy, one who is never critical in any winning coalition?
questions.solution: Without $P_1$ the most weight is 3 + 3 + 1 = 7, so every winning coalition contains $P_1$; and $P_1$ with $P_4$ is only 6, so it also contains $P_2$ or $P_3$. Such a coalition already has at least 8 without $P_4$, so $P_4$ is never critical. $P_2$ is critical in $(P_1, P_2)$ and $P_3$ in $(P_1, P_3)$, each of weight 8. So $P_4$ is the dummy.

solve.work: Winning: P1P2, P1P3, P1P2P3, P1P2P4, P1P3P4, all; P2P3P4=7 loses. P4 removed from P1P2P4 (8) or P1P3P4 (8) still wins; never critical. P4.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: A weighted voting system has quota 10 and three players with weights 12, 3 and 2. How many of the players are dummies?
questions.solution: $P_1$ has weight 12, which wins alone, and the other two together have only 5, so they lose. A coalition wins exactly when it contains $P_1$, and then removing $P_2$ or $P_3$ never changes the result. Only $P_1$ is ever critical, so 2 players are dummies.

solve.work: P1 (12) is a dictator; P2 and P3 never critical: 2 dummies.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system, $P_1$ is critical 5 times, $P_2$ 3 times, $P_3$ once and $P_4$ once across all the winning coalitions. A player's Banzhaf power index is that player's count divided by the total of all the counts. What is the Banzhaf power index of $P_1$?
questions.solution: The total of the counts is 5 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 10. For $P_1$ the index is 5 / 10 = 1/2.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 4, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 3, 2 and 1. The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$, $(P_1, P_3)$ and $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$. In how many of these is $P_1$ critical?
questions.solution: Without $P_1$, the coalitions become $P_2$ alone (2), $P_3$ alone (1) and $(P_2, P_3)$ (3). All are below 4, so $P_1$ is critical in all 3 winning coalitions.

solve.work: Without P1: P2=2, P3=1, P2P3=3, all <4. Critical in all 3.

questions.stem: How is a player's Banzhaf power index found?
choices: Count the orders in which the player is pivotal and divide by the number of orders
Divide the player's weight by the total weight of all players
Divide the number of winning coalitions that contain the player by the number of all coalitions
Count the times the player is critical in winning coalitions and divide by the total of all players' counts
questions.answer: Count the times the player is critical in winning coalitions and divide by the total of all players' counts
questions.solution: The Banzhaf index compares how often each player is critical. The pivotal-orders count belongs to the Shapley-Shubik index, and a weight share or a share of coalitions does not measure power directly.

solve.answer: Count the times the player is critical in winning coalitions and divide by the total of all players' counts
solve.work: Definition of Banzhaf index.

questions.stem: Three players have Banzhaf power indices that add up to 1. The index of $P_1$ is 1/2 and the index of $P_2$ is 1/3. What is the Banzhaf power index of $P_3$?

Four players with weights 3, 2, 1 and 1 (for $P_1$ to $P_4$) join a coalition one at a time, in the order $P_3$, $P_4$, $P_2$, $P_1$. The quota is 5, and the pivotal player is the one whose joining first brings the total to 5 or more. Who is pivotal?
questions.solution: The running totals are 1 after $P_3$, 2 after $P_4$, 4 after $P_2$, and 7 after $P_1$. The total first reaches 5 when $P_1$ joins, so $P_1$ is pivotal.

solve.work: Running totals 1, 2, 4, 7: P1 brings it to 5 or more.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with three players, $P_1$ is a dictator: $P_1$ wins alone, and any coalition without $P_1$ loses. What is the Shapley-Shubik power index of $P_1$?
questions.solution: The other players cannot reach the quota without $P_1$, so the total first reaches the quota exactly when $P_1$ joins, whatever the order. $P_1$ is pivotal in all 6 orders, and the index is 6/6 = 1.

solve.work: P1 is pivotal in every order (total reaches quota exactly when P1 joins). Index 1.

questions.stem: How is a player's Shapley-Shubik power index found?
choices: Count the times the player is critical in winning coalitions and divide by all players' counts
Divide the player's weight by the total weight of all players
Count the orders of the players in which that player is pivotal and divide by the number of orders
Divide the quota by the player's weight
questions.answer: Count the orders of the players in which that player is pivotal and divide by the number of orders
questions.solution: The Shapley-Shubik index uses orders of joining. The count of critical positions is the Banzhaf index, and neither a weight share nor a quota ratio measures it.

solve.answer: Count the orders of the players in which that player is pivotal and divide by the number of orders
solve.work: Shapley-Shubik definition.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 3, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 2, 1 and 1. The players join one at a time, and there are 6 possible orders. In how many of the orders is $P_1$ pivotal?
questions.solution: Orders and pivotal player: 123:P2, 132:P3, 213:P1, 231:P1, 312:P1, 321:P1. $P_1$ is pivotal in 4 of the 6 orders.

solve.work: P1 first (2 orders): second joiner pivotal. P1 second or third (4 orders): P1 pivotal. 4.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system, how does the power of a player with more weight compare with that of a player with less weight?
choices: It is always exactly in proportion to the weights
It is sometimes smaller than the lighter player's
It is at least as large, but it need not be larger
questions.answer: It is at least as large, but it need not be larger
questions.solution: A heavier player can do everything a lighter one can in any coalition, so the heavier player's power is never smaller. It can be equal, though: in a system with quota 14 and weights 6, 5, 4 and 3, the players of weight 4 and 3 have equal Banzhaf power.

solve.answer: It is at least as large, but it need not be larger
solve.work: Power indices are monotone in weight: never smaller, but can be equal (e.g. both dummies).

questions.stem: A party holds 40% of the total weight in a weighted voting system. Which statement is correct about its share of the power?
choices: It can differ from 40%, because power depends on how often the party is critical or pivotal
It is exactly 40%, because power always matches the share of the weight
It is always less than 40%, because the quota is more than half
It is always more than 40%, because large parties join winning coalitions
questions.answer: It can differ from 40%, because power depends on how often the party is critical or pivotal
questions.solution: Power depends on how often a party can turn a losing coalition into a winning one, which is not the same as its share of the weight. For example, with 40, 30 and 30 votes and a quota of 51, any two parties win, so each party has 1/3 of the power, less than the 40% party's share of the votes.

solve.answer: It can differ from 40%, because power depends on how often the party is critical or pivotal
solve.work: Power depends on criticality, not weight share.

questions.stem: Two parties hold 60 and 40 of the 100 votes on a council, and a motion needs at least 51 votes. What is the Banzhaf power index of the party with 40 votes?
questions.solution: The 40-vote party can never help a coalition win: 60 votes win alone, and 40 votes lose alone. So it is never critical, and its index is 0. The 60-vote party has all the power.

solve.work: 60 >= 51 alone and 40 < 51: the 60 party is a dictator; the 40 party is never critical. Index 0.

questions.stem: Which of these shows that a weighted voting system gives a member less power than the member's votes suggest?
choices: The weights add up to the total number of votes
A member with votes is a dummy, never critical in any winning coalition
The quota is more than half of the total weight
Two members have different numbers of votes
questions.answer: A member with votes is a dummy, never critical in any winning coalition
questions.solution: A dummy holds votes but can never change the result, so its power is zero, less than its votes suggest. Adding up the weights, a quota above half and unequal weights are all normal and not signs of unfairness by themselves.

solve.answer: A member with votes is a dummy, never critical in any winning coalition
solve.work: A dummy holds votes but has zero power.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 11, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 8, 5, 4 and 3. A coalition is written as the list of its players. Which of these coalitions is a losing coalition?
questions.solution: A coalition loses when its total weight is below the quota, 11. $(P_2, P_3)$ has $5 + 4 = 9$, which loses. $(P_1, P_4)$ has 11, $(P_1, P_3)$ has 12 and $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ has 12, so all three win.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 14, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 9, 6, 5 and 4. How many coalitions of exactly 2 players are winning coalitions?
questions.solution: The six pairs have totals $9 + 6 = 15$, $9 + 5 = 14$, $9 + 4 = 13$, $6 + 5 = 11$, $6 + 4 = 10$ and $5 + 4 = 9$. Only the totals 15 and 14 reach the quota of 14, so 2 pairs win.

questions.stem: A committee has 6 voters, including Ana. A coalition is any group of one or more of the voters. How many coalitions include Ana?
questions.solution: Ana is in the coalition. Each of the other 5 voters is either in or out, which gives $2^5 = 32$ choices. Every one of these groups includes Ana, so there are 32 coalitions.

solve.work: Ana plus any subset of the other 5: 2^5 = 32.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 8, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 5, 3, 2 and 2. A player has veto power if no coalition without that player can win. Which statement is true?
choices: $P_1$ has veto power but is not a dictator
questions.answer: $P_1$ has veto power but is not a dictator
questions.solution: Without $P_1$ the others have only $3 + 2 + 2 = 7$, below 8, so $P_1$ has veto power. But $P_1$ alone has 5, below 8, so $P_1$ is not a dictator. Without $P_2$ the others have $5 + 2 + 2 = 9$, so $P_2$ has no veto power. $P_4$ is critical in the winning coalition $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$, with total 9, so $P_4$ is not a dummy.

solve.answer: $P_1$ has veto power but is not a dictator
solve.work: Total 12. Without P1: 3+2+2 = 7 < 8, so P1 has veto; P1 alone 5 < 8, not a dictator. P4 is critical in (P1,P3,P4) = 9 (dropping P4 gives 7), so not a dummy. Without P2: 9 >= 8, so P2 has no veto.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 6, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 4, 3 and 2. A player's Banzhaf power index is the number of times the player is critical divided by the total number of times all players are critical. What is the Banzhaf power index of $P_1$?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ with 7, $(P_1, P_3)$ with 6 and $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ with 9; $(P_2, P_3)$ has only 5. In $(P_1, P_2)$ both players are critical, and in $(P_1, P_3)$ both are. In $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ only $P_1$ is critical (without $P_1$ the total is 5; without $P_2$ it is 6 and without $P_3$ it is 7, both still winning). So $P_1$ is critical 3 times and $P_2$ and $P_3$ once each: 5 in all. The index of $P_1$ is $3/5$.

solve.work: Winning: {P1,P2}=7 (both critical), {P1,P3}=6 (both critical), {P1,P2,P3}=9 (only P1 critical: removing P1 leaves 5). Counts P1 3, P2 1, P3 1; total 5. P1 = 3/5.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 5, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 3, 2 and 1. Which list gives the Banzhaf power indices of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$, in that order?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ with 5 and $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ with 6. In $(P_1, P_2)$ both players are critical. In $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$, $P_1$ and $P_2$ are critical (the totals without them are 3 and 4), but $P_3$ is not (the total without $P_3$ is still 5). The counts are 2, 2 and 0, total 4, so the indices are 1/2, 1/2 and 0. The weights 3, 2, 1 would give 1/2, 1/3, 1/6, but power is not the same as weight.

solve.work: Winning: {P1,P2}=5 (both critical), {P1,P2,P3}=6 (P1 and P2 critical, P3 not). {P1,P3}=4 loses. Counts 2,2,0 of 4: 1/2, 1/2, 0.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 5, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are 3, 2 and 2. The players join in each of the 6 possible orders, and the pivotal player in an order is the one whose joining first brings the total weight to the quota or more. What is the Shapley-Shubik power index of $P_1$?
questions.solution: Check each order and find who brings the total to at least 5. $P_1, P_2, P_3$: 3 then 5, so $P_2$. $P_1, P_3, P_2$: 3 then 5, so $P_3$. $P_2, P_1, P_3$: 2 then 5, so $P_1$. $P_2, P_3, P_1$: 2, 4, then 7, so $P_1$. $P_3, P_1, P_2$: 2 then 5, so $P_1$. $P_3, P_2, P_1$: 2, 4, then 7, so $P_1$. $P_1$ is pivotal in 4 of the 6 orders, so the index is $4/6 = 2/3$.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 12, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 6, 5, 4 and 3. The players join in the order $P_3$, $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_4$. The pivotal player is the one whose joining first brings the total weight to the quota or more. Which player is pivotal in this order?
questions.solution: Add the weights in order: $P_3$ gives 4, then $P_1$ gives $4 + 6 = 10$, then $P_2$ gives $10 + 5 = 15$. The total first reaches 12 when $P_2$ joins, so $P_2$ is pivotal.

solve.work: P3: 4; then P1: 10 < 12; then P2: 15 >= 12. P2 is pivotal.

questions.stem: Three parties hold 49, 48 and 3 of the 100 votes on a council, and a motion needs at least 51 votes. The smallest party holds 3% of the votes. Which statement about its Banzhaf power is true?
choices: Its power is about 3% of the total, matching its share of the votes
Its power is 0, because it can never be critical
Its power equals each other party's, exactly one third of the total
Its power is smaller than each other party's, but greater than 0
questions.answer: Its power equals each other party's, exactly one third of the total
questions.solution: Every pair of parties has at least 51 votes ($49 + 48 = 97$, $49 + 3 = 52$, $48 + 3 = 51$), and no single party does. In each winning pair both parties are critical; in the coalition of all three nobody is critical. So each party is critical twice, and each has Banzhaf power 1/3, despite the smallest party holding only 3% of the votes.

solve.answer: Its power equals each other party's, exactly one third of the total
solve.work: Any two parties reach 51 (97, 52, 51); one alone does not. Each is critical in its two 2-party coalitions, none in the grand coalition: 2,2,2, so each has 1/3.

questions.stem: Which statement about power in a weighted voting system is correct?
choices: A player's power always equals the player's weight divided by the total weight
A player's power depends only on the quota, not on the weights
The player with the largest weight always has more power than every other player
A player's power depends on how often that player can turn a losing coalition into a winning one
questions.answer: A player's power depends on how often that player can turn a losing coalition into a winning one
questions.solution: Power measures how often a player matters, that is, how often joining turns a losing coalition into a winning one (or, equivalently, leaving breaks a winning one). It is not the same as the share of the weight: for example, with weights 49, 48 and 3 and quota 51 all three players have equal power. A player with the largest weight can have the same power as others, so it is not always greater.

solve.answer: A player's power depends on how often that player can turn a losing coalition into a winning one
solve.work: Power is measured by being critical/pivotal, i.e. turning losing coalitions into winning ones. Largest weight can tie (e.g. 49/48/3), power is not proportional to weight, and weights matter.

questions.stem: Four voters have weights 10, 8, 6 and 4, and a motion needs a quota of 20. How many of the groups of exactly 3 voters can pass the motion?
questions.solution: The four groups of 3 have weights 10+8+6 = 24, 10+8+4 = 22, 10+6+4 = 20 and 8+6+4 = 18. The first three reach 20, so 3 groups win.

questions.stem: A weighted voting system has voters with weights 6, 5, 3 and 2. A quota is allowed if it is more than half of the total weight and not more than the total weight. Which of these numbers cannot be the quota?
questions.solution: The total weight is 6 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 16, so an allowed quota is more than 8 and at most 16. The numbers 9, 12 and 16 are allowed. The number 8 is exactly half, not more than half, so it is not allowed.

solve.work: Total 16; quota must be >8 and <=16. 8 is not more than half.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system the quota is 10, and the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 7, 5, 3 and 1. A coalition is written as the list of its players. Which of these coalitions wins?
questions.solution: $(P_1, P_3)$ has weight 7 + 3 = 10, which reaches the quota. The others have weights 7 + 1 = 8, 5 + 3 = 8 and 5 + 3 + 1 = 9, all below 10.

questions.stem: A school board has 8 members. How many different coalitions of exactly 2 members can be formed?
questions.solution: There are 8 × 7 = 56 ordered pairs, and each pair appears twice, so 56 / 2 = 28.

questions.stem: Five players join a coalition one at a time. In how many of the possible orders does $P_3$ join first?
questions.solution: Once $P_3$ is first, the other four players can follow in any order: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.

solve.work: P3 first, the other 4 in 4!=24 orders.

questions.stem: In the Shapley-Shubik method, a system has 6 players. In how many different orders can the players join the coalition one at a time?
questions.solution: The first player can be any of 6, the next any of 5, and so on: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 8, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 5, 4, 3 and 2. In how many winning coalitions is $P_3$ critical?
questions.solution: $P_3$ is critical in $(P_1, P_3)$ (weight 8), $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ (weight 10), $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ (weight 9). That is 3 coalitions.

solve.work: Winning: P1P2, P1P3, P1P2P3, P1P2P4, P1P3P4, P2P3P4, all. P3 critical in P1P3 (5), P1P3P4 (7), P2P3P4 (6); not in P1P2P3 (9) or all (11). 3.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 10, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 8, 2, 1 and 1. A player has veto power if no coalition without that player can win. Which statement is true?
choices: $P_1$ has veto power and there are no dummies
questions.answer: $P_1$ has veto power and there are no dummies
questions.solution: Without $P_1$ the most weight is 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, so $P_1$ has veto power. $P_1$ alone has 8, below 10, so there is no dictator. $(P_1, P_2)$ has exactly 10, so $P_2$ is critical there. $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ has exactly 10, so $P_3$ and $P_4$ are critical there. So there are no dummies. $P_2$ does not have veto power, because $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ wins without $P_2$.

solve.answer: $P_1$ has veto power and there are no dummies
solve.work: Winning: P1P2(10), P1P2P3, P1P2P4, P1P3P4(10), all. P1 has veto (others total 4). P2 no veto (P1P3P4 wins). P4 critical in P1P3P4, P3 too, so no dummies. P1 not dictator (8<10).

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 14, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 6, 5, 4 and 3. A player has veto power if no coalition without that player can win. How many of the four players have veto power?
questions.solution: Without $P_1$ the other three total 12, below 14. Without $P_2$ they total 13, below 14. Without $P_3$ they total 14, which wins, and without $P_4$ they total 15, which wins. So only $P_1$ and $P_2$ have veto power: 2 players.

solve.work: Total 18. Without P1: 12<14 veto; without P2: 13 veto; without P3: 14 not; without P4: 15 not. 2.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 9, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $P_4$ and $P_5$ are 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1. The coalition $(P_1, P_3, P_4, P_5)$ has total weight 11. Which players are critical in it?
questions.solution: Without $P_1$ the weight is 6, below 9, so $P_1$ is critical. Without $P_3$ it is 8, below 9, so $P_3$ is critical. Without $P_4$ it is 9 and without $P_5$ it is 10; both still win, so they are not critical. The critical players are $P_1$ and $P_3$.

solve.work: 11-5=6 lose (P1 critical), 11-3=8 lose (P3 critical), 11-2=9 win, 11-1=10 win.

questions.stem: A council has four members with weights 6, 4, 3 and 2, and a motion passes when the supporters' weights total at least 11. A member's Banzhaf power index is the number of times the member is critical divided by the total of all members' counts. Find the Banzhaf power index of the member with weight 4.
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 13, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ 12, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ 11, $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 15. The critical counts are 4, 2, 2, 2, total 10. The member with weight 4 is critical 2 times, so the index is 2/10 = 1/5.

solve.work: Quota 11, weights 6,4,3,2 (total 15). Winning: 6+4+3=13 (all three critical), 6+4+2=12 (all three critical), 6+3+2=11 (all three critical), all 15 (only 6 critical). Counts: 6:4, 4:2, 3:2, 2:2; total 10. Index of weight 4 = 2/10 = 1/5.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 10, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 8, 2, 1 and 1. Which list gives their Banzhaf power indices in that order?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 10, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 11, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ 11, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ 10, $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 12. The critical counts are 5, 3, 1, 1, total 10, so the indices are 5/10, 3/10, 1/10, 1/10. The other lists are the weight shares, the Shapley-Shubik indices, and a guess that the three small players are equal.

solve.work: Winning: P1P2, P1P2P3, P1P2P4, P1P3P4, all. Counts P1 5, P2 3, P3 1, P4 1; total 10: 1/2, 3/10, 1/10, 1/10.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 14, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 6, 5, 4 and 3. A player's Banzhaf power index is the number of times the player is critical divided by the total of all players' counts. What is the Banzhaf power index of $P_3$?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 15, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ 14, $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 18. The critical counts are 3, 3, 1, 1, total 8. $P_3$ is critical once, so its index is 1/8.

solve.work: Winning: P1P2P3(15), P1P2P4(14), all(18). Counts: P1 3, P2 3, P3 1 (in P1P2P3), P4 1; total 8. P3 = 1/8.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 7, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 4, 3, 2 and 1. Which statement about the Banzhaf power indices is true?
choices: $P_3$ and $P_4$ have the same index, even though their weights differ
questions.answer: $P_3$ and $P_4$ have the same index, even though their weights differ
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 7, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 9, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ 8, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ 7, $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 10. The critical counts are 5, 3, 1, 1 out of 10. So $P_3$ and $P_4$ are tied at 1/10; $P_2$ has 3 times $P_3$'s index; $P_1$ has 1/2; and $P_4$ is critical once, so it is not a dummy.

solve.answer: $P_3$ and $P_4$ have the same index, even though their weights differ
solve.work: Counts: P1 5, P2 3, P3 1, P4 1 (total 10). P3 and P4 both 1/10 despite weights 2 and 1. Others false (P2 is 3x P3; P4 not dummy; P1 = 1/2).

questions.stem: A voting body has four members, $P_1$ to $P_4$, with weights 5, 4, 3 and 2, and a motion passes with total weight at least 10. Members join a coalition one at a time in each of the 24 possible orders. The Shapley-Shubik power index of a member is the fraction of the orders in which that member is pivotal. Find the index of $P_1$.

solve.work: Enumerating 24 orders: P1 pivotal 12, others 4 each. 12/24=1/2.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 9, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 7, 3, 2 and 1. Which list gives their Shapley-Shubik power indices in that order?
questions.solution: Pivotal player in each of the 24 orders: 1234:P2, 1243:P2, 1324:P3, 1342:P3, 1423:P2, 1432:P3, 2134:P1, 2143:P1, 2314:P1, 2341:P1, 2413:P1, 2431:P1, 3124:P1, 3142:P1, 3214:P1, 3241:P1, 3412:P1, 3421:P1, 4123:P2, 4132:P3, 4213:P1, 4231:P1, 4312:P1, 4321:P1. The pivot counts are 16, 4, 4, 0, so the indices are 16/24, 4/24, 4/24, 0. The other lists are the weight shares, the Banzhaf indices, and a guess that the weakest player has power.

solve.work: Enumeration: pivotal counts 16, 4, 4, 0 of 24: 2/3, 1/6, 1/6, 0.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 7, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 5, 3, 2 and 2. The four players join in each of the 24 possible orders. In how many of these orders is $P_2$ the pivotal player, the one whose joining first brings the total to 7 or more?

solve.work: Enumeration: pivotal counts P1 12, P2 4, P3 4, P4 4. P2 = 4.

questions.stem: Five players with weights 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2 (for $P_1$ to $P_5$) join a coalition in the order $P_5$, $P_3$, $P_1$, $P_4$, $P_2$. A coalition wins at weight 14 or more. Which player is pivotal?
questions.solution: The running totals are 2, 6, 12, 15 and 20. The total first reaches 14 when $P_4$ joins, so $P_4$ is pivotal.

solve.work: Totals: P5 2, P3 6, P1 12, P4 15 >= 14. P4 pivotal.

questions.stem: A board has three members with 5, 4 and 1 votes, and a motion needs 6 votes. The member with 1 vote holds 10% of all the votes. What is that member's Banzhaf power index?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 9, $(P_1, P_3)$ 6, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 10. The critical counts are 3, 1, 1, total 5. The 1-vote member is critical once, so its index is 1/5 (20% of the power).

solve.work: Winning: 5+4, 5+1, 5+4+1. Counts: 5-vote 3, 4-vote 1, 1-vote 1; total 5. Index 1/5.

questions.stem: A council has three members with 2, 1 and 1 votes, and a motion needs 3 votes. The member with 2 votes holds half of the votes. Which statement about that member's Banzhaf power is true?
choices: The member has exactly 1/2 of the power, matching its share of the votes
The member has 2/5 of the power, less than its share of the votes
The member has 3/5 of the power, more than its share of the votes
The member has all of the power, as a dictator
questions.answer: The member has 3/5 of the power, more than its share of the votes
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 3, $(P_1, P_3)$ 3, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 4. The critical counts are 3, 1, 1, total 5, so the 2-vote member has 3/5 of the Banzhaf power. It is not a dictator, since 2 votes alone do not reach 3.

solve.answer: The member has 3/5 of the power, more than its share of the votes

questions.stem: Three towns of equal population send representatives to a board with 3, 2 and 2 votes, and a motion needs 4 votes. Which statement is true?
choices: The 3-vote town has the most Banzhaf power, so the system favors it
The 3-vote town is a dictator, so the other towns have no power
The two 2-vote towns have no power, because they cannot win together
Each town has the same Banzhaf power, so the unequal votes do not favor any town
questions.answer: Each town has the same Banzhaf power, so the unequal votes do not favor any town
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 5, $(P_1, P_3)$ 5, $(P_2, P_3)$ 4, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 7. Every pair of towns wins (the two 2-vote towns together have 4). The critical counts are 2, 2, 2, so each town has 1/3 of the power.

solve.answer: Each town has the same Banzhaf power, so the unequal votes do not favor any town
solve.work: Every pair wins (5,5,4), all three: no one critical. Each critical twice: equal power.

questions.stem: A council has 15 members: five heavy members with 7 votes each and ten light members with 1 vote each. A motion needs 39 of the 45 votes. Which statement is true?
choices: Each heavy member has veto power, and no member is a dummy
The ten light members are dummies
A heavy member is a dictator
Only one of the heavy members has veto power
questions.answer: Each heavy member has veto power, and no member is a dummy
questions.solution: Without one heavy member the most votes available is 4 × 7 + 10 = 38, below 39, so every heavy member has veto power. With at most four heavy members the most votes is 28 + 10 = 38, so a winning coalition needs all five heavy members (35 votes) and at least 4 light ones. In a coalition with exactly 4 light members, each light member is critical (losing one leaves 38). So no member is a dummy, and no single member comes near 39 votes alone.

solve.answer: Each heavy member has veto power, and no member is a dummy
solve.work: Without one heavy: 28+10=38<39, so each heavy has veto. All heavies (35) + 4 lights = 39: each light critical there, so no dummies. No dictator.

questions.stem: A board has five members with 1 vote each, and a motion needs 3 votes. A member is critical in a winning coalition if the coalition would lose without that member. Counting every winning coalition, how many times in total are the members critical?
questions.solution: A coalition of 3 members wins, and each of its 3 members is critical (removing one leaves 2). There are 5 × 4 × 3 / (3 × 2 × 1) = 10 such coalitions, so 10 × 3 = 30 critical positions. Coalitions of 4 or 5 members still win after losing one member, so nobody is critical there.

solve.work: Only 3-member coalitions have critical members: C(5,3)=10, each with 3 critical: 30.

questions.stem: In a voting body the quota is the smallest whole number that is at least two thirds of the total weight. Five voters have weights 9, 7, 5, 4 and 3. What is the quota?
questions.solution: The total weight is $9 + 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 28$. Two thirds of 28 is $18\frac{2}{3}$. The smallest whole number that is at least that is 19.

solve.work: Total 9+7+5+4+3 = 28. 2/3 of 28 = 18.67; smallest whole number at least that is 19.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 11, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 7, 5, 3 and 2. A winning coalition is minimal if it loses whenever any one of its members leaves. A coalition is written as the list of its players. Which statement lists all the minimal winning coalitions?
questions.solution: $(P_1, P_2)$ has 12, and loses if either leaves (7 or 5). $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ has 12 and loses if any one leaves (5, 9 or 10). No other coalition is minimal: $(P_1, P_3)$ has 10, $(P_1, P_4)$ has 9 and $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ has 10, so these lose, and every other winning coalition contains one of the two minimal ones.

solve.work: Winning: {P1,P2}=12, {P1,P2,P3}=15, {P1,P2,P4}=14, {P1,P3,P4}=12, all = 17. {P2,P3,P4}=10 loses. Minimal: {P1,P2} and {P1,P3,P4} (removing any member drops below 11); the 3-member ones with P1,P2 stay winning without P3 or P4.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 8, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 4, 3, 2 and 1. A player has veto power if no coalition without that player can win. Which players have veto power?
questions.answer: $P_1$ and $P_2$ only
questions.solution: Check the total of everyone else. Without $P_1$: $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$, below 8. Without $P_2$: $4 + 2 + 1 = 7$, below 8. Without $P_3$: $4 + 3 + 1 = 8$, which wins. Without $P_4$: $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$, which wins. So only $P_1$ and $P_2$ have veto power.

solve.answer: $P_1$ and $P_2$ only
solve.work: Total 10. Without P1: 6 < 8 (veto). Without P2: 7 < 8 (veto). Without P3: 8 (no veto). Without P4: 9 (no veto). P1 and P2 only.

questions.stem: A council has four members, $P_1$ to $P_4$, with weights 6, 4, 3 and 2, and a motion passes when the supporters' weights total at least 10. Find the Banzhaf power index of $P_2$: the number of times $P_2$ is critical, divided by the total number of times all four members are critical.
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ with 10, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ with 13, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ with 12, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ with 11 and all four with 15. $P_1$ is critical in all 5. $P_2$ is critical in $(P_1, P_2)$, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ and $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$: 3 times. $P_3$ is critical only in $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$, and so is $P_4$: once each.
