The total is $5 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 10$, so the index of $P_2$ is $3/10$.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 51, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 40, 30, 20 and 10. Which list gives the Banzhaf power indices of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$, in that order?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$, $(P_1, P_3)$, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$, $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ and all four. Counting the times each player is critical gives $P_1$: 5, $P_2$: 3, $P_3$: 3, $P_4$: 1, a total of 12. The indices are 5/12, 3/12 = 1/4, 1/4 and 1/12. (The weights alone would suggest 2/5, 3/10, 1/5, 1/10.)

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 6, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 4, 3, 2 and 1. The players join one at a time in each of the 24 possible orders, and the pivotal player is the one whose joining first brings the total weight to the quota or more. The Shapley-Shubik power index of a player is the fraction of the orders in which that player is pivotal. What is the Shapley-Shubik power index of $P_4$?
questions.solution: $P_4$ (weight 1) is pivotal only if the players before $P_4$ total exactly 5: then $P_4$ brings the total to 6, while a total of 6 or more before it would mean $P_4$ is not needed. The only players that total 5 are $P_2$ and $P_3$ ($3 + 2$). So the order is $P_2, P_3, P_4, P_1$ or $P_3, P_2, P_4, P_1$: 2 orders. The index is $2/24 = 1/12$.

solve.work: P4 (weight 1) is pivotal when the players before it total exactly 5. Subsets of {4,3,2} totalling 5: only {3,2}. Orders: 2! before x 1! after = 2. Index 2/24 = 1/12.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 9, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 5, 4, 3 and 2. The players join in each of the 24 possible orders, and the pivotal player is the one whose joining first brings the total weight to the quota or more. In how many of the 24 orders is $P_2$ the pivotal player?
questions.solution: $P_2$ is pivotal when the players before $P_2$ total less than 9 but, with $P_2$'s 4, reach 9 or more, so they total from 5 to 8. The sets that work are $(P_1)$ with 5, $(P_3, P_4)$ with 5, $(P_1, P_3)$ with 8 and $(P_1, P_4)$ with 7. ($(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ has 10, already enough.) For a set of $k$ players before $P_2$ there are $k! \times (3 - k)!$ orders: $1! \times 2! = 2$ for $(P_1)$, and $2! \times 1! = 2$ for each of the other three. The total is $2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8$.

solve.work: P2 (4) pivotal when predecessors total 5 to 8. Subsets of {5,3,2}: {5}=5 (1!2! = 2 orders), {5,3}=8 (2), {5,2}=7 (2), {3,2}=5 (2). Total 8.

questions.stem: A weighted voting system with three players is written $[q: w_1, w_2, w_3]$, with quota $q$ and weights $w_1$, $w_2$ and $w_3$ for $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$. Which system gives all three players the same Shapley-Shubik power index?
questions.solution: In $[3: 2, 2, 1]$ no single player reaches 3, but any two players do, so the pivotal player is always the second to join. Each player is second in 2 of the 6 orders, so all three have index 1/3. In $[5: 3, 2, 1]$, $P_3$ is never pivotal. In $[4: 3, 2, 1]$, $P_1$ is pivotal in 4 of 6 orders. In $[3: 3, 1, 1]$, $P_1$ alone reaches the quota and is always pivotal.

solve.work: [3:2,2,1]: no one alone wins, every pair wins, so the second player is always pivotal: 1/3 each. [5:3,2,1]: P3 a dummy. [3:3,1,1]: P1 a dictator. [4:3,2,1]: P1 pivotal 4 of 6.

questions.stem: A county board has six members with 31, 31, 28, 21, 2 and 2 votes, and a motion needs at least 58 of the 115 votes. A dummy is a member who is never critical in any winning coalition. How many of the six members are dummies?
questions.solution: The three largest members have 31, 31 and 28 votes. Any two of them have at least $31 + 28 = 59$ votes, which is enough, and each is critical when only two of them are in the coalition. A coalition with at most one of them has at most $31 + 21 + 2 + 2 = 56$ votes, which is not enough, even with all three smaller members. So the members with 21, 2 and 2 votes can never turn a losing coalition into a winning one: they are dummies, despite holding 21 of the 115 votes. The answer is 3.

solve.work: Any two of 31, 31, 28 reach 58 (62, 59). Any coalition with at most one of them has at most 31+21+2+2 = 56 < 58. So a coalition wins exactly when it has two of the big three; the 21 and both 2s are never critical: 3 dummies.

questions.stem: Three players have weights 7, 3 and 2, and the quota is 12, the total weight, so a motion passes only if all three vote for it. Which statement is true?
choices: All three players have equal power, even though their weights differ
$P_1$ has the most power, in proportion to its larger weight
$P_1$ is a dictator, because it has the largest weight
$P_2$ and $P_3$ are dummies, because their weights are small
questions.answer: All three players have equal power, even though their weights differ
questions.solution: Only the coalition of all three players has total weight 12. If any one player leaves, the total drops below 12, so each player is critical in that one coalition and nowhere else. Each player is also pivotal in 2 of the 6 orders (the last to join). So the three have equal power (1/3 each), whatever their weights.

solve.answer: All three players have equal power, even though their weights differ
solve.work: Only winning coalition is all three; each is critical in it, so each has Banzhaf (and Shapley-Shubik) index 1/3: equal power.

questions.stem: A club has seven voters with weights 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 2. A motion needs a quota that is more than 60% of the total weight, and the club uses the smallest whole number that works. What is the quota?
questions.solution: The total weight is 8+6+5+4+3+2+2 = 30. Sixty percent of 30 is 18, and the quota must be more than that, so the smallest whole number is 19.

solve.work: Total 30; 60% is 18; smallest whole number more than 18 is 19.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 8, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 5, 4, 3 and 2. A winning coalition is minimal if it would lose whenever any one of its members left. Which choice lists all the minimal winning coalitions?
questions.solution: $(P_1, P_2)$ has weight 9 and $(P_1, P_3)$ has weight 8; each loses if either member leaves. $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ has weight 9, and it loses if any member leaves (4+3 = 7, 4+2 = 6, 3+2 = 5). $(P_1, P_4)$ has weight 7 and loses. Any other winning coalition contains one of these three, so it is not minimal.

solve.work: Winning: P1P2=9, P1P3=8, P2P3P4=9, and supersets. P1P4=7 loses. P1P2P3, P1P2P4, P1P3P4 are not minimal (drop P3/P4 still wins). Minimal: P1P2, P1P3, P2P3P4.

questions.stem: A board has four members with weights 4, 3, 2 and 2, and the quota is 7. How many different coalitions of one or more members win?
A voting body has total weight 21 and quota 12. The coalition $X$ has total weight 10. Which statement is correct about the coalition made of all the voters who are not in $X$?
choices: It loses, because its weight 11 is less than the quota 12
It wins, because its weight 11 is more than half of the total weight 21
It loses, because it has fewer members than $X$
questions.answer: It loses, because its weight 11 is less than the quota 12
questions.solution: The voters outside $X$ have weight 21 - 10 = 11. That is less than the quota 12, so they lose too. Being more than half of the total weight (10.5) is not enough; a coalition must reach the quota.

solve.answer: It loses, because its weight 11 is less than the quota 12
solve.work: Complement weight 21-10=11 < 12, loses.

questions.stem: A committee has 7 voters. A coalition is any group of one or more voters. How many coalitions have at least 2 voters?
questions.solution: There are 2^7 = 128 groups, including the empty one. Remove the empty group (1) and the 7 groups of a single voter: 128 - 1 - 7 = 120.

solve.work: 2^7-1=127 nonempty, minus 7 singles = 120.

questions.stem: The 5 players of a system join one at a time, and there are 120 possible orders. In how many of them does $P_2$ join before $P_4$?
questions.solution: For every order in which $P_2$ comes before $P_4$, swapping the two gives an order in which $P_4$ comes first. So exactly half of the orders qualify: 120 / 2 = 60.

solve.work: By symmetry half of 120 = 60.

questions.stem: A council has 7 voters, including Dev. How many coalitions of exactly 3 voters do not include Dev?
questions.solution: Without Dev there are 6 voters. The number of ways to choose 3 of them is 6 × 5 × 4 / (3 × 2 × 1) = 20. (15 counts the coalitions that do include Dev; 35 counts all coalitions of 3.)

solve.work: Choose 3 from the other 6: C(6,3)=20.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: The weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 9, 3, 2 and 1, so the total weight is 15. The quota must be more than half of the total and at most the total. A dictator is a player who wins alone while every coalition without that player loses. For which of these quotas is $P_1$ a dictator?
questions.solution: With quota 8, $P_1$ wins alone (9 is at least 8), and the others together have only 3 + 2 + 1 = 6, which loses. With quota 10, 12 or 15, $P_1$ alone has 9, which is too little to win.

solve.work: Dictator needs q<=9 and q>6 (others 6): q=8 or 9. Among options only 8 (and 8>7.5 is allowed).

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: A system is written $[q: w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4]$, with the quota first and then the weights of $P_1$ to $P_4$. A dummy is a player who is never critical in any winning coalition. Which of these systems has exactly two dummies?
questions.solution: In $[8: 4, 4, 2, 1]$ a coalition needs both 4s, since 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 is too small. Those two already total 8, so $P_3$ and $P_4$ are never critical, and there are 2 dummies. In $[9: 7, 3, 2, 1]$ only $P_4$ is a dummy; in $[10: 6, 5, 3, 2]$ nobody is; in $[7: 8, 3, 2, 1]$ $P_1$ wins alone and the other three are dummies.

solve.work: [8:4,4,2,1]: only coalitions with P1 and P2 win (P1P3P4=7, P2P3P4=7 lose), so P3, P4 are dummies: exactly two. [9:7,3,2,1] has one dummy (P4); [10:6,5,3,2] none; [7:8,...] three.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 16, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $P_4$ and $P_5$ are 8, 6, 4, 2 and 1. How many of the five players are dummies, never critical in any winning coalition?
questions.solution: $P_5$ (weight 1) would be critical only in a coalition whose weight is exactly 16 including $P_5$, which means the rest add up to exactly 15. The other weights 8, 6, 4 and 2 are all even, so no group of them adds to 15. $P_5$ is a dummy. The others are not dummies. In $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$, of weight 18, removing $P_1$, $P_2$ or $P_3$ leaves 10, 12 or 14, all below 16, so all three are critical. In $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$, of weight 16, removing $P_4$ leaves 14, so $P_4$ is critical. So there is 1 dummy.

solve.work: Total 21. Critical counts: P1 6, P2 6, P3 2, P4 2, P5 0 (removing 1 from any winning coalition >=16 leaves... checked all 2^5 coalitions). One dummy, P5.

questions.skill: Critical players, dictators, veto power and dummies
questions.stem: In a weighted voting system both $P_1$ and $P_2$ have veto power, which means no coalition without that player can win. Which statement is true of every winning coalition?
choices: It contains exactly one of $P_1$ and $P_2$
It may lack both $P_1$ and $P_2$ if its weight is large enough
questions.answer: It contains both $P_1$ and $P_2$
questions.solution: A winning coalition without $P_1$ is impossible, because $P_1$ has veto power. For the same reason it cannot lack $P_2$. So every winning coalition contains both.

solve.answer: It contains both $P_1$ and $P_2$
solve.work: Each veto player must be in every winning coalition.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 9, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $P_4$ and $P_5$ are 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1. Across all the winning coalitions, the five players are critical a total of 25 times. What is the Banzhaf power index of $P_2$?
questions.solution: $P_2$ is critical in $(P_1, P_2)$ (weight 9), $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ (weight 12), $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ (weight 11), $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ (weight 9), $(P_1, P_2, P_5)$ (weight 10), $(P_1, P_2, P_4, P_5)$ (weight 12), $(P_2, P_3, P_4, P_5)$ (weight 10). That is 7 times, so the index is 7/25.

solve.work: Enumerating 13 winning coalitions: counts 9,7,5,3,1 (total 25). P2 = 7/25.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 11, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 7, 5, 4 and 2. Which list gives their Banzhaf power indices in that order?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 12, $(P_1, P_3)$ 11, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 16, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ 14, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ 13, $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 11, $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 18. The critical counts are 5, 3, 3, 1, total 12, so the indices are 5/12, 3/12, 3/12, 1/12. The list 7/18, 5/18, 2/9, 1/9 is the weight shares, 2/7, 2/7, 2/7, 1/7 counts only the minimal winning coalitions, and 3/10, 1/4, 1/4, 1/5 counts the winning coalitions each player belongs to instead of the times each is critical.

questions.stem: Five panel members carry 5, 4, 3, 2 and 2 votes, and a motion passes with at least 11 votes. Count how many times each member is critical across all winning coalitions. The Banzhaf power index of a member is that count divided by the sum of the five counts. What is the index of the member with 5 votes?
questions.solution: The member with weight 5 is critical in $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ (weight 12), $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ (weight 11), $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ (weight 14), $(P_1, P_2, P_5)$ (weight 11), $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_5)$ (weight 14), $(P_1, P_2, P_4, P_5)$ (weight 13), $(P_1, P_3, P_4, P_5)$ (weight 12). The five members' counts are 7, 7, 3, 3, 3, a total of 23. So the index is 7/23.

solve.work: Total 16, quota 11. Enumerating: counts 5-vote 7, 4-vote 7, 3-vote 3, each 2-vote 3; total 23. Index 7/23.

questions.stem: A motion needs 9 votes to pass, and $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ carry 8, 3, 1 and 1 votes. Which of these gives the Banzhaf power indices of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$, in order?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 11, $(P_1, P_3)$ 9, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 12, $(P_1, P_4)$ 9, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ 12, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ 10, $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 13. $P_1$ is critical in 7 of them and each other player in 1, a total of 10. The other lists are the weight shares, the result of leaving out the coalition of all four players, and the Shapley-Shubik indices.

solve.work: Winning: P1 with any other. P1P2, P1P3, P1P4 (both critical), P1P2P3, P1P2P4, P1P3P4, all (P1 only). Counts 7,1,1,1: 7/10, 1/10, 1/10, 1/10.

questions.stem: Five players carry 3, 3, 2, 1 and 1 votes ($P_1$ to $P_5$), and a motion needs 6 votes to pass. Which statement about their Banzhaf power is true?
choices: $P_3$ has 3 times the Banzhaf power of $P_4$, though its weight is only twice as large
$P_3$ has twice the Banzhaf power of $P_4$, in line with its weight
$P_3$ and $P_4$ have the same Banzhaf power
questions.answer: $P_3$ has 3 times the Banzhaf power of $P_4$, though its weight is only twice as large
questions.solution: The critical counts are 8, 8, 6, 2, 2. $P_3$ is critical 6 times and $P_4$ 2 times, a ratio of 3 to 1. $P_1$ is critical 8 times, more than $P_3$.

solve.answer: $P_3$ has 3 times the Banzhaf power of $P_4$, though its weight is only twice as large
solve.work: Enumerating: counts 8, 8, 6, 2, 2 (total 26). P3 3/13, P4 1/13: three times, weight only twice.

questions.stem: A board has four members with weights 6, 4, 3 and 2. A motion passes with weight at least 9. In each of the 24 orders of joining, the pivotal member is the one whose joining first brings the total to 9 or more. What is the Shapley-Shubik power index of the member with weight 3?

solve.work: Enumeration: counts 10, 6, 6, 2 of 24. Weight 3 member: 6/24=1/4.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 12, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 8, 5, 3 and 2. Which list gives their Shapley-Shubik power indices in that order?
questions.solution: Pivotal player in each of the 24 orders: 1234:P2, 1243:P2, 1324:P2, 1342:P4, 1423:P2, 1432:P3, 2134:P1, 2143:P1, 2314:P1, 2341:P1, 2413:P1, 2431:P1, 3124:P2, 3142:P4, 3214:P1, 3241:P1, 3412:P1, 3421:P1, 4123:P2, 4132:P3, 4213:P1, 4231:P1, 4312:P1, 4321:P1. The pivot counts are 14, 6, 2, 2, so the indices are 14/24, 6/24, 2/24, 2/24. The second list is the Banzhaf indices and the third the weight shares.

questions.stem: A system has quota 4 and four players with weights 3, 1, 1 and 1 for $P_1$ to $P_4$. The players join one at a time in each of the 24 possible orders, and the pivotal player is the one whose joining first brings the total to 4 or more. What is the Shapley-Shubik power index of $P_1$?
questions.solution: If $P_1$ joins first, the total is 3 and the next player to join is pivotal, not $P_1$. This happens in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders. In every other order, $P_1$ joins after at least one weight-1 player: the total before is 1 to 3, below 4, and after it is 4 or more. So $P_1$ is pivotal in 24 - 6 = 18 orders, and the index is 18/24 = 3/4.

solve.work: If P1 joins first, the next player brings 3 to 4 and is pivotal (6 orders). Otherwise P1 is pivotal: after one, two or three 1-vote players the total is below 4 until P1 joins. 18/24 = 3/4.

questions.stem: In a weighted voting system with quota 9, the weights of $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ are 5, 3, 3 and 2, and the players join in each of the 24 possible orders. Which statement is true?
choices: $P_2$ is pivotal in exactly 1/5 of the orders
$P_1$ is pivotal in exactly 2/5 of the orders
$P_1$ is pivotal in exactly half of the orders
questions.answer: $P_1$ is pivotal in exactly half of the orders
questions.solution: Pivotal player in each order: 1234:P3, 1243:P4, 1324:P2, 1342:P4, 1423:P2, 1432:P3, 2134:P3, 2143:P4, 2314:P1, 2341:P1, 2413:P1, 2431:P1, 3124:P2, 3142:P4, 3214:P1, 3241:P1, 3412:P1, 3421:P1, 4123:P2, 4132:P3, 4213:P1, 4231:P1, 4312:P1, 4321:P1. The pivot counts are 12, 4, 4, 4 out of 24: $P_1$ has 1/2, and each other player has 1/6. The values 1/5 and 2/5 are Banzhaf indices, not Shapley-Shubik ones.

solve.answer: $P_1$ is pivotal in exactly half of the orders
solve.work: Enumeration: counts 12, 4, 4, 4 of 24. P1 pivotal in exactly half.

questions.stem: A system has five players, and there are 120 possible orders in which they can join. $P_1$ is pivotal in 48 orders and $P_2$ in 36 orders. The other three players are pivotal equally often. What is the Shapley-Shubik power index of $P_5$?
questions.solution: The other three players are pivotal in 120 - 48 - 36 = 36 orders altogether, so 36 / 3 = 12 orders each. The index of $P_5$ is 12/120 = 1/10.

questions.stem: A board has three members with 4, 3 and 2 votes. Its quota is first set at 5 and later raised to 7. Which statement about Banzhaf power is true?
choices: At quota 5 the 4-vote member has the most power; at quota 7 all three have equal power
At quota 5 the three members have equal power; at quota 7 the 2-vote member has none
At quota 5 the 2-vote member has none; at quota 7 all three have equal power
The powers are the same at both quotas, because the votes did not change
questions.answer: At quota 5 the three members have equal power; at quota 7 the 2-vote member has none
questions.solution: At quota 5 any two members win, and each member is critical in two of the three winning pairs, so each has 1/3. At quota 7 only $(4, 3)$ and all three win; the 2-vote member is critical in neither, so it is a dummy and the other two have 1/2 each.

solve.answer: At quota 5 the three members have equal power; at quota 7 the 2-vote member has none
solve.work: Quota 5: every pair wins, all critical in pairs, none in the triple: equal. Quota 7: only {4,3} and {4,3,2} win; 2-vote never critical.

questions.stem: A council has four members with 6, 5, 3 and 2 votes, and a motion needs 10 votes. How many times as much Banzhaf power does the 6-vote member have as the 5-vote member?
questions.solution: The winning coalitions are $(P_1, P_2)$ 11, $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ 14, $(P_1, P_2, P_4)$ 13, $(P_1, P_3, P_4)$ 11, $(P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 10, $(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4)$ 16. The critical counts are 4, 4, 2, 2. The 6-vote and 5-vote members are each critical 4 times, so their powers are equal and the ratio is 1.

solve.work: Enumeration: counts 4, 4, 2, 2. 6-vote and 5-vote equal: ratio 1.

questions.stem: Five people share a prize that Dana values at 150 dollars. In a fair division, each person must receive a share that he or she values as at least $\frac{1}{5}$ of the whole. What is the least value, in dollars, that Dana can place on her share?
questions.solution: A fair share for 5 people is $\frac{1}{5}$ of the whole, by the player's own values: $150\div5=30$ dollars.

questions.stem: In a fair division among 4 players, what must each player believe about his or her own share?
choices: It is worth at least $\frac{1}{2}$ of the total, by his or her own values
It is worth at least $\frac{1}{4}$ of the total, by his or her own values
It is exactly the same size as every other player's share
It is worth more than any other player's share, by his or her own values
questions.answer: It is worth at least $\frac{1}{4}$ of the total, by his or her own values
questions.solution: A fair (proportional) division gives each of the $n$ players a share worth at least $\frac{1}{n}$ of the total, as that player values it. With 4 players this is $\frac{1}{4}$. Players need not agree on values, and shares need not be equal in size.

solve.answer: It is worth at least $\frac{1}{4}$ of the total, by his or her own values
solve.work: Fair (proportional) share among 4: at least 1/4 of the total by one's own values.

questions.stem: Ana cuts a cake into two pieces, Bea chooses one of them, and Ana takes the other. Why should Ana cut two pieces that she values equally?
choices: She takes the larger piece, so the cut does not matter to her at all
Bea must receive a piece of exactly half the size of the cake
Bea always chooses the piece that Ana values the least of the two
She may get either piece, so both should be worth the same to her
questions.answer: She may get either piece, so both should be worth the same to her
questions.solution: Ana does not know which piece Bea will choose. If she cuts two pieces she values equally, she gets a piece worth half the cake to her whichever one is left. If she cut unevenly, Bea could leave her the smaller one.

solve.answer: She may get either piece, so both should be worth the same to her
solve.work: The divider does not know which piece she will get, so she makes both worth half to her.

questions.stem: Ana and Bea share a cake by the divider-chooser method. Ana values the whole cake at 24 dollars. She cuts it into two pieces that she values equally, Bea chooses a piece, and Ana takes the other. How many dollars is Ana's piece worth to her?
questions.solution: Ana values the two pieces equally, so each is worth half of 24 dollars to her, and she is happy with whichever one is left: $24\div2=12$ dollars.

solve.work: Equal halves in her view: 24 / 2 = 12.

questions.stem: Three players share a cake by the lone-divider method. The divider values the whole cake at 60 dollars and cuts it into three pieces that she values equally. How many dollars is each piece worth to the divider?
questions.solution: Three pieces of equal value share 60 dollars, so each is worth $60\div3=20$ dollars to the divider.

questions.stem: Ana, Ben and Cy share a cake by the lone-chooser method. Ana and Ben first split the cake between them, and each then cuts his or her own share into three pieces. Cy takes one piece from Ana's pieces and one from Ben's pieces. How many pieces does Cy get?
questions.solution: Cy chooses one piece from each of the two sets of three pieces, so Cy gets $1+1=2$ pieces.

solve.work: One from Ana's pieces and one from Ben's: 2.

questions.stem: Ann, Ben and Cal bid on a bike and a canoe. In the sealed-bids method, a player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by the number of players. Ann bids 60 dollars for the bike and 90 dollars for the canoe. What is Ann's fair share, in dollars?
questions.solution: Ann's bids total $60+90=150$ dollars. With 3 players, her fair share is $150\div3=50$ dollars.

questions.stem: In the sealed-bids method, who receives an item?
choices: The player who bid the most for it
The player who bid the least for it
The player with the largest fair share
A player chosen at random among the bidders
questions.answer: The player who bid the most for it
questions.solution: Each item goes to the player who bid the most for it. Cash payments then even out the differences.

solve.answer: The player who bid the most for it
solve.work: Each item goes to the highest bidder.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which fair-division method uses cash payments between the players to make up differences in value?
questions.answer: Sealed bids
questions.solution: In sealed bids, items go to the highest bidders, and players who receive more than their fair share pay cash to those who receive less. The other three methods divide a cake without money changing hands.

solve.answer: Sealed bids
solve.work: Sealed bids settles with cash payments.

questions.stem: Sam values a whole inheritance at 150 dollars, and it is shared by 3 people. A division is fair to a person when he or she values his or her share at $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole or more. Which of these shares is NOT fair to Sam?
choices: A share that Sam values at 49 dollars
A share that Sam values at 50 dollars
A share that Sam values at 52 dollars
A share that Sam values at 75 dollars
questions.answer: A share that Sam values at 49 dollars
questions.solution: A fair share for Sam is worth at least 150 / 3 = 50 dollars to him. The shares worth 50, 52 and 75 dollars are fair. A share worth 49 dollars is below 50, so it is not fair.

solve.answer: A share that Sam values at 49 dollars
solve.work: Fair share = 150/3 = 50 dollars. 52, 75 and 50 are at least 50; 49 is below 50, so not fair.

questions.stem: Eight friends share a prize. A division is fair to a friend when he or she values his or her own share at $\frac{1}{8}$ of the whole prize or more. What is the least percent of the whole prize that a friend can value his or her share at?
questions.solution: One eighth of 100 percent is 100 / 8 = 12.5 percent.

solve.work: Fair means at least 1/8 of the prize; 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5 percent.

questions.stem: Three players share a prize that Ann values at 60 points in all. A division is fair to Ann when she values her own share at $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole or more. In which case is the division fair to Ann?
choices: Ann values her share at 18 points and the other two shares at 20 and 22 points
Ann values her share at 19 points and the other two shares at 19 and 22 points
Ann values her share at 22 points and the other two shares at 28 and 10 points
Ann values her share at 15 points and the other two shares at 25 and 20 points
questions.answer: Ann values her share at 22 points and the other two shares at 28 and 10 points
questions.solution: A fair share is worth at least 60 / 3 = 20 points to Ann. When she values her share at 22 points, that is enough, even though she values another share at 28. The shares she values at 18, 19 or 15 points are all less than 20.

solve.answer: Ann values her share at 22 points and the other two shares at 28 and 10 points
solve.work: 1/3 of 60 = 20. A: 22 (22+28+10=60) is at least 20, fair. B 19, C 15, D 18 are below 20.

questions.stem: In the divider-chooser method, what happens after the divider has cut the cake?
choices: The chooser takes the piece he or she prefers, and the divider takes the other piece
The divider takes the piece he or she prefers, and the chooser takes the other piece
The two players flip a coin to decide which piece each one takes
The chooser takes the heavier piece, and the divider takes the lighter one
questions.answer: The chooser takes the piece he or she prefers, and the divider takes the other piece
questions.solution: The chooser looks at both pieces and takes the one he or she values more. The divider receives the remaining piece. This is why the divider cuts two pieces that he or she values equally.

solve.answer: The chooser takes the piece he or she prefers, and the divider takes the other piece
solve.work: Divider cuts, chooser picks the piece he or she prefers, divider gets the other.

questions.stem: Tom is the chooser in the divider-chooser method. He values the two pieces at 70 percent and 30 percent of the whole cake, and he takes the piece he prefers. What percent of the whole cake does he get, in his own view?
questions.solution: Tom takes the piece he values more, the one worth 70 percent to him.

solve.work: He takes the piece he values at 70 percent.

questions.stem: A cake weighs 800 grams and is the same all the way through, and Rae values every part of it equally. As the divider, she cuts it into two pieces that she values equally. How many grams does each piece weigh?
questions.solution: Equal value to Rae means equal weight here, so each piece weighs 800 / 2 = 400 grams.

solve.work: Uniform value, equal value means equal weight: 800/2 = 400 g.

questions.stem: In the lone-divider method with 4 players, into how many pieces does the divider cut the cake?
questions.solution: The divider cuts one piece for each player, so 4 pieces. The three choosers each get one and the divider keeps the last.

solve.work: Lone divider cuts into N = 4 pieces.

questions.stem: In the lone-divider method with N players, what does each chooser do after the divider has cut the cake?
choices: He or she takes turns picking a piece, starting with the youngest player
He or she cuts one of the pieces again into N smaller pieces, which the other players then choose from
He or she secretly declares fair each piece worth at least $\frac{1}{N}$ of the cake to him or her
He or she names the single piece that is worth the most to him or her, and the divider gives that piece up
questions.answer: He or she secretly declares fair each piece worth at least $\frac{1}{N}$ of the cake to him or her
questions.solution: Each chooser decides alone which of the pieces he or she would accept as a fair share, those worth at least 1/N of the cake. The method then gives each chooser a piece he or she declared fair.

solve.answer: He or she secretly declares fair each piece worth at least $\frac{1}{N}$ of the cake to him or her
solve.work: Each chooser independently (secretly) declares the pieces worth at least 1/N to him or her. Option D.

questions.stem: A chooser values four pieces at 10, 30, 35 and 25 percent of the whole cake. In the lone-divider method with four players, a chooser declares a piece fair if he values it at 25 percent or more. How many pieces does he declare fair?
questions.solution: The pieces worth 30, 35 and 25 percent are at least 25 percent, so he declares those 3 pieces fair. The 10 percent piece is not fair.

solve.work: Pieces at least 25: 30, 35, 25 -> 3 pieces.

questions.stem: In the lone-chooser method with 4 players, three players first divide the cake among themselves, and each of them cuts his or her own share into pieces for the fourth player to choose from. Into how many pieces does each of the three cut his or her share?
questions.solution: The chooser is to take one piece from each share, and each share is cut into as many pieces as there are players. With 4 players, each share is cut into 4 pieces.

solve.work: In lone-chooser with N=4 each of the three cuts his share into 4 pieces.

questions.stem: In the lone-chooser method with 3 players, Ana and Ben first split the cake between them. Who cuts the pieces that Cy chooses from?
choices: Cy cuts each of the two shares into 3 pieces that he values equally, and then Ana and Ben pick
Ana cuts her own share into 3 pieces that she values equally, and Ben does the same with his
Ana cuts the whole cake into 3 pieces that she values equally, and Ben and Cy then choose
Ana and Ben each cut the other's share into 3 pieces that the other one values equally
questions.answer: Ana cuts her own share into 3 pieces that she values equally, and Ben does the same with his
questions.solution: Ana and Ben each cut their own share into 3 pieces of equal value to themselves. Cy then chooses one piece from each of the two shares.

solve.answer: Ana cuts her own share into 3 pieces that she values equally, and Ben does the same with his
solve.work: Ana and Ben each cut their own share into 3 pieces they value equally; Cy picks one from each. Option C.

questions.stem: In the lone-chooser method, Ana cuts her share into 3 pieces that she values equally, and then Cy takes one of them. What fraction of her share does Ana keep?
questions.solution: Ana is left with the other 2 of the 3 equal pieces, so she keeps 2/3 of her share.

solve.work: She keeps 2 of 3 equal pieces: 2/3 of her share.

questions.stem: Ann and Bo own a motorbike together and use the sealed-bids method. Ann bids 70 dollars and Bo bids 50 dollars. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by the number of players. What is Bo's fair share, in dollars?
questions.solution: Bo's bids total 50 dollars, and there are 2 players, so his fair share is 50 / 2 = 25 dollars.

solve.work: Bo's bids total 50; fair share 50/2 = 25.

questions.stem: In the sealed-bids method, which kind of player pays money into the pool?
choices: A player who wins no items at all, so that he or she is not left out of the division
The player who made the single highest bid on any one item
A player who wins items worth more to him or her than his or her fair share
Every player, each paying the same amount into the pool
questions.answer: A player who wins items worth more to him or her than his or her fair share
questions.solution: A player whose items, valued by his or her own bids, are worth more than his or her fair share pays the difference into the pool. A player who wins less than his or her fair share is paid from the pool instead.

solve.answer: A player who wins items worth more to him or her than his or her fair share
solve.work: A player whose items exceed his or her fair share pays the excess into the pool. Option C.

questions.stem: Ann, Bo and Cy bid 45, 36 and 60 dollars for a kayak, using the sealed-bids method. A player's fair share is his or her bid divided by 3. The winner pays into the pool the amount by which the kayak is worth more to the winner than the winner's fair share. How many dollars does the winner pay into the pool?
questions.solution: Cy bid the most, 60 dollars, so he wins. His fair share is 60 / 3 = 20 dollars. He pays 60 - 20 = 40 dollars into the pool.

solve.work: Cy wins with 60; fair share 60/3 = 20; pays 60-20 = 40.

questions.stem: In the sealed-bids method, Eve's fair share is 90 dollars, and the items she wins are worth 60 dollars by her own bids. How many dollars does she receive from the pool, before any leftover money is split?
questions.solution: Her items are worth 90 - 60 = 30 dollars less than her fair share, so she is paid 30 dollars from the pool.

solve.work: She is paid 90 - 60 = 30.

questions.stem: Two players use the method of markers on 10 lots in a row. Each player secretly places one marker that splits the lots into 2 groups of equal worth to that player. A marks after lot 4 and B marks after lot 6. The player whose marker is further left wins the lots up to his or her marker, and the other player wins the lots after his or her marker. Lots won by neither player are left over. How many lots are left over?
questions.solution: A's marker is further left, so A wins lots 1 to 4. B wins the lots after lot 6, which are lots 7 to 10. Lots 5 and 6 are won by neither player, so 2 lots are left over.

solve.work: A wins 1-4, B wins 7-10; lots 5 and 6 left over: 2.

questions.stem: In the method of markers, what does each player do first?
choices: He or she bids an amount of cash for each of the lots in the row, and the highest bid wins it
He or she marks the row of lots into groups that are all worth the same to him or her
He or she cuts the row into groups that all have the same number of lots
He or she picks the one lot that he or she wants the most and takes it
questions.answer: He or she marks the row of lots into groups that are all worth the same to him or her
questions.solution: Each player, in secret, places markers in the row so that the groups between the markers are of equal worth in that player's own view. The groups need not have the same number of lots.

solve.answer: He or she marks the row of lots into groups that are all worth the same to him or her
solve.work: Each player first places markers splitting the row into groups of equal worth to him or her. Option A.

questions.stem: A player places markers after lots 5 and 9 to split 12 lots in a row into 3 groups: the lots up to the first marker, the lots after the first marker up to the second, and the lots after the second marker. How many lots are in the middle group?
questions.solution: The groups are lots 1 to 5, lots 6 to 9 and lots 10 to 12. The middle group has 9 - 5 = 4 lots.

solve.work: Middle group lots 6 to 9: 4 lots.

questions.stem: Five players use the method of markers. Each player places markers that split the row of lots into 5 groups that are worth the same to that player. How many markers does each player place?
questions.solution: To make 5 groups in a row you need 4 dividing markers, one fewer than the number of groups.

solve.work: 5 groups need 4 markers.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which method can be used to divide items such as a boat and a piano among several people when the items cannot be cut up and the people are able to pay cash?
questions.answer: Sealed bids
questions.solution: Sealed bids uses cash payments to even out the differences in value, so the items need not be cut. The other three methods are about cutting a divisible thing, such as a cake, into pieces.

solve.answer: Sealed bids
solve.work: Indivisible items with cash payments: sealed bids.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which of these methods is used for exactly two players?
questions.answer: Divider-chooser
questions.solution: In divider-chooser one player cuts and the other chooses, so it is a method for two players. The other methods are written for any number of players.

solve.answer: Divider-chooser
solve.work: Divider-chooser is the two-player method.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: What does the sealed-bids method need that the divider-chooser method does not need?
choices: A cake that can be cut into pieces of any size
Exactly two players who take turns
Players who are able to pay cash into a pool
A referee who values the cake for them
questions.answer: Players who are able to pay cash into a pool
questions.solution: In sealed bids some players pay into a pool and others are paid from it, so every player must be able to pay. Divider-chooser needs a divisible object and two players but no cash.

solve.answer: Players who are able to pay cash into a pool
solve.work: Sealed bids needs players able to pay cash into the pool. Option B.

questions.stem: Players A and B share 10 items in a row, numbered 1 to 10, by the method of markers. Each player marks the point that splits the row into two parts of equal worth to him or her. The player whose marker is further left receives the items to the left of his or her own marker, and the other player receives the items to the right of his or her own marker. Items between the two markers are left over, to be divided in another way. A's marker is after item 4 and B's marker is after item 7. How many items are left over?
questions.solution: A's marker is further left, so A receives items 1 to 4. B receives the items to the right of B's own marker, items 8 to 10. Items 5, 6 and 7 are between the markers, so 3 items are left over: $7-4=3$.

solve.work: A's marker (after item 4) is further left, so A takes items 1-4. B takes the items to the right of B's marker (after item 7): items 8-10. Items 5, 6, 7 are left over: 3 items.

questions.stem: Ana cuts a cake into two pieces and Bea chooses one by the divider-chooser method. Bea values the two pieces at 18 dollars and 12 dollars. By how many dollars does the value of the piece Bea chooses exceed her fair share, which is half of the cake's value to her?
questions.solution: Bea values the whole cake at $18+12=30$ dollars, so her fair share is 15 dollars. She chooses the 18-dollar piece, which is $18-15=3$ dollars more than her fair share.

solve.work: Bea's total 30, fair share 15; she chooses 18: 18 - 15 = 3.

questions.stem: Two players divide a cake by the divider-chooser method. Which statement is true afterward?
choices: The divider may think the chooser's piece is worth more than hers
The chooser may think she received less than half of the cake
Both players must value the two pieces in exactly the same way
Each player thinks his or her piece is worth at least half
questions.answer: Each player thinks his or her piece is worth at least half
questions.solution: The divider values both pieces equally, so each is worth half to her whichever she gets. The chooser takes the piece she values more, which is worth at least half to her. So both are satisfied; they need not agree on how the pieces compare.

solve.answer: Each player thinks his or her piece is worth at least half
solve.work: Divider values both halves equally; chooser takes the one she values at least half. Both think they have at least half.

questions.stem: Dana cuts a cake into piece 1, piece 2 and piece 3, which she values equally. Eli declares pieces 1 and 2 fair. Fay declares only piece 2 fair. Which assignment follows the lone-divider method?
choices: Eli gets piece 1, Fay gets piece 2, Dana gets piece 3
Eli gets piece 2, Fay gets piece 1, Dana gets piece 3
Eli gets piece 1, Fay gets piece 3, Dana gets piece 2
Eli gets piece 2, Fay gets piece 3, Dana gets piece 1
questions.answer: Eli gets piece 1, Fay gets piece 2, Dana gets piece 3
questions.solution: Each chooser must receive a piece he or she declared fair. Fay declared only piece 2, so Fay gets piece 2. Eli then gets piece 1, his other fair piece. Dana, the divider, takes the piece left over, piece 3.

solve.answer: Eli gets piece 1, Fay gets piece 2, Dana gets piece 3
solve.work: Fay accepts only piece 2, so Fay gets 2; Eli gets 1; Dana gets 3.

questions.stem: In the lone-divider method, why must the divider cut the cake into pieces that all have equal value to the divider?
choices: She chooses her piece first, so she wants all the pieces to look alike
The choosers must all receive pieces of exactly equal size
She gets the piece left over, so every piece must be fair to her
The choosers will each take the piece the divider values least
questions.answer: She gets the piece left over, so every piece must be fair to her
questions.solution: The divider gets whichever piece is left after the choosers are served. To be sure of a fair share whichever piece that is, she cuts so that every piece is worth $\frac{1}{n}$ of the cake to her.

solve.answer: She gets the piece left over, so every piece must be fair to her
solve.work: The divider takes whatever piece is left, so every piece must be a fair share to her.

questions.stem: In the lone-divider method with three players, a chooser declares a piece fair if she values it at $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole cake or more. She values the three pieces at 20 percent, 35 percent and 45 percent of the whole cake. How many pieces does she declare fair?
questions.solution: A piece is fair to her if it is worth at least about $33.3$ percent. The pieces worth 35 percent and 45 percent qualify; the 20 percent piece does not. She declares 2 pieces fair.

solve.work: 1/3 is about 33.3%. 35% and 45% qualify, 20% does not: 2.

questions.stem: Ana, Ben and Cy share a cake by the lone-chooser method. Ana and Ben split it, and Ana ends up with half of the cake in her own view. She cuts her half into three pieces that she values equally, and Cy takes one of them. What fraction of the whole cake, in Ana's view, is the piece Cy takes?
questions.solution: Ana's half is worth $\frac{1}{2}$ of the cake to her. Each of her three equal pieces is $\frac{1}{2}\div3=\frac{1}{6}$ of the whole cake.

questions.stem: Dee and Eli inherit a piano and a sofa and use the sealed-bids method. Dee bids 400 dollars for the piano and 100 for the sofa. Eli bids 300 for the piano and 200 for the sofa. Each item goes to its highest bidder. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 2. A player whose items are worth more than the fair share (by his or her own bids) pays the difference into a pool, and a player whose items are worth less is paid the difference from the pool. Whatever is left in the pool is split equally. How many dollars in cash does Eli receive in all?
questions.solution: Dee wins the piano and Eli wins the sofa. Fair shares: Dee $\frac{500}{2}=250$, Eli $\frac{500}{2}=250$. Dee's piano is worth 150 more than her share, so she pays 150. Eli's sofa is worth 50 less than his share, so he is paid 50. The 100 dollars left over is split equally, 50 each. Eli receives $50+50=100$ dollars (and Dee pays $150-50=100$).

solve.work: Dee gets piano (400), Eli sofa (200). Fair shares: Dee 250, Eli 250. Dee pays 150; Eli receives 50. Pool 100, split 50 each. Eli receives 50 + 50 = 100.

questions.stem: A division is envy-free if no player values another player's share more than his or her own. Ann values her own share at 40 percent of the cake, Bo's share at 35 percent and Cy's share at 25 percent. Bo values Ann's share at 30 percent, his own at 30 percent and Cy's at 40 percent. Cy values Ann's share at 30 percent, Bo's at 30 percent and his own at 40 percent. Which statement is true?
choices: Only Ann envies another player's share, because Bo's share is worth 35 percent to her
Only Bo envies another player's share, because he values Cy's share more than his own
Ann and Cy both envy another player's share, because each values another share at 30 percent or more
Nobody envies another player's share, so the division is envy-free, because every player holds a share worth 30 or more
questions.answer: Only Bo envies another player's share, because he values Cy's share more than his own
questions.solution: Ann values her own share (40) more than the others (35 and 25), so she does not envy anyone. Cy values his own share (40) more than the others (30 and 30), so he does not either. Bo values Cy's share at 40, which is more than his own 30, so Bo envies Cy. Only Bo envies another player.

solve.answer: Only Bo envies another player's share, because he values Cy's share more than his own
solve.work: Ann: own 40 vs 35, 25 - no envy. Bo: own 30 but Cy's 40 - envies Cy. Cy: own 40 vs 30, 30 - no envy. Only Bo envies.

questions.stem: A division among four players is proportional when each player values his or her own share at 25 percent of the whole or more. Players A, B, C and D value their own shares at 31, 24, 25 and 22 percent of the whole. How many of the four players have a share that meets this requirement?
questions.solution: A share meets the requirement when it is worth 25 percent or more to its owner. That is true for A (31) and C (25, exactly enough). It is not true for B (24) or D (22). So 2 players are satisfied.

solve.work: Need at least 25: A 31 yes, B 24 no, C 25 yes, D 22 no. Count 2.

questions.stem: Two players divide a cake. Ana values her own piece at 55 percent of the whole cake. Bo values his own piece at 47 percent of the whole cake. Which statement must be true?
choices: Ana values Bo's piece at more than she values her own piece, 55 percent
The division is proportional, because 55 and 47 are both close to half of the cake
Each player values his or her own piece at more than the other player's piece
Bo values Ana's piece at 53 percent, which is more than he values his own piece
questions.answer: Bo values Ana's piece at 53 percent, which is more than he values his own piece
questions.solution: Bo values the two pieces at 100 percent in all. His own piece is 47, so Ana's piece is 100 - 47 = 53 percent to him, which is more than 47. Ana values Bo's piece at only 100 - 55 = 45 percent, less than her own. The division is not proportional because Bo's 47 is below 50, and Bo values Ana's piece more than his own.

solve.answer: Bo values Ana's piece at 53 percent, which is more than he values his own piece
solve.work: Two pieces make the whole. Ana values Bo's piece at 45 < 55, so A false. Bo values Ana's piece at 100-47 = 53 > 47, so B true. C false for Bo. D false: Bo has 47 < 50.

questions.stem: Ana and Bea share a cake by the divider-chooser method. Bea values the whole cake at 50 dollars, and she values the two pieces that Ana cuts at 22 dollars and 28 dollars. Bea chooses first. How many dollars is Ana's piece worth to Bea?
questions.solution: Bea takes the piece she values at 28 dollars. Ana is left with the piece worth 22 dollars to Bea (50 - 28 = 22).

solve.work: Bea picks first and takes the 28-dollar piece; Ana gets the other, worth 22 to Bea.

questions.stem: Ana is the divider. She cuts a cake into two pieces that she values at 60 percent and 40 percent of the cake, instead of equally, and Bea then chooses. What can happen?
choices: Ana is sure to receive the piece worth 60 percent to her, because she was the one who made the cut
Bea must take the piece worth 40 percent to Ana, because the chooser always takes the smaller piece
Bea may choose the piece worth 60 percent to Ana, leaving Ana with less than half of the cake in her view
Ana is guaranteed at least 50 percent of the cake in her own view, whatever the two pieces are worth to her
questions.answer: Bea may choose the piece worth 60 percent to Ana, leaving Ana with less than half of the cake in her view
questions.solution: Bea takes the piece she prefers, and that may be the one Ana values at 60 percent. Then Ana gets the 40 percent piece, less than half in her view. Only a cut into two pieces of equal value to the divider guarantees her a fair share.

solve.answer: Bea may choose the piece worth 60 percent to Ana, leaving Ana with less than half of the cake in her view
solve.work: Bea may take the 60 percent piece (to Ana), leaving Ana 40 percent < half. Option B.

questions.stem: A straight strip of land 100 meters long is shared by the divider-chooser method. The divider values the first 40 meters at 5 dollars per meter and the remaining 60 meters at 2 dollars per meter. She cuts the strip once so that she values the two pieces equally. How many meters from the start of the strip is the cut?
questions.solution: The whole strip is worth 40 x 5 + 60 x 2 = 200 + 120 = 320 dollars to her, so each piece must be worth 160 dollars. The first 40 meters are worth 200 dollars, which is more than 160, so the cut falls inside them: 160 / 5 = 32 meters.

solve.work: Total value = 40*5 + 60*2 = 320; half = 160. First 40 m worth 200 > 160, so cut at 160/5 = 32 m.

questions.stem: Ann cuts a cake into pieces numbered 1, 2 and 3 for the lone-divider method. Bo declares pieces 1 and 3 fair, and Cy declares only piece 3 fair. Each chooser must get a piece he declared fair, and Ann receives the piece that is left. Which numbered piece does Ann receive?
questions.solution: Cy declared only piece 3, so Cy must get piece 3. Bo then gets piece 1, which is the other piece he declared. The piece left for Ann is piece 2.

solve.work: Cy must get 3, so Bo gets 1, Ann gets 2.

questions.stem: In the lone-divider method with three players, Bo values the three pieces in the ratio $5 : 6 : 9$. A chooser declares a piece fair if it is worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole cake to him. How many pieces does Bo declare fair?
questions.solution: The parts add up to 5 + 6 + 9 = 20, so the pieces are worth 25, 30 and 45 percent of the cake to Bo. One third is about 33.3 percent, so only the 45 percent piece is fair. Bo declares 1 piece.

solve.work: Total parts 20; 1/3 is 6.67 parts. Only 9 parts (45 percent) qualifies; 6/20 = 30 percent does not. 1 piece.

questions.stem: In the lone-divider method with three players, Cy values the whole cake at 90 dollars, and he values pieces A, B and C at 24, 30 and 36 dollars. A piece is fair to him if it is worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole cake to him. Which pieces does Cy declare fair?
questions.answer: Pieces B and C
questions.solution: One third of 90 dollars is 30 dollars. Piece B is worth exactly 30 and piece C is worth 36, so both are fair. Piece A, at 24 dollars, is not.

solve.answer: Pieces B and C
solve.work: 1/3 of 90 = 30. A 24 no, B 30 yes, C 36 yes. Pieces B and C.

questions.stem: Ana and Ben split a cake and Ana gets a share she values at $\frac{1}{2}$ of the whole cake. In the lone-chooser method she cuts her share into three pieces that she values equally, and Cy takes one of them. What fraction of the whole cake does Ana keep, in her own view?
questions.solution: Ana keeps 2 of her 3 equal pieces, which is 2/3 of her share. Her share is worth 1/2 of the cake to her, so she keeps 1/2 x 2/3 = 1/3 of the cake.

questions.stem: Ana, Ben and Cy use the lone-chooser method. Cy values the three pieces of Ana's share at 12, 16 and 22 percent of the whole cake, and the three pieces of Ben's share at 15, 15 and 20 percent. Cy takes the piece he values most from each share. What percent of the whole cake does Cy receive, in his own view?
questions.solution: Cy takes the 22 percent piece from Ana's share and the 20 percent piece from Ben's share. In total 22 + 20 = 42 percent.

solve.work: Best from Ana's share 22, from Ben's share 20; total 42.

questions.stem: In the lone-chooser method with 4 players, three players divide the cake among themselves, and each of them cuts his or her own share into 4 pieces. The fourth player, Dee, will choose one piece from each share. How many pieces are there in all for Dee to choose among?
questions.solution: Each of the 3 shares is cut into 4 pieces, so there are 3 x 4 = 12 pieces. Dee chooses 1 piece from each share, so she receives 3 pieces.

solve.work: 3 shares x 4 pieces = 12 pieces.

questions.stem: Ann, Bo and Cy co-own a cabin and one of them will keep it. They use the sealed-bids method with bids of 120 dollars from Ann, 90 dollars from Bo and 60 dollars from Cy. A player's fair share is his or her bid divided by 3. The winner pays into the pool the amount by which the cabin is worth more to the winner than the winner's fair share, each of the others is paid his or her fair share from the pool, and the money left over is split equally among the three players. How many dollars does Ann pay in NET, that is, the amount she pays into the pool minus her equal share of the leftover?
questions.solution: Ann wins. Her fair share is 120 / 3 = 40, so she pays 120 - 40 = 80 dollars into the pool. Bo is paid 90 / 3 = 30 and Cy is paid 60 / 3 = 20, so 50 dollars leaves the pool. The leftover is 80 - 50 = 30 dollars, and each player gets 30 / 3 = 10. Ann's net payment is 80 - 10 = 70 dollars.

solve.work: Ann wins; fair share 40; pays 120-40 = 80. Bo paid 30, Cy paid 20. Leftover 80-50 = 30, each gets 10. Ann net 80-10 = 70.

questions.stem: Fay and Gus use the sealed-bids method for a bike and a desk. Fay bids 80 dollars for the bike and 40 for the desk. Gus bids 50 for the bike and 70 for the desk. Each item goes to its highest bidder. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 2. A player whose items are worth more than the fair share (by his or her own bids) pays the difference into the pool, and a player whose items are worth less is paid the difference from the pool. How many dollars are left in the pool after all of these payments?
questions.solution: Fay's fair share is (80 + 40) / 2 = 60 dollars and Gus's is (50 + 70) / 2 = 60 dollars. Fay wins the bike, worth 80 to her, so she pays 80 - 60 = 20 dollars in. Gus wins the desk, worth 70 to him, so he pays 70 - 60 = 10 dollars in. Nobody is paid from the pool, so 20 + 10 = 30 dollars are left.

solve.work: Bike to Fay (80), desk to Gus (70). Fay fair 120/2=60, pays 20. Gus fair 60, pays 10. Pool 30.

questions.stem: Ann, Bo and Cy use the sealed-bids method for a ring, a vase and a lamp. Ann bids 40, 90 and 20 dollars for them, in that order. Bo bids 60, 50 and 10 dollars. Cy bids 50, 80 and 80 dollars. Which list shows who wins each item?
choices: Bo gets the ring, Ann gets the vase and Cy gets the lamp
Ann gets the ring, Bo gets the vase and Cy gets the lamp
Bo gets the ring, Cy gets the vase and Ann gets the lamp
Cy gets the ring, Ann gets the vase and Bo gets the lamp
questions.answer: Bo gets the ring, Ann gets the vase and Cy gets the lamp
questions.solution: Each item goes to the highest bidder. For the ring the bids are 40, 60 and 50, so Bo wins. For the vase they are 90, 50 and 80, so Ann wins. For the lamp they are 20, 10 and 80, so Cy wins.

solve.answer: Bo gets the ring, Ann gets the vase and Cy gets the lamp
solve.work: Ring: 40/60/50 Bo. Vase: 90/50/80 Ann. Lamp: 20/10/80 Cy. Option C.

questions.stem: Ann, Bo and Cy use the sealed-bids method for a canoe and a tent. Ann bids 120 dollars for the canoe and 30 for the tent. Bo bids 90 for the canoe and 60 for the tent. Cy bids 60 for the canoe and 90 for the tent. Items go to the highest bidders. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 3. Each player pays the pool, or is paid from it, the difference between the items won (by his or her own bids) and the fair share, and the leftover is split equally. How many dollars in cash does Bo receive in all, counting his equal share of the leftover?
questions.solution: Ann wins the canoe and Cy wins the tent, so Bo wins nothing. Every fair share is 150 / 3 = 50 dollars. Ann pays 120 - 50 = 70 and Cy pays 90 - 50 = 40, so 110 dollars goes in. Bo is paid 50, so the leftover is 110 - 50 = 60 dollars, and each player gets 20. Bo receives 50 + 20 = 70 dollars in all.

solve.work: Canoe Ann (120), tent Cy (90). Fair shares 150/3 = 50 each. Ann pays 70; Bo has nothing, paid 50; Cy pays 40. Pool 70+40-50 = 60, each 20. Bo gets 50+20 = 70.

questions.stem: Three players use the method of markers on 12 lots in a row. Each player's two markers split the lots into 3 groups of equal worth to that player: the lots up to the first marker, the lots after the first marker up to the second, and the lots after the second marker. A marks after lots 3 and 7, B after lots 4 and 9, and C after lots 5 and 8. The player whose first marker is leftmost wins his or her first group. Of the other two, the one whose second marker is further left wins his or her middle group, and the last player wins his or her last group. Which lots does B win?
questions.answer: Lots 10 to 12
questions.solution: The first markers are at 3, 4 and 5, so A wins A's first group, lots 1 to 3. Of B and C, the second markers are at 9 and 8, so C is further left and wins C's middle group, lots 6 to 8. B is last and wins B's last group, the lots after lot 9, which are lots 10 to 12.

solve.answer: Lots 10 to 12
solve.work: First markers A3, B4, C5: A wins lots 1-3. Of B and C, second markers B9, C8: C wins middle 6-8. B wins his last group 10-12.

questions.stem: Two players use the method of markers on 15 lots in a row. Each places one marker that splits the lots into 2 groups of equal worth to that player. A marks after lot 6 and B marks after lot 10. The player whose marker is further left wins the lots up to his or her marker, and the other player wins the lots after his or her marker. How many lots does B win?
questions.solution: A's marker is further left, so A wins lots 1 to 6. B wins the lots after lot 10, which are lots 11 to 15. That is 15 - 10 = 5 lots.

solve.work: A (6) is left: wins 1-6. B wins lots after 10: 11-15, 5 lots.

questions.stem: A player values 7 lots in a row at 7, 5, 3, 4, 6, 2 and 3 points, in order. She places one marker to split the lots into 2 groups of equal worth to her. After which lot does she place the marker?
questions.solution: The lots are worth 7 + 5 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 30 points in all, so each group must be worth 15. The first three lots are worth 7 + 5 + 3 = 15 and the other four are worth 4 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15. The marker goes after lot 3.

solve.work: Total 30, half 15. Cumulative 7, 12, 15 -> after lot 3.

questions.stem: In the method of markers with two players, how can some lots be left over?
choices: The players refuse the lots that they value the least, and those lots are then left over in the row
Lots are left over only if both players place their markers in the same place
The last player has to give back lots until the other player has half of the lots
Each winner takes only his or her own group, so the lots between the two markers go to neither
questions.answer: Each winner takes only his or her own group, so the lots between the two markers go to neither
questions.solution: The leftmost marker wins everything up to it, and the other player wins everything after his or her marker. The lots in between are in neither group, so they are left over. If the markers were in the same place, there would be none left over.

solve.answer: Each winner takes only his or her own group, so the lots between the two markers go to neither
solve.work: Each winner takes only his own group; lots between the markers go to neither. Option C.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which is an advantage of the method of markers over the sealed-bids method?
choices: No lots are ever left over to be shared another way
No cash needs to be paid between the players
The lots do not have to be in any particular order
Every player is given the same number of lots
questions.answer: No cash needs to be paid between the players
questions.solution: In the method of markers each player simply receives lots, with no payments. But some lots may be left over, the lots are placed in a row, and the groups can have different numbers of lots.

solve.answer: No cash needs to be paid between the players
solve.work: Markers needs no cash; sealed bids does. Option B.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which is a weakness of the method of markers?
choices: Players have to pay cash into a pool to make up for differences in value between them
A player may receive less than a fair share in his or her own view
The lots must be cut into pieces of any size so that every player gets an equal group
Some lots may be left over, and they have to be shared out by another method
questions.answer: Some lots may be left over, and they have to be shared out by another method
questions.solution: The lots between the winners' groups are won by nobody and must be divided some other way. Each winner does get one of his or her own equal groups, so no payments are needed and no lot has to be cut.

solve.answer: Some lots may be left over, and they have to be shared out by another method
solve.work: Leftover lots must be shared another way. Option C. (A is false: each gets a fair share in own view.)

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which is a weakness of the lone-chooser method compared with the lone-divider method?
choices: It can only be used to divide items that cannot be cut
It gives the last player less than a fair share
It needs every player to pay cash into a pool
It needs many more cuts as players are added
questions.answer: It needs many more cuts as players are added
questions.solution: In lone-divider one player cuts the cake once, into as many pieces as there are players. In lone-chooser each of the earlier players cuts his or her own share again, and the number of pieces grows quickly with the number of players. It still gives every player a fair share, and no cash is needed.

solve.answer: It needs many more cuts as players are added
solve.work: Lone-chooser needs many more cuts as N grows (N! pieces) vs N pieces for lone-divider. Option A.

questions.stem: Four heirs share a cabin by the sealed-bids method. Ann bids 180 dollars, Ben 120, Cy 100 and Di 80. Each heir's fair share is his or her bid divided by 4. The top bidder keeps the cabin and pays into a pool the amount by which that bid exceeds the fair share. Each of the others receives cash equal to his or her fair share from the pool. Money left in the pool is then split equally among all four heirs. In all, how many dollars in cash does Cy receive?
questions.solution: Fair shares are 45 (Ann), 30 (Ben), 25 (Cy) and 20 (Di). Ann keeps the cabin and pays $180-45=135$ dollars into the pool. Ben, Cy and Di receive $30+25+20=75$ dollars from it, so $135-75=60$ dollars is left. Split four ways, each heir gets 15 dollars more. Cy receives $25+15=40$ dollars.

solve.work: Fair shares: Ann 180/4=45, Ben 30, Cy 25, Di 20. Ann keeps the cabin and pays 180-45=135 into the pool. Ben, Cy, Di receive 30+25+20=75 from the pool, leaving 60. Split equally: 15 each. Cy receives 25+15=40 dollars.

questions.stem: Players A and B divide 15 items in a row, numbered 1 to 15, using markers. Each places one marker splitting the row into two parts that he or she values equally. The player with the marker further left takes every item to the left of it. The other player takes every item to the right of his or her own marker. Anything between the markers is left over. A's marker is after item 6, and B's marker is further right. B ends up with 5 items. How many items are left over?
questions.solution: A's marker is further left, so A takes items 1 to 6, which is 6 items. B takes 5 items from the right end, items 11 to 15. That leaves items 7 to 10 between the markers: $15-6-5=4$ items.

solve.work: A's marker after item 6 is further left, so A takes items 1-6. B takes the 5 items to the right of B's marker, i.e. items 11-15, so B's marker is after item 10. Left over: items 7-10, which is 4 items.

questions.stem: Ann, Ben and Cy share a cake by the lone-chooser method. Ann and Ben first split the cake into two halves by divider-chooser. Each of them then cuts the half he or she received into three pieces that he or she thinks are equal. Cy takes the one piece he likes best from each half. Cy values the whole cake at 60 dollars. Which statement about Cy's two pieces must be true?
choices: Together they are worth exactly 20 dollars to Cy
Together they are worth at least 30 dollars to Cy
Together they are worth at least 20 dollars to Cy
Together they are worth at least 40 dollars to Cy
questions.answer: Together they are worth at least 20 dollars to Cy
questions.solution: In each half, Cy takes the piece he likes best out of three, so it is worth at least one third of that half to him. The two halves together are worth 60 dollars to Cy, so his two pieces are worth at least $\frac{1}{3}\times 60=20$ dollars to him. It could be more, so it need not be exactly 20 dollars.

solve.answer: Together they are worth at least 20 dollars to Cy
solve.work: Each half is cut into three pieces; in Cy's valuation the best of three pieces is worth at least 1/3 of that half. So Cy's two pieces are worth at least 1/3 of his value of the whole cake: 60/3 = 20 dollars. Nothing guarantees 30 or 40, and exactly 20 is not forced.

questions.stem: A long cake, the same thickness all along, is cut by one straight cut into a left piece and a right piece. The left half of the cake is chocolate and the right half is vanilla. Ana values any amount of chocolate three times as much as the same amount of vanilla. She cuts the cake so that she values the two pieces equally. What fraction of the whole cake is the left piece?
questions.solution: Let the whole cake have length 1. Chocolate (length $\frac{1}{2}$) is worth $3\times\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}$ to Ana and vanilla is worth $\frac{1}{2}$, so the cake is worth 2 and each piece must be worth 1. The left piece lies within the chocolate, where each unit of length is worth 3, so its length is $\frac{1}{3}$ of the cake.

solve.work: Value: chocolate 3 per unit length, vanilla 1. Total = 3(1/2) + 1(1/2) = 2; half = 1. Left piece of length x <= 1/2: 3x = 1, x = 1/3.

questions.stem: Ann (the divider) cuts a cake into pieces 1, 2, 3 and 4 for the lone-divider method. Ben declares pieces 1 and 2 fair, Cy declares pieces 2 and 3 fair, and Dee declares only piece 1 fair. Each chooser must get a piece he or she declared fair. Which piece does Ann receive?
questions.answer: Piece 4
questions.solution: Dee declared only piece 1, so Dee gets piece 1. Ben then gets piece 2 (his other fair piece). Cy then gets piece 3. The piece nobody was given, piece 4, goes to Ann, the divider.

solve.answer: Piece 4
solve.work: Dee must get 1, so Ben gets 2, Cy gets 3, Ann gets 4.

questions.stem: Ana, Ben and Cy share a cake by the lone-chooser method. Ana and Ben split the cake, and each cuts his or her half into three pieces. Cy then takes one piece from each half, the one he values most. Cy values the three pieces of Ana's half at 10, 14 and 20 percent of the whole cake, and the three pieces of Ben's half at 18, 20 and 18 percent. What percent of the whole cake does Cy get, in his own view?
questions.solution: Cy takes his favorite piece from each half: 20 percent from Ana's half and 20 percent from Ben's half. Total: $20+20=40$ percent, which is more than the $\frac{1}{3}$ (about 33 percent) he is entitled to.

solve.work: Best of Ana's: 20; best of Ben's: 20. Total 40.

questions.stem: In the lone-chooser method with three players, why does the chooser, Cy, end up with a share worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the cake to him?
choices: He chooses last, so the pieces that are left over are the ones he values most
Ana and Ben cut the pieces to match his values, so all six are worth the same to him
He takes the two largest pieces by size, which are always worth over $\frac{1}{3}$
He takes his favorite piece from each half, worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of that half
questions.answer: He takes his favorite piece from each half, worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of that half
questions.solution: Cy takes his favorite of the three pieces in each half. The best of three pieces is worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of that half to him, so the two pieces together are worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the two halves, which is $\frac{1}{3}$ of the cake.

solve.answer: He takes his favorite piece from each half, worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of that half
solve.work: Each half is cut into 3; his favorite of 3 is at least 1/3 of that half's value to him, so total at least 1/3 of the cake.

questions.stem: Ann, Ben and Cal use the sealed-bids method for a boat and a tent. Ann bids 150 dollars for the boat and 60 for the tent. Ben bids 120 for the boat and 240 for the tent. Cal bids 40 for the boat and 20 for the tent. Each item goes to its highest bidder; a player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 3; each player pays or is paid the difference between the value of the items won (by his or her own bids) and the fair share; money left over is split equally among the three. How many dollars in cash does Cal receive?
questions.solution: Ann wins the boat and Ben wins the tent. Fair shares: Ann 70, Ben 120, Cal 20. Ann's items are worth $150-70=80$ more than her share; Ben's are worth $240-120=120$ more; Cal has no items and is owed 20. The pool left over is $80+120-20=180$ dollars, so each player gets 60 of it. Cal receives $20+60=80$ dollars. (Ann pays $80-60=20$ and Ben pays $120-60=60$, which adds to Cal's 80.)

solve.work: Boat to Ann (150), tent to Ben (240). Fair shares: Ann 70, Ben 120, Cal 20. Ann pays 80, Ben pays 120, Cal receives 20. Pool 180, 60 each. Cal: 20 + 60 = 80.

questions.stem: Ann, Ben and Cal use the sealed-bids method for a bike and a piano. Ann bids 50 dollars for the bike and 160 for the piano. Ben bids 100 for the bike and 80 for the piano. Cal bids 230 for the bike and 10 for the piano. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 3; each player pays or is paid the difference between the value of the items won (by his or her own bids) and the fair share; money left over is split equally among the three. How many dollars in cash does Ben receive?
questions.solution: Cal wins the bike and Ann wins the piano. Fair shares: Ann 70, Ben 60, Cal 80. Ann's piano is worth $160-70=90$ more than her share; Cal's bike is worth $230-80=150$ more; Ben has no items and is owed 60. The pool left over is $90+150-60=180$ dollars, so each player gets 60 of it. Ben receives $60+60=120$ dollars.

solve.work: Bike to Cal (230), piano to Ann (160); Ben wins nothing. Fair shares: Ann 70, Ben 60, Cal 80. Ann pays 90, Cal pays 150, Ben receives 60. Pool 180, 60 each. Ben: 60 + 60 = 120.

questions.stem: In the method of markers, why does each player receive a fair share?
choices: Each player wins exactly the group of lots that he or she values the most
Each player wins the same number of lots as every other player does
Each player's winnings include one of that player's own equal groups
The last player is allowed to choose any of the lots that remain
questions.answer: Each player's winnings include one of that player's own equal groups
questions.solution: Each player marks the lots into $n$ groups of equal worth to that player. The group a player wins runs at least as far as that player's own group would have, so it contains one of the player's own equal-worth groups, which is worth $\frac{1}{n}$ of the lots to that player.

solve.answer: Each player's winnings include one of that player's own equal groups
solve.work: Each player's lots contain one of the equal-value segments he marked, worth 1/N to him.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which is a weakness of the sealed-bids method?
choices: It cannot be used when the items cannot be cut into smaller pieces
It can leave a player with less than a fair share in his or her own view
It needs one player to act as the divider of every one of the items
A player who wins more than a fair share must be able to pay the extra
questions.answer: A player who wins more than a fair share must be able to pay the extra
questions.solution: Sealed bids works for items that cannot be cut and gives every player at least a fair share, but it needs money: a winner who owes cash must be able to pay it, and a bidder with little cash may be unable to compete fairly.

solve.answer: A player who wins more than a fair share must be able to pay the extra
solve.work: A winner of items worth more than the fair share must pay cash: needs enough money. Sealed bids works for indivisible items and guarantees fair shares.

questions.stem: A division among three players is called proportional when each player believes his or her share is worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the total. Which statement about proportional divisions is correct?
choices: Some player may believe another player's share is worth more than her own
No player can believe another player's share is worth more than her own
Every player must believe her share is worth exactly $\frac{1}{3}$ of the total
All three shares must be exactly the same size as one another
questions.answer: Some player may believe another player's share is worth more than her own
questions.solution: Being proportional only says each player got at least $\frac{1}{3}$ by her own values. A player could value her own share at $\frac{1}{3}$ and another player's share at $\frac{1}{2}$, and so envy that player. Shares also need not be equal in size or in value.

solve.answer: Some player may believe another player's share is worth more than her own
solve.work: Proportional is not envy-free: e.g. own share 34%, another's 60%. So some player may value another's share more.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: In the sealed-bids method, which statement is true of every player after the leftover money is shared out?
choices: Every player receives at least one of the items
Some player may receive items and cash worth less than his or her fair share
The items and cash he or she receives are worth at least his or her fair share
A player who wins no item receives no cash
questions.answer: The items and cash he or she receives are worth at least his or her fair share
questions.solution: Each player receives the value of the items won, minus the difference from the fair share (settled in cash), plus an equal share of the leftover money. That totals the fair share plus a part of the leftover, so it is at least the fair share by the player's own bids. A player who wins no item still receives cash, and not every player wins an item.

solve.answer: The items and cash he or she receives are worth at least his or her fair share
solve.work: Each player gets at least the fair share, plus a nonnegative part of the surplus.

questions.stem: Why is every proportional division between two players also envy-free?
choices: The two pieces are always cut to exactly the same size, so neither player can prefer the piece the other player took
Each player values the other player's piece at exactly 50 percent of the cake, so no one can prefer it
The divider cuts after seeing how the chooser values the cake, so envy between the two cannot happen
Each player values both pieces at 100 percent in all, so a piece worth 50 or more leaves the other worth 50 or less
questions.answer: Each player values both pieces at 100 percent in all, so a piece worth 50 or more leaves the other worth 50 or less
questions.solution: For one player, the values of the two pieces add up to the whole. In a proportional division the player's own piece is worth at least half, so the other piece is worth at most half, and he or she does not value it more. That is exactly envy-free. (The pieces need not be the same size, and a player need not value the other piece at exactly half.)

solve.answer: Each player values both pieces at 100 percent in all, so a piece worth 50 or more leaves the other worth 50 or less
solve.work: To each player the two pieces total 100 percent; if own piece >= 50 then other <= 50, so no envy. Option C.

questions.stem: Three players divide a cake. A division is proportional when each player values his or her own share at $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole or more, and envy-free when no player values another's share more than his or her own. Ann values the shares of Ann, Bo and Cy at 36, 40 and 24 percent. Bo values them at 33, 34 and 33 percent. Cy values them at 30, 20 and 50 percent. Which statement is true?
choices: It is both proportional and envy-free
It is proportional but not envy-free
It is envy-free but not proportional
It is neither proportional nor envy-free
questions.answer: It is proportional but not envy-free
questions.solution: Each player values his or her own share at 36, 34 and 50 percent, all at least 33.3 percent, so the division is proportional. Ann values Bo's share (40) more than her own (36), so she envies Bo and the division is not envy-free.

solve.answer: It is proportional but not envy-free
solve.work: Proportional: Ann 36, Bo 34, Cy 50 all >= 33.3, yes. Envy: Ann values Bo's 40 > her 36, so not envy-free. Proportional but not envy-free.
