questions.stem: Dev and four others share an estate, and Dev values the whole estate at 350 dollars. A division is fair to him when the items and cash he ends up with are worth at least $\frac{1}{5}$ of 350 dollars to him. He receives a boat he values at 90 dollars, pays some cash into a pool, and later gets 6 dollars back as his share of the money left over. What is the most he can pay into the pool and still have a fair share, in dollars?
questions.solution: His fair share is 350 / 5 = 70 dollars. He ends with the boat (90 dollars) plus 6 dollars back, minus what he pays in. So 90 + 6 - x must be at least 70, which gives x at most 26 dollars.

questions.stem: A long rectangular cake is 100 centimeters long, with the same thickness all along. The divider values the first 20 centimeters at 2 dollars per centimeter and the other 80 centimeters at 5 dollars per centimeter. She makes one straight cut across it so that she values the two pieces equally. How many centimeters from the first end is the cut?
questions.solution: The whole cake is worth 20 x 2 + 80 x 5 = 40 + 400 = 440 dollars to her, so each piece must be worth 220 dollars. The first 20 centimeters are worth only 40 dollars, so she needs another 220 - 40 = 180 dollars from the part worth 5 dollars per centimeter: 180 / 5 = 36 centimeters. The cut is at 20 + 36 = 56 centimeters.

solve.work: Total = 20*2 + 80*5 = 440; half 220. First 20 cm = 40; need 180 more at 5/cm = 36 cm. Cut at 20+36 = 56 cm.

questions.stem: Why is the chooser in the divider-chooser method sure to receive a piece worth at least half of the cake to him or her?
choices: The two pieces together are worth the whole cake to the chooser, so the piece he or she prefers is worth at least half
The divider cuts the pieces to have equal value for the chooser as well as for the divider, so either piece is half
The chooser takes the larger piece by size, and the larger piece is always worth half the cake or more to him or her
The chooser may take both pieces for himself or herself if the divider's cut leaves him or her with less than half
questions.answer: The two pieces together are worth the whole cake to the chooser, so the piece he or she prefers is worth at least half
questions.solution: The two pieces add up to the whole cake in the chooser's view. They cannot both be worth less than half, so the one he or she prefers is worth at least half. The divider cuts equally only in his or her own view, and nobody may take both pieces.

solve.answer: The two pieces together are worth the whole cake to the chooser, so the piece he or she prefers is worth at least half
solve.work: The two pieces total the whole to the chooser, so the larger in his view is at least half. Option B.

questions.stem: Ana and Bea share a cake by the divider-chooser method. Ana cuts two pieces that she values equally. Bea values the two pieces at 40 percent and 60 percent of the cake, takes her favorite, and Ana takes the other. Ana's value of her own piece and Bea's value of her own piece are each a percent of the whole cake in that person's own view. What is the sum of these two percents?
questions.solution: Ana values her piece at half, 50 percent. Bea takes the piece worth 60 percent to her. The sum is 50 + 60 = 110. It can be more than 100, because the two players do not value the cake in the same way.

solve.work: Ana's piece is worth 50 to her (equal cut). Bea takes her favorite, 60. Sum 50+60 = 110.

questions.stem: Ann cuts a cake into pieces A, B, C and D for the lone-divider method with four players. Ben declares pieces B and C fair, Cy declares only piece B fair, and Dee declares pieces A and B fair. Each chooser must be given a piece he or she declared fair, and Ann receives the piece that is left. Which piece does Ben receive?
questions.answer: Piece C
questions.solution: Cy declared only piece B, so Cy gets B. Dee then must take A, the other piece she declared. Ben is left with C, the other piece he declared. Ann receives piece D.

solve.answer: Piece C
solve.work: Cy only B, so Cy gets B. Dee then must get A. Ben gets C. Ann gets D.

questions.stem: Ann cuts a cake into pieces A, B, C and D for the lone-divider method with four players. Ben declares pieces A and B fair, Cy declares pieces B and C fair, and Dee declares pieces C and D fair. In how many different ways can the three choosers each be given a different piece that he or she declared fair? (Ann takes the piece that is left in each case.)
questions.solution: If Ben takes A, Cy can take B (then Dee takes C or D: 2 ways) or C (then Dee takes D: 1 way). If Ben takes B, Cy must take C and Dee takes D: 1 way. In all there are 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 ways.

solve.work: Ben {A,B}, Cy {B,C}, Dee {C,D}. Ben A: Cy B, Dee C or D (2); Cy C, Dee D (1). Ben B: Cy C, Dee D (1). Total 4.

questions.stem: In the lone-divider method with three players, which statement is guaranteed to be true afterward?
choices: Each chooser believes his or her piece is the most valuable of the three pieces
All three pieces are worth the same amount to every player
The divider believes the piece she receives is worth more than each of the other two pieces
Each chooser believes his or her piece is worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole cake
questions.answer: Each chooser believes his or her piece is worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole cake
questions.solution: A chooser is only given a piece he or she declared fair, worth at least 1/3. The chooser may still think another piece is worth more, so the division need not be envy-free. The divider values all three pieces equally, and the other players need not.

solve.answer: Each chooser believes his or her piece is worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the whole cake
solve.work: Each chooser gets a piece he declared fair, worth at least 1/3 to him. Option C; others not guaranteed.

questions.stem: In the lone-chooser method with three players, Ana ends the first step with a share she values at least $\frac{1}{2}$ of the cake, and she cuts it into three pieces that she values equally. Why is her final share, after Cy takes one of the pieces, worth at least $\frac{1}{3}$ of the cake to her?
choices: She keeps 2 of her 3 equal pieces, which is $\frac{2}{3}$ of a share worth at least $\frac{1}{2}$ of the cake to her
Cy always takes the piece that Ana values the most, so what is left is worth exactly $\frac{1}{3}$ of the cake to her
Ana values all three pieces at $\frac{1}{2}$ of the cake, so any two of them are worth the whole
Cy is only allowed to take a piece that Ana values at less than $\frac{1}{3}$ of the cake
questions.answer: She keeps 2 of her 3 equal pieces, which is $\frac{2}{3}$ of a share worth at least $\frac{1}{2}$ of the cake to her
questions.solution: Ana values her three pieces equally, so each is worth at least 1/6 of the cake to her. After Cy takes one, she keeps two pieces, worth at least 2 x 1/6 = 1/3 of the cake. Cy may take any piece, and Ana does not decide which.

solve.answer: She keeps 2 of her 3 equal pieces, which is $\frac{2}{3}$ of a share worth at least $\frac{1}{2}$ of the cake to her
solve.work: She keeps 2/3 of a share worth >= 1/2, so >= 1/3. Option B.

questions.stem: In the lone-chooser method with four players, three players divide a cake and each cuts his or her own share into 4 pieces that he or she values equally. Dee values the three shares at 40, 35 and 25 percent of the whole cake, and she takes her favorite piece from each share. What is the least percent of the whole cake she is sure to receive in her own view?
questions.solution: Dee's favorite piece of a share is worth at least 1/4 of that share to her, because the 4 pieces together are worth the whole share. So she gets at least 40/4 + 35/4 + 25/4 = 10 + 8.75 + 6.25 = 25 percent.

solve.work: Best of 4 pieces of a share is at least 1/4 of it: (40+35+25)/4 = 25 at least.

questions.stem: Ana, Ben and Cy use the lone-chooser method. Cy values Ana's share at 50 percent of the whole cake, and its three pieces are in the ratio $1 : 2 : 2$ to him. He values Ben's share at 50 percent of the whole cake, and its three pieces are in the ratio $1 : 1 : 2$ to him. Cy takes his favorite piece from each share. What percent of the whole cake does he receive in his own view?
questions.solution: Ana's pieces are 1/5, 2/5 and 2/5 of 50 percent, so the best is 2/5 x 50 = 20 percent. Ben's pieces are 1/4, 1/4 and 2/4 of 50 percent, so the best is 2/4 x 50 = 25 percent. Together 20 + 25 = 45 percent.

questions.stem: Ann, Bo and Cy use the sealed-bids method for a sofa, a desk and a piano. Ann bids 260, 80 and 200 dollars for them, in that order. Bo bids 200, 120 and 70 dollars. Cy bids 80, 70 and 240 dollars. Items go to the highest bidders. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 3. Each player pays the pool, or is paid from it, the difference between the items won (by his or her own bids) and the fair share, and the leftover is split equally. How many dollars does Cy pay in NET, that is, the amount he pays into the pool minus his equal share of the leftover?
questions.solution: Ann wins the sofa, Bo the desk and Cy the piano. The fair shares are 540 / 3 = 180 for Ann, 390 / 3 = 130 for Bo and 390 / 3 = 130 for Cy. Ann pays 260 - 180 = 80 into the pool, Cy pays 240 - 130 = 110, and Bo is paid 130 - 120 = 10. The leftover is 80 + 110 - 10 = 180 dollars, so each player gets 60. Cy's net payment is 110 - 60 = 50 dollars.

solve.work: Sofa Ann 260, desk Bo 120, piano Cy 240. Fair: Ann 540/3=180, Bo 390/3=130, Cy 390/3=130. Ann pays 80, Bo paid 10, Cy pays 110. Leftover 80+110-10 = 180, each 60. Cy net 110-60 = 50.

questions.stem: Ann, Bo and Cy use the sealed-bids method for a kayak, a tent and a stove. Ann bids 80, 120 and 130 dollars for them, in that order. Bo bids 260, 150 and 70 dollars. Cy bids 300, 60 and 30 dollars. Items go to the highest bidders. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 3. Each player pays the pool, or is paid from it, the difference between the items won (by his or her own bids) and the fair share, and the leftover is split equally. Bo's net cash is what he receives minus what he pays in. What is the value of his items, by his own bids, plus his net cash, in dollars?
questions.solution: The kayak goes to Cy, the tent to Bo and the stove to Ann. Bo's fair share is 480 / 3 = 160, and his tent is worth 150 to him, so he is paid 10 from the pool. Ann's fair share is 110 and she pays 130 - 110 = 20. Cy's fair share is 130 and he pays 300 - 130 = 170. The leftover is 20 + 170 - 10 = 180 dollars, so each gets 60. Bo's net cash is 10 + 60 = 70, and 150 + 70 = 220 dollars. (This is his fair share, 160, plus 60.)

solve.work: Kayak Cy 300, tent Bo 150, stove Ann 130. Fair: Ann 330/3=110, Bo 480/3=160, Cy 390/3=130. Ann pays 20, Bo paid 10, Cy pays 170. Leftover 180, each 60. Bo net cash 10+60 = 70. Items 150 + 70 = 220.

questions.stem: Ann, Ben and Cy use the sealed-bids method for a truck and a trailer. Ann bids 50 and 100 dollars for them, in that order. Ben bids 170 and 220 dollars. Cy bids 70 and 110 dollars. Items go to the highest bidders. A player's fair share is the total of his or her bids divided by 3. Each player pays the pool, or is paid from it, the difference between the items won (by his or her own bids) and the fair share, and the leftover is split equally. How many dollars does Ben pay in NET, that is, the amount he pays into the pool minus his equal share of the leftover?
questions.solution: Ben wins both items, worth 170 + 220 = 390 dollars by his bids. His fair share is 390 / 3 = 130, so he pays 390 - 130 = 260 dollars into the pool. Ann is paid her fair share, (50 + 100) / 3 = 50, and Cy is paid (70 + 110) / 3 = 60. The leftover is 260 - 50 - 60 = 150 dollars, so each player gets 50. Ben's net payment is 260 - 50 = 210 dollars.

solve.work: Ben wins both (170, 220) = 390. Fair: Ann 150/3=50, Ben 390/3=130, Cy 180/3=60. Ben pays 260; Ann paid 50, Cy paid 60. Leftover 150, each 50. Ben net 260-50 = 210.

questions.stem: Which of these is a risk of bidding more for an item than it is truly worth to you, in the sealed-bids method?
choices: The item goes to the second-highest bidder, so a high bid only helps your rivals
Your fair share becomes smaller, since it is found by dividing your bids by a larger number
You may win the item and pay more for it than it is worth to you, ending below your true fair share
Your bid is thrown out, because the highest bid on each item is disqualified from the method and ignored
questions.answer: You may win the item and pay more for it than it is worth to you, ending below your true fair share
questions.solution: A bid above your true value can win you the item, and you then pay into the pool an amount based on that bid. You may end up with something that costs you more than it is worth to you, and so with less than your true fair share. The highest bid wins and is never thrown out, and inflating your bids makes your fair share larger, not smaller.

solve.answer: You may win the item and pay more for it than it is worth to you, ending below your true fair share
solve.work: Overbidding can win the item at a price above its true worth, leaving you below your true fair share. Option D.

questions.stem: A player values 8 lots in a row at 5, 3, 2, 6, 4, 1, 3 and 6 points, in order. She places two markers that split the lots into 3 groups of equal worth to her. After which lot does her second marker go?
questions.solution: The lots are worth 5 + 3 + 2 + 6 + 4 + 1 + 3 + 6 = 30 points, so each group must be worth 10. The groups are lots 1 to 3 (5 + 3 + 2 = 10), lots 4 and 5 (6 + 4 = 10) and lots 6 to 8 (1 + 3 + 6 = 10). The markers go after lots 3 and 5, so the second marker is after lot 5.

solve.work: Total 30, third 10. Cumulative 5, 8, 10 (lot 3), 16, 20 (lot 5), then 1+3+6 = 10. Second marker after lot 5.

questions.stem: Two players use the method of markers on 10 lots in a row, each placing one marker. The player whose marker is further left wins the lots up to it, the other player wins the lots after his or her marker, and if the markers are in the same place a coin toss decides who takes the left group. In which case are no lots left over?
choices: A marks after lot 4 and B marks after lot 5
A marks after lot 5 and B marks after lot 5
A marks after lot 3 and B marks after lot 7
A marks after lot 2 and B marks after lot 6
questions.answer: A marks after lot 5 and B marks after lot 5
questions.solution: Lots are left over exactly when the markers are in different places: the lots between them belong to neither player. With both markers after lot 5, one player wins lots 1 to 5 and the other wins lots 6 to 10, so nothing is left over. If A marks after lot 4 and B after lot 5, lot 5 is left over. If A marks after lot 3 and B after lot 7, lots 4 to 7 are left over. If A marks after lot 2 and B after lot 6, lots 3 to 6 are left over.

solve.answer: A marks after lot 5 and B marks after lot 5
solve.work: A: lot 5 left. B: lots 3-6 left. C: same place, one takes 1-5, other 6-10, none left. D: lots 4-7 left. Option C.

questions.stem: Three players use the method of markers on 10 lots in a row. Each player's two markers split the lots into 3 groups of equal worth to that player: the lots up to the first marker, the lots after the first marker up to the second, and the lots after the second marker. A marks after lots 2 and 6, B after lots 3 and 5, and C after lots 4 and 8. The player whose first marker is leftmost wins his or her first group. Of the other two, the one whose second marker is further left wins his or her middle group, and the last player wins his or her last group. Which lots are left over?
questions.answer: Lots 3, 6, 7 and 8
questions.solution: The first markers are at 2, 3 and 4, so A wins lots 1 and 2. Of B and C, the second markers are at 5 and 8, so B wins B's middle group, lots 4 and 5. C is last and wins the lots after lot 8, which are lots 9 and 10. The lots no one wins are 3, 6, 7 and 8.

solve.answer: Lots 3, 6, 7 and 8
solve.work: First markers A2, B3, C4: A wins 1-2. Second markers B5, C8: B wins middle 4-5. C wins last 9-10. Left over 3, 6, 7, 8.

questions.stem: Two players use the method of markers on 8 lots in a row. Each places one marker that splits the lots into 2 groups of equal worth to that player. A values the lots at 6, 4, 5, 3, 2, 4, 3 and 3 points, in order. B values them at 2, 3, 4, 3, 3, 4, 5 and 6 points. The player whose marker is further left wins the lots up to it, and the other player wins the lots after his or her marker. How many lots does B win?
questions.solution: A's lots total 30 points, so half is 15, and 6 + 4 + 5 = 15: A's marker is after lot 3. B's lots total 30 too, and 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 15: B's marker is after lot 5. A's marker is further left, so A wins lots 1 to 3 and B wins the lots after lot 5, which are lots 6 to 8. B wins 3 lots.

solve.work: A: total 30, cumulative 6, 10, 15 -> marker after lot 3. B: total 30, cumulative 2, 5, 9, 12, 15 -> after lot 5. A wins 1-3; B wins lots 6-8: 3 lots.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which statement is true of the divider-chooser, lone-divider, lone-chooser and sealed-bids methods when every player acts honestly?
choices: Each player is sure that no other player received a better share than his or her own
Each player is sure of a share worth at least $\frac{1}{N}$ of the whole to him or her, with N players
Each player ends up with a share of exactly the same size as every other player's share, measured by weight
No player has to cut, bid or declare anything, since the result is decided by lot
questions.answer: Each player is sure of a share worth at least $\frac{1}{N}$ of the whole to him or her, with N players
questions.solution: All four methods are designed to give each player a proportional, or fair, share: at least 1/N of the whole in that player's own view. They do not promise that nobody envies another share, they do not give equal-sized shares, and they all need players to cut, declare or bid.

solve.answer: Each player is sure of a share worth at least $\frac{1}{N}$ of the whole to him or her, with N players
solve.work: All four are proportional: each honest player gets at least 1/N in own view. Envy-freeness is not guaranteed. Option C.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: Which statement about the sealed-bids method is true?
choices: Each item goes to the player who bid the most for it, so someone who values it highly gets it
Each player wins the same number of items, so that no one is left out of the division of the items
The player with the largest fair share wins all of the items, and pays the others for them
No cash is ever needed, because the items are simply divided up according to their bids
questions.answer: Each item goes to the player who bid the most for it, so someone who values it highly gets it
questions.solution: In sealed bids every item is given to its highest bidder. Players may win different numbers of items, or none, and cash payments make up the differences. A fair share is only the amount used to decide payments.

solve.answer: Each item goes to the player who bid the most for it, so someone who values it highly gets it
solve.work: Each item goes to the highest bidder. Option B.

questions.skill: Strengths and fairness of the methods
questions.stem: In the lone-divider method with three players, Bo declares a piece fair when it is worth only 30 percent of the cake to him. What can go wrong for Bo?
choices: He is certain to get the piece that is most valuable to him, because he declared it
He has to pay cash to the divider for the piece, because it was a poor piece to begin with
He may be given that piece, which is worth less than the fair share of one third to him
The divider has to cut all of the pieces again to suit his declaration
questions.answer: He may be given that piece, which is worth less than the fair share of one third to him
questions.solution: A chooser may be given any piece he declared fair. A piece worth 30 percent is below one third (about 33.3 percent), so if he receives it he gets less than a fair share. Nothing guarantees him his favorite piece, and the method uses no cash and no second cut.

solve.answer: He may be given that piece, which is worth less than the fair share of one third to him
solve.work: He may be given a piece worth only 30 percent < 1/3 to him. Option C.

questions.stem: A country has 4 states and 14 seats to share among them. The total population of the 4 states is 840,000. What is the standard divisor?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is the total population divided by the number of seats: $840000 \div 14 = 60000$ people per seat.

questions.stem: The standard divisor is 250 people per seat. Cedar has a population of 3,100. What is Cedar's standard quota?
questions.solution: The standard quota is the state's population divided by the standard divisor: $3100 \div 250 = 12.4$.

questions.stem: The Jefferson method rounds every modified quota down. A state's modified quota is 6.98. How many seats does that state receive?
questions.solution: Rounding down means dropping the decimal part, even when it is close to 1. So 6.98 becomes 6 seats.

solve.work: Round 6.98 down: 6.

questions.stem: The Adams method rounds every modified quota up to the next whole number. A state's modified quota is 4.02. How many seats does that state receive?
questions.solution: Rounding up moves any quota that is not a whole number to the next whole number, even when the decimal part is tiny. So 4.02 becomes 5 seats.

solve.work: Round 4.02 up: 5.

questions.stem: The Webster method rounds each modified quota to the nearest whole number. A state's modified quota is 6.52. How many seats does that state receive?
questions.solution: The decimal part, 0.52, is more than one half, so 6.52 rounds up to 7 seats.

solve.work: 6.52 rounds to 7.

questions.stem: Three states have standard quotas of 4.35, 7.62 and 2.03, and there are 14 seats to share. In the Hamilton method, every state first gets its lower quota. How many seats are left over to be given out?
questions.solution: The lower quotas are 4, 7 and 2, which use $4 + 7 + 2 = 13$ seats. That leaves $14 - 13 = 1$ seat.

questions.stem: Which of these apportionment methods does NOT use a modified divisor?
questions.answer: Hamilton
questions.solution: The Hamilton method uses only the standard divisor and gives leftover seats to the largest decimal parts. Jefferson, Adams and Webster each adjust the divisor until the rounded quotas add up to the number of seats.

solve.answer: Hamilton
solve.work: Hamilton uses the standard divisor and largest remainders.

questions.stem: The average constituency of a state is its number of people per seat. Which state has the largest average constituency? North has 3000 people and 10 seats. East has 2100 people and 6 seats. South has 2200 people and 5 seats. West has 1900 people and 5 seats.
questions.answer: South
questions.solution: Divide each population by its seats: North 300, East 350, South 440, West 380. South has the most people per seat. North has the largest population, but it also has the most seats.

solve.answer: South
solve.work: North 300, East 350, South 440, West 380. South largest.

questions.stem: What is the goal of an apportionment method?
choices: To give every state the same number of seats, whatever its size
To find out which state has the largest population of all
To keep adding seats until every state is perfectly happy
To share a fixed number of seats among states by population
questions.answer: To share a fixed number of seats among states by population
questions.solution: Apportionment shares a fixed number of whole seats among groups in proportion to their populations, as fairly as whole numbers allow.

solve.answer: To share a fixed number of seats among states by population
solve.work: Apportionment shares a fixed number of seats by population.

questions.stem: Four states share 13 seats. Their standard quotas are Aspen 5.3, Birch 3.9, Cedar 2.5 and Dogwood 1.3. In the Hamilton method, which state is first in line for a leftover seat?
questions.answer: Birch
questions.solution: The lower quotas are 5, 3, 2 and 1, which use 11 of the 13 seats. Leftover seats go to the largest decimal parts. The decimal parts are 0.3, 0.9, 0.5 and 0.3, and Birch's 0.9 is the largest.

solve.answer: Birch
solve.work: Lower quotas 5+3+2+1 = 11, 2 left. Largest fractional part: Birch 0.9.

questions.stem: A school board has 9 seats to share among 5 districts. The districts have 54,000 people in all. What is the standard divisor?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is the total population divided by the number of seats: 54,000 / 9 = 6,000 people per seat.

questions.stem: The standard divisor is 1,200 people per seat. Rowan County has a population of 8,820. What is the standard quota of Rowan County?
questions.solution: The standard quota is the population divided by the standard divisor: 8,820 / 1,200 = 7.35.

questions.stem: What do the standard quotas of all the states add up to?
choices: The total population of all of the states
The total number of seats that are to be shared
The value of the standard divisor
The number of states that are sharing seats
questions.answer: The total number of seats that are to be shared
questions.solution: Each standard quota is a state's population divided by the standard divisor, which is the total population divided by the number of seats. Adding all the quotas gives the total population divided by the standard divisor, which is the number of seats.

solve.answer: The total number of seats that are to be shared
solve.work: Sum of quotas = total population / SD = number of seats. Option A.

questions.stem: The standard divisor is 40,000 people per seat. Which of these populations has a standard quota between 6 and 7?
Which of these is a problem of apportionment?
choices: Sharing the seats of a legislature among the states according to their populations
Choosing which one candidate wins the seat in a single district election by counting the votes
Cutting a cake into two pieces so that both people get a piece that is fair to each of them
Counting how many people live in each state in a census
questions.answer: Sharing the seats of a legislature among the states according to their populations
questions.solution: Apportionment means dividing a fixed number of seats among groups, such as states, in proportion to their populations. Counting people, electing one candidate and cutting a cake are different problems.

solve.answer: Sharing the seats of a legislature among the states according to their populations
solve.work: Apportionment: sharing seats among states by population. Option D.

questions.stem: In the Hamilton method, a state's standard quota is 6.45. The state first gets its lower quota. If it is also given one of the leftover seats, how many seats does the state have in all?
questions.solution: The lower quota of 6.45 is 6. With one leftover seat the state has 6 + 1 = 7 seats.

solve.work: Lower quota 6, plus one leftover seat = 7.

questions.stem: In the Hamilton method, which states receive the leftover seats after every state has its lower quota?
choices: The states with the largest populations, one seat each
The states whose standard quotas have the smallest decimal parts, one seat each
The states whose standard quotas have the largest decimal parts, one seat each
Every state in turn, starting with the state with the smallest population
questions.answer: The states whose standard quotas have the largest decimal parts, one seat each
questions.solution: After the lower quotas are given, the remaining seats go one at a time to the states with the largest decimal parts (the part after the decimal point) of their standard quotas.

solve.answer: The states whose standard quotas have the largest decimal parts, one seat each
solve.work: Hamilton gives leftovers to largest decimal parts, one each. Option A.

questions.stem: Four states share 13 seats by the Hamilton method. Their lower quotas are 5, 3, 2 and 1. How many leftover seats are there to give out?
questions.solution: The lower quotas give 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 11 seats. There are 13 - 11 = 2 leftover seats.

questions.stem: In the Jefferson method, a state has 4,750 people and the modified divisor is 500. How many seats does the state receive?
questions.solution: The modified quota is 4,750 / 500 = 9.5. The Jefferson method rounds every modified quota down, so the state receives 9 seats.

solve.work: 4750/500 = 9.5, rounded down to 9.

questions.stem: In the Jefferson method, a trial modified divisor gives a total of 22 seats when only 20 seats are to be shared. What should be done next?
choices: Try a smaller modified divisor, so that the modified quotas get larger
Take a seat from each of the two states with the smallest decimal parts
Round the modified quotas up instead of down, to settle the total
Try a larger modified divisor, so that the modified quotas get smaller
questions.answer: Try a larger modified divisor, so that the modified quotas get smaller
questions.solution: Each state's modified quota is its population divided by the divisor. A larger divisor makes every quota smaller and so lowers the total number of seats. The Jefferson method keeps rounding down and only changes the divisor.

solve.answer: Try a larger modified divisor, so that the modified quotas get smaller
solve.work: Too many seats: larger divisor to make quotas smaller. Option D.

questions.stem: The Jefferson method is used with the modified divisor 20. Three towns have populations, in thousands, of 155, 97 and 48. How many seats do the three towns receive in all?
questions.solution: The modified quotas are 155 / 20 = 7.75, 97 / 20 = 4.85 and 48 / 20 = 2.4. Rounding down gives 7, 4 and 2, which is 13 seats in all.

questions.stem: In the Adams method, a state has 6,010 people and the modified divisor is 1,000. How many seats does the state receive?
questions.solution: The modified quota is 6,010 / 1,000 = 6.01. The Adams method rounds every modified quota up, so the state receives 7 seats.

solve.work: 6.01 rounded up to 7.

questions.stem: When every quota is rounded up, the total is at least the number of seats. To bring the total down to exactly the number of seats, the Adams method uses a modified divisor that is
choices: equal to the total number of seats
equal to the population of the smallest state
questions.answer: larger than the standard divisor
questions.solution: A larger divisor makes each modified quota smaller, so fewer quotas are pushed up to the next whole number, and the total falls. A smaller divisor would make the total grow.

solve.answer: larger than the standard divisor
solve.work: Rounding up gives too many; larger divisor brings it down. Option C.

questions.stem: The Adams method is used with the modified divisor 20. Three towns have populations, in thousands, of 133, 87 and 41. How many seats do the three towns receive in all?
questions.solution: The modified quotas are 133 / 20 = 6.65, 87 / 20 = 4.35 and 41 / 20 = 2.05. Rounding each up gives 7, 5 and 3, which is 15 seats in all.

questions.stem: In the Webster method, a state has 4,380 people and the modified divisor is 1,000. How many seats does the state receive?
questions.solution: The modified quota is 4,380 / 1,000 = 4.38. The Webster method rounds to the nearest whole number, and 4.38 is nearest to 4, so the state receives 4 seats.

solve.work: 4.38 rounds to 4.

questions.stem: In the Webster method, rounding each quota to the nearest whole number gives one seat fewer than the number to be shared. What is done next?
choices: Use a larger divisor, so that the modified quotas get smaller
Give the extra seat to the state with the largest population
Use a smaller divisor, so that the modified quotas get larger
Round all of the quotas up instead of to the nearest whole number
questions.answer: Use a smaller divisor, so that the modified quotas get larger
questions.solution: The total is too small, so the modified quotas must grow. Dividing by a smaller number gives larger quotas, so more of them round up. The method keeps rounding to the nearest whole number and only changes the divisor.

solve.answer: Use a smaller divisor, so that the modified quotas get larger
solve.work: Too few seats: smaller divisor to make quotas larger. Option A.

questions.stem: Four states share 13 seats. Their standard quotas are 5.4, 3.7, 2.6 and 1.3. The Webster method is used with the standard divisor, rounding each quota to the nearest whole number. How many seats are given out in all?
questions.solution: The quotas round to 5, 4, 3 and 1, which is 5 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 13 seats, exactly the number to be shared.

questions.stem: In the Huntington-Hill method, a modified quota between 7 and 8 is rounded up if it is more than the geometric mean $\sqrt{7 \times 8}$, which is about 7.48, and down otherwise. A state's modified quota is 7.6. How many seats does it receive?
questions.solution: The modified quota 7.6 is more than the cutoff 7.48, so it is rounded up to 8 seats.

solve.work: 7.6 > 7.48, rounded up to 8.

questions.stem: In the Huntington-Hill method, the cutoff for rounding a modified quota between two whole numbers is their geometric mean. What is the square of the cutoff between 5 and 6?
questions.solution: The cutoff is $\sqrt{5 \times 6}$, so its square is 5 x 6 = 30. The cutoff itself is about 5.48.

solve.work: Cutoff sqrt(30); its square is 30.

questions.stem: In the Huntington-Hill method, a modified quota between 3 and 4 is rounded up if it is more than $\sqrt{3 \times 4}$, which is about 3.46, and down otherwise. A state's modified quota is 3.4. How many seats does it receive?
questions.solution: The modified quota 3.4 is less than the cutoff 3.46, so it is rounded down to 3 seats.

solve.work: 3.4 < 3.46, rounded down to 3.

questions.stem: Which of these methods rounds every modified quota up to the next whole number?
questions.answer: Adams
questions.solution: The Jefferson method rounds every quota down, the Adams method rounds every quota up, and the Webster and Huntington-Hill methods round to a nearby whole number using a cutoff.

solve.answer: Adams
solve.work: Adams rounds every quota up.

questions.stem: The average constituency of a state is its number of people per seat. Oak has 45,000 people and 9 seats. What is the average constituency of Oak?
questions.solution: The average constituency is 45,000 / 9 = 5,000 people per seat.

questions.stem: The average constituency of a state is its number of people per seat. Lake has 4,800 people and 8 seats, Hill has 3,500 people and 5 seats, Bay has 2,160 people and 3 seats, and Glen has 5,700 people and 10 seats. Which state has the smallest average constituency?
questions.answer: Glen
questions.solution: The averages are Lake 4,800 / 8 = 600, Hill 3,500 / 5 = 700, Bay 2,160 / 3 = 720 and Glen 5,700 / 10 = 570. The smallest is Glen, with 570 people per seat.

solve.answer: Glen
solve.work: Lake 600, Hill 700, Bay 720, Glen 570. Smallest Glen.

questions.stem: Use the Hamilton method to share 20 seats among four states. Their populations, in thousands, are Aspen 372, Birch 241, Cedar 117 and Dogwood 70. How many seats does Dogwood receive?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is $800 \div 20 = 40$. The standard quotas are 9.3, 6.025, 2.925 and 1.75. The lower quotas 9, 6, 2 and 1 use 18 seats, so 2 are left over. The largest decimal parts are 0.925 (Cedar) and 0.75 (Dogwood), so Cedar gets 3 and Dogwood gets 2.

solve.work: Total 800, SD 40. Quotas: A 9.3, B 6.025, C 2.925, D 1.75. Lower sum 18; 2 seats to C (.925) and D (.75). Dogwood 2.

questions.stem: Use the Hamilton method to share 21 seats among four states. Their populations, in thousands, are Aspen 262, Birch 250, Cedar 113 and Dogwood 47. Which list gives the seats for Aspen, Birch, Cedar and Dogwood, in that order?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is $672 \div 21 = 32$. The quotas are about 8.19, 7.81, 3.53, 1.47. The lower quotas 8, 7, 3 and 1 use 19 seats, so 2 are left over. They go to the largest decimal parts, Birch (0.81) and Cedar (0.53), giving 8, 8, 4, 1.

questions.stem: In the Jefferson method, 15 seats are shared among four states whose populations, in thousands, are Aspen 283, Birch 193, Cedar 155 and Dogwood 134. The modified divisor 45 gives a total of exactly 15 seats. How many seats does Dogwood receive?
questions.solution: Divide each population by 45 and round down: about 6.29, 4.29, 3.44, 2.98 become 6, 4, 3 and 2, which total 15. Dogwood's modified quota is 2.98, which rounds down to 2.

questions.stem: In the Adams method, 18 seats are shared among four states whose populations, in thousands, are Aspen 329, Birch 321, Cedar 169 and Dogwood 99. The modified divisor 55 gives a total of exactly 18 seats. How many seats does Cedar receive?
questions.solution: Divide each population by 55 and round up: about 5.98, 5.84, 3.07, 1.80 become 6, 6, 4 and 2, which total 18. Cedar's modified quota is 3.07, which rounds up to 4.

questions.stem: In the Webster method, 21 seats are shared among four states whose populations, in thousands, are Aspen 199, Birch 193, Cedar 122 and Dogwood 116. Dividing by the standard divisor and rounding each quota to the nearest whole number gives exactly 21 seats, so no change of divisor is needed. How many seats does Birch receive?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is $630 \div 21 = 30$. The quotas are about 6.63, 6.43, 4.07, 3.87. Rounded to the nearest whole number they are 7, 6, 4 and 4, which total 21. Birch's quota 6.43 rounds down to 6.

questions.stem: The Huntington-Hill method decides whether to round a modified quota that lies between 4 and 5 up or down by comparing it with a cutoff. What is the cutoff?
questions.answer: $\sqrt{4 \times 5}$
questions.solution: The Huntington-Hill cutoff is the geometric mean of the two whole numbers around the quota: $\sqrt{4 \times 5} \approx 4.47$. A quota above it rounds up to 5, and a quota below it rounds down to 4. The arithmetic mean, 4.5, is the Webster cutoff.

solve.answer: $\sqrt{4 \times 5}$
solve.work: Huntington-Hill uses the geometric mean sqrt(n(n+1)) = sqrt(20).

questions.stem: The quota rule says a state's number of seats should be either its standard quota rounded down or its standard quota rounded up. A state's standard quota is 7.4. What is the greatest number of seats the quota rule allows it to receive?
questions.solution: The lower quota is 7 and the upper quota is 8. The quota rule allows 7 or 8 seats, so the greatest is 8.

solve.work: Upper quota of 7.4 is 8.

questions.stem: Which method is used today to divide the 435 seats of the United States House of Representatives among the states?
questions.answer: Huntington-Hill
questions.solution: The Huntington-Hill method has been used for the House since 1941. Hamilton, Jefferson and Webster were used in earlier years.

solve.answer: Huntington-Hill
solve.work: Huntington-Hill, used since 1941.

questions.stem: Which statement is true?
choices: Adams tends to favor states with large populations.
Jefferson tends to favor states with small populations.
Jefferson tends to favor states with large populations.
Hamilton rounds every quota up to the next whole number.
questions.answer: Jefferson tends to favor states with large populations.
questions.solution: Jefferson rounds down, so it must use a smaller divisor to reach the total, and that helps the states with large populations. Adams rounds up and so tends to favor small states. Hamilton rounds quotas down first and then gives leftover seats to the largest decimal parts.

solve.answer: Jefferson tends to favor states with large populations.
solve.work: Jefferson (rounding down) favors large states; Adams favors small; Hamilton does not round all up.

questions.stem: In the Jefferson method, the lower quotas found with the standard divisor add up to 18, but there are 20 seats to share. What must be done?
choices: Use a divisor larger than the standard divisor and round down again
Give the 2 extra seats to the states with the largest decimal parts
Round every quota up instead of down, as the Adams method does
Use a divisor smaller than the standard divisor and round down again
questions.answer: Use a divisor smaller than the standard divisor and round down again
questions.solution: A smaller divisor makes every quota larger, so more quotas reach the next whole number when rounded down. The total rises until it reaches 20. Giving leftover seats to the largest decimal parts is the Hamilton method, and rounding up is the Adams method.

solve.answer: Use a divisor smaller than the standard divisor and round down again
solve.work: Too few seats: quotas must grow, so divide by a smaller divisor, then round down.

questions.stem: A council of 12 seats is shared among four wards. Their populations, in thousands, are 138, 96, 78 and 48. What is the standard quota of the ward with the largest population?
questions.solution: The total population is 138 + 96 + 78 + 48 = 360 thousand. The standard divisor is 360 / 12 = 30 thousand per seat. The largest ward's standard quota is 138 / 30 = 4.6.

questions.stem: Twenty seats are shared among four districts with populations, in thousands, of 410, 255, 187 and 148. How many of the districts have a standard quota greater than 3?
questions.solution: The total is 410 + 255 + 187 + 148 = 1,000 thousand, so the standard divisor is 1,000 / 20 = 50 thousand. The standard quotas are 8.2, 5.1, 3.74 and 2.96. Three of them are greater than 3.

solve.work: Total 1000, SD 50: 8.2, 5.1, 3.74, 2.96. Greater than 3: three.

questions.stem: Seventeen seats are shared by the Hamilton method among four counties, Marlow, Norton, Oakdale and Pinecrest, with populations, in thousands, of 332, 178, 114 and 56. How many seats does Norton receive?
questions.solution: The total is 680 thousand, so the standard divisor is 680 / 17 = 40. The standard quotas are 8.30, 4.45, 2.85 and 1.40, with lower quotas 8, 4, 2 and 1, which use 15 seats. Two seats are left over, and they go to the largest decimal parts, 0.85 (Oakdale) and 0.45 (Norton). Norton receives 4 + 1 = 5 seats.

questions.stem: Four states share 20 seats. Their standard quotas are 7.46, 5.38, 4.45 and 2.71. Which list gives their seats by the Hamilton method, in the same order?
questions.solution: The lower quotas are 7, 5, 4 and 2, which use 18 seats, so 2 seats are left over. The largest decimal parts are 0.71 (the fourth state) and 0.46 (the first state), so those two states get one more seat each: 8, 5, 4 and 3.

questions.stem: Twenty-two seats are shared by the Hamilton method among five towns, Alder, Bishop, Cole, Dunmore and Easton, with populations, in thousands, of 193, 190, 116, 84 and 77. How many seats do Dunmore and Easton receive together?
questions.solution: The total is 660 thousand, so the standard divisor is 660 / 22 = 30. The standard quotas are 6.43, 6.33, 3.87, 2.80 and 2.57, with lower quotas 6, 6, 3, 2 and 2, which use 19 seats. Three seats are left over and go to the largest decimal parts: 0.87 (Cole), 0.80 (Dunmore) and 0.57 (Easton). Dunmore and Easton receive 3 + 3 = 6 seats.

questions.stem: Twenty seats are shared among five regions by the Jefferson method. Their populations, in thousands, are 292, 241, 132, 78 and 57. The modified divisor 35 gives exactly 20 seats. How many seats does the region with 57 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: With the modified divisor 35 the modified quotas are 8.34, 6.89, 3.77, 2.23 and 1.63, and the Jefferson method rounds down: 8, 6, 3, 2 and 1, which is 20 seats. The region with 57 thousand people receives 1 seat.

questions.stem: Twelve seats are shared by the Jefferson method among three towns with populations, in thousands, of 241, 231 and 128. Which modified divisor gives exactly 12 seats?
questions.solution: With 44 the modified quotas are 5.48, 5.25 and 2.91, which round down to 5, 5 and 2: 12 seats. With 40 they are 6.03, 5.78 and 3.2, giving 6 + 5 + 3 = 14. With 48 they are 5.02, 4.81 and 2.67, giving 5 + 4 + 2 = 11. With 50 they are 4.82, 4.62 and 2.56, giving 4 + 4 + 2 = 10.

questions.stem: The standard divisor is 50. In the Jefferson method, the lower quotas found with it give only 18 of the 20 seats. Which modified divisor might the method use next?
questions.solution: Rounding down with the standard divisor gives too few seats, so the modified quotas must get larger. That needs a divisor smaller than 50, and only 46 is smaller. A divisor of 50 gives the same 18 seats again, and larger divisors give fewer.

solve.work: Too few seats under Jefferson: smaller divisor, 46.

questions.stem: Eighteen seats are shared by the Adams method among four states with populations, in thousands, of 488, 255, 118 and 39. The modified divisor 56 gives exactly 18 seats. How many seats does the state with 118 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: With the modified divisor 56 the modified quotas are 8.71, 4.55, 2.11 and 0.70, and the Adams method rounds up: 9, 5, 3 and 1, which is 18 seats. The state with 118 thousand people receives 3 seats.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Adams method is true?
choices: Every state receives at least one seat, however small its population
A state with a very small population can receive no seats at all, as in the Jefferson method
Every modified quota is rounded down to the whole number below it
It tends to favor the states with the largest populations
questions.answer: Every state receives at least one seat, however small its population
questions.solution: The Adams method rounds every modified quota up, so any state with a positive population gets at least 1 seat. Rounding up is what helps small states most, so the method favors them rather than the large states.

solve.answer: Every state receives at least one seat, however small its population
solve.work: Adams rounds up, so every state with people gets at least 1. Option B.

questions.stem: Twenty seats are shared by the Webster method among five regions with populations, in thousands, of 395, 201, 157, 25 and 22. The modified divisor 42 gives exactly 20 seats. How many seats does the region with 22 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: With the modified divisor 42 the modified quotas are 9.40, 4.79, 3.74, 0.60 and 0.52, and the Webster method rounds to the nearest whole number: 9, 5, 4, 1 and 1, which is 20 seats. The region with 22 thousand people has a modified quota of 0.52, which rounds to 1, so it receives 1 seat.

questions.stem: Twenty seats are shared among four districts by the Webster method, with populations, in thousands, of 415, 333, 133 and 119. Dividing by the standard divisor and rounding each quota to the nearest whole number gives exactly 20 seats, so no change of divisor is needed. How many seats does the district with 333 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 1,000 thousand, so the standard divisor is 1,000 / 20 = 50. The quotas are 8.30, 6.66, 2.66 and 2.38, which round to 8, 7, 3 and 2, which is 20 seats. The district with 333 thousand people receives 7 seats.

questions.stem: In the Huntington-Hill method, a state's modified quota is 4.48. How many seats does the state receive?
questions.solution: The quota lies between 4 and 5, so the cutoff is $\sqrt{4 \times 5} = \sqrt{20}$, which is about 4.472. Since $4.48^2$ is about 20.07, which is more than 20, the quota 4.48 is more than the cutoff and is rounded up to 5 seats. (The Webster method would round it down to 4, because it is less than 4.5.)

questions.stem: Which of these modified quotas is rounded up by the Huntington-Hill method but rounded down by the Webster method?
questions.solution: Between 3 and 4 the Huntington-Hill cutoff is $\sqrt{12}$, about 3.464, while the Webster cutoff is 3.5. A quota between 3.464 and 3.5 is rounded up by Huntington-Hill and down by Webster. Only 3.47 is in that range: 3.40 is rounded down by both, and 3.52 and 3.61 are rounded up by both.

solve.work: HH cutoff 3.464, Webster 3.5. 3.47 is between: up by HH, down by Webster.

questions.stem: Twenty seats are shared by the Huntington-Hill method among five regions with populations, in thousands, of 280, 230, 151, 107 and 32. The modified divisor 43 gives exactly 20 seats. How many seats does the region with 107 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The modified quotas are 6.51, 5.35, 3.51, 2.49 and 0.74. The cutoffs are $\sqrt{42}$ = 6.48 between 6 and 7, $\sqrt{30}$ = 5.48 between 5 and 6, $\sqrt{12}$ = 3.46 between 3 and 4, $\sqrt{6}$ = 2.45 between 2 and 3, and 0 between 0 and 1. So the quotas round to 7, 5, 4, 3 and 1: 20 seats. The region with 107 thousand people has quota 2.49, which is above 2.45, so it receives 3 seats.

questions.stem: Fourteen seats are shared among four districts with populations, in thousands, of 290, 102, 98 and 70. The Jefferson method gives them 8, 2, 2 and 2 seats, and the Adams method gives them 6, 3, 3 and 2 seats. How many more seats does the largest district receive from the Jefferson method than from the Adams method?
questions.solution: The largest district receives 8 seats from the Jefferson method and 6 from the Adams method, which is 8 - 6 = 2 more.

questions.stem: The average constituency of a state is its number of people per seat. A county with 21,000 people has 3 seats, and a fourth seat is added. What is the average constituency of the county after the fourth seat is added?
questions.solution: The average constituency is now 21,000 / 4 = 5,250 people per seat. (It was 7,000 before.)

questions.stem: The quota rule says that a state's number of seats must be its lower quota or its upper quota. A state's standard quota is 4.7. Which numbers of seats satisfy the quota rule for this state?
questions.answer: 4 or 5 seats
questions.solution: The lower quota of 4.7 is 4 and the upper quota is 5. The quota rule allows either of them, so 4 or 5 seats.

solve.answer: 4 or 5 seats
solve.work: Lower 4, upper 5. Option C.

questions.stem: Which of these methods never breaks the quota rule?
questions.answer: Hamilton
questions.solution: The Hamilton method gives every state its lower quota and then at most one more seat, so it always stays within the quota rule. The divisor methods, including Jefferson, Adams and Huntington-Hill, can give a state seats outside its lower and upper quotas.

solve.answer: Hamilton
solve.work: Hamilton always gives lower or upper quota.

questions.stem: Which of these methods tends to favor states with small populations?
questions.answer: Adams
questions.solution: Rounding every modified quota up helps small states the most, so the Adams method tends to favor them. The Jefferson method, which rounds down, tends to favor large states. The Webster method is close to neutral, and the Hamilton method has no systematic lean for a particular size.

solve.answer: Adams
solve.work: Adams favors small states.

questions.stem: Which of these describes the Alabama paradox?
choices: A state with faster population growth than another state loses a seat to that state at the next apportionment
A new state is added with the extra seats it deserves, yet some old states' seats change among themselves
A state receives more seats than its upper quota or fewer seats than its lower quota in the apportionment
A state loses a seat when the total number of seats is increased, although no state's population has changed
questions.answer: A state loses a seat when the total number of seats is increased, although no state's population has changed
questions.solution: In the Alabama paradox the populations stay the same and only the total number of seats goes up, yet some state ends up with fewer seats than before. The other descriptions are the population paradox, the new-states paradox and a violation of the quota rule.

solve.answer: A state loses a seat when the total number of seats is increased, although no state's population has changed
solve.work: Alabama paradox: more seats in total, a state loses one. Option D.

questions.stem: Which of these describes the population paradox?
choices: A state loses a seat when the total number of seats is increased, although no state's population has changed
A new state is added with the extra seats it deserves, yet some old states' seats change among themselves
A state with faster population growth than another state loses a seat to that state at the next apportionment
A state receives more seats than its upper quota or fewer seats than its lower quota in the apportionment
questions.answer: A state with faster population growth than another state loses a seat to that state at the next apportionment
questions.solution: In the population paradox, the populations change between two apportionments. A state that grew faster in percentage ends up with fewer seats, because the seat goes to a state that grew more slowly. The other descriptions are the Alabama paradox, the new-states paradox and a quota-rule violation.

solve.answer: A state with faster population growth than another state loses a seat to that state at the next apportionment
solve.work: Population paradox: faster-growing state loses a seat to another. Option C.

questions.stem: Which of these describes the new-states paradox?
choices: A state loses a seat when the total number of seats is increased, although no state's population has changed
A state with faster population growth than another state loses a seat to that state at the next apportionment
A new state is added with the extra seats it deserves, yet some old states' seats change among themselves
A state receives more seats than its upper quota or fewer seats than its lower quota in the apportionment
questions.answer: A new state is added with the extra seats it deserves, yet some old states' seats change among themselves
questions.solution: In the new-states paradox, a new state joins and the total number of seats is raised by the number the new state deserves. The old states' populations have not changed, but one old state gains a seat from another. The other descriptions are the Alabama paradox, the population paradox and a quota-rule violation.

solve.answer: A new state is added with the extra seats it deserves, yet some old states' seats change among themselves
solve.work: New-states paradox: adding a state with its fair seats changes old states' seats. Option D.

questions.stem: In the Jefferson method, 14 seats are shared among four states whose populations, in thousands, are Aspen 316, Birch 306, Cedar 199 and Dogwood 103. Which modified divisor gives exactly 14 seats?
questions.solution: Divide each population by the divisor and round down, then add. With 60 the seats are 5, 5, 3 and 1, a total of 14. With 50 the total is 17, with 66 (the standard divisor) it is 12, and with 70 it is 11.

questions.stem: Use the Adams method to share 18 seats among four states. Their populations, in thousands, are Aspen 257, Birch 234, Cedar 97 and Dogwood 42. How many seats does Dogwood receive?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is $630 \div 18 = 35$. Rounding the quotas up (about 7.34, 6.69, 2.77, 1.20) gives 8, 7, 3 and 2, a total of 20, which is 2 too many. A larger divisor is needed. With 40 the quotas are about 6.43, 5.85, 2.43, 1.05, which round up to 7, 6, 3 and 2, a total of 18. Dogwood gets 2.

solve.work: Total 630, SD 35: ceilings 8+7+3+2 = 20, too many. d=40: A 6.43->7, B 5.85->6, C 2.43->3, D 1.05->2 = 18. Dogwood drops to 1 only at d>=42, where total is 7+6+3+1 = 17, so any valid divisor gives Dogwood 2.

questions.stem: Use the Webster method to share 14 seats among four states. Their populations, in thousands, are Aspen 287, Birch 256, Cedar 212 and Dogwood 141. How many seats does Aspen receive?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is $896 \div 14 = 64$. The quotas, about 4.48, 4.00, 3.31, 2.20, round to 4, 4, 3 and 2, a total of 13, which is 1 too few. A smaller divisor is needed. With 62 the quotas are about 4.63, 4.13, 3.42, 2.27, which round to 5, 4, 3 and 2, a total of 14. Aspen gets 5.

questions.stem: Use the Huntington-Hill method to share 16 seats among four states. Their populations, in thousands, are Aspen 259, Birch 173, Cedar 78 and Dogwood 50. How many seats does Dogwood receive?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is $560 \div 16 = 35$. The quotas are about 7.40, 4.94, 2.23, 1.43. The cutoffs are $\sqrt{7 \times 8} \approx 7.48$, $\sqrt{4 \times 5} \approx 4.47$, $\sqrt{2 \times 3} \approx 2.45$ and $\sqrt{1 \times 2} \approx 1.41$. The quotas round to 7, 5, 2 and 2, which total 16, so this divisor works. Dogwood's quota 1.43 is above 1.41, so it rounds up to 2.

questions.stem: Twelve seats are shared among four states whose populations, in thousands, are Aspen 231, Birch 195, Cedar 140 and Dogwood 106. Which state receives one more seat under the Jefferson method than under the Hamilton method?
questions.answer: Birch
questions.solution: Hamilton: the standard divisor is $672 \div 12 = 56$, the quotas are about 4.13, 3.48, 2.50, 1.89, and the leftover seats go to Dogwood (0.89) and Cedar (0.50), giving 4, 3, 3, 2. Jefferson: with the divisor 48 the quotas (about 4.81, 4.06, 2.92, 2.21) round down to 4, 4, 2, 2, a total of 12. Birch gains a seat and Cedar loses one.

solve.answer: Birch
solve.work: Total 672, SD 56. Quotas A 4.125, B 3.482, C 2.5, D 1.893. Hamilton: 4,3,2,1 + seats to D and C: 4,3,3,2. Jefferson: d=48: 4.81->4, 4.06->4, 2.92->2, 2.21->2 = 12 (valid for d in (46.67, 48.75]). Jefferson 4,4,2,2. Birch gains one.

questions.stem: Three states have populations, in thousands, of Aspen 470, Birch 330 and Cedar 200. The Hamilton method first shares 7 seats among them, and then shares 8 seats among the same states. Which statement is true?
choices: Cedar loses a seat when the total goes from 7 to 8.
Aspen loses a seat when the total goes from 7 to 8.
Birch loses a seat when the total goes from 7 to 8.
No state loses a seat when the total goes from 7 to 8.
questions.answer: Cedar loses a seat when the total goes from 7 to 8.
questions.solution: With 7 seats the quotas are 3.29, 2.31, 1.40, the lower quotas use 6 seats, and the leftover seat goes to Cedar (0.40), giving 3, 2, 2. With 8 seats the quotas are 3.76, 2.64, 1.60, the lower quotas use 6 seats, and the 2 leftover seats go to Aspen (0.76) and Birch (0.64), giving 4, 3, 1. Cedar falls from 2 seats to 1 although there is one more seat to share: this is the Alabama paradox.

solve.answer: Cedar loses a seat when the total goes from 7 to 8.
solve.work: Total 1000. 7 seats: quotas 3.29, 2.31, 1.40; lower 6, extra to C: 3,2,2. 8 seats: 3.76, 2.64, 1.6; lower 6, extras to A and B: 4,3,1. Cedar loses a seat (Alabama paradox).

questions.stem: Four states with populations, in thousands, Aspen 259, Birch 109, Cedar 88 and Dogwood 38 share 19 seats. The standard divisor is 26, and the Jefferson method gives the states 11, 4, 3 and 1 seats, in that order. Which statement is true?
choices: Aspen gets less than its lower quota, so Jefferson breaks the quota rule.
Aspen gets more than its upper quota, so Jefferson breaks the quota rule.
Every state gets its lower or upper quota, so the quota rule holds.
Dogwood gets more than its upper quota, so Jefferson breaks the quota rule.
questions.answer: Aspen gets more than its upper quota, so Jefferson breaks the quota rule.
questions.solution: The standard quotas are about 9.96, 4.19, 3.38, 1.46. Aspen's quota 9.96 has an upper quota of 10, but Jefferson gives it 11 seats. The other states stay within their lower and upper quotas: Birch 4 (4 or 5), Cedar 3 (3 or 4), Dogwood 1 (1 or 2).

solve.answer: Aspen gets more than its upper quota, so Jefferson breaks the quota rule.
solve.work: Quotas with SD 26: A 9.96, B 4.19, C 3.38, D 1.46. Aspen's upper quota is 10 but gets 11 (check d=23.5: 11,4,3,1 = 19). Upper-quota violation.

questions.stem: State X has 5400 people and 9 seats. State Y has 2100 people and 3 seats. One seat is moved from X to Y, so X has 8 seats and Y has 4. After the move, how many more people per seat does X have than Y has?
questions.solution: After the move X has $5400 \div 8 = 675$ people per seat and Y has $2100 \div 4 = 525$ people per seat. The difference is $675 - 525 = 150$. Before the move the averages were 600 and 700, a difference of 100, so the move made the averages less equal.

questions.stem: In the Webster method, 14 seats are shared among four states whose populations, in thousands, are Aspen 336, Birch 309, Cedar 244 and Dogwood 175. Which modified divisor gives exactly 14 seats?
questions.solution: Divide each population by the divisor, round to the nearest whole number, then add. With 72 the seats are 5, 4, 3 and 2, a total of 14. With 68 the total is 17, and with both 76 (the standard divisor) and 80 it is 13.

questions.stem: After a new census, the Hamilton method takes a seat away from State X, whose population grew by 8 percent, and gives it to State Y, whose population grew by only 2 percent. The total number of seats did not change. Which of these describes what happened?
choices: A violation of the upper quota
questions.answer: The population paradox
questions.solution: A state that grows faster loses a seat to a state that grows more slowly, with the total number of seats unchanged. This is the population paradox. The Alabama paradox needs the total number of seats to change, and the new-states paradox needs a new state to join.

solve.answer: The population paradox
solve.work: Faster-growing state loses a seat to slower-growing one, seats fixed: population paradox.

questions.stem: A state has 192,000 people and a standard quota of 6.4. There are 20 seats to share in all. What is the total population of all of the states, in people?
questions.solution: The standard divisor is 192,000 / 6.4 = 30,000 people per seat. The total population is the standard divisor times the number of seats: 30,000 x 20 = 600,000.

questions.stem: Twenty-six seats are shared by the Hamilton method among five regions with populations, in thousands, of 472, 223, 150, 107 and 88. How many seats does the region with 107 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 1,040 thousand, so the standard divisor is 1,040 / 26 = 40. The standard quotas are 11.80, 5.575, 3.75, 2.675 and 2.20, with lower quotas 11, 5, 3, 2 and 2, which use 23 seats. Three seats are left over and go to the largest decimal parts: 0.80 (472), 0.75 (150) and 0.675 (107). The region with 107 thousand people gets 2 + 1 = 3 seats.

questions.stem: Four states share 20 seats by the Hamilton method. Their standard quotas are 6.46, 5.41, 4.44 and 3.69. Which state is rounded up even though the decimal part of its standard quota is less than 0.5?
questions.answer: The state with standard quota 6.46
questions.solution: The lower quotas 6, 5, 4 and 3 use 18 seats, so 2 seats are left over. They go to the two largest decimal parts, 0.69 and 0.46. The state with quota 6.46 gets a seat even though 0.46 is less than 0.5. The state with quota 3.69 also gets one, but its decimal part is more than 0.5.

solve.answer: The state with standard quota 6.46
solve.work: Lower 6,5,4,3 = 18; 2 left go to .69 and .46. 6.46 rounded up though < .5.

questions.stem: Eighteen seats are shared by the Hamilton method among four islands with populations, in thousands, of 532, 200, 128 and 40. How many seats does the island with 40 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 900 thousand, so the standard divisor is 900 / 18 = 50. The standard quotas are 10.64, 4.00, 2.56 and 0.80, with lower quotas 10, 4, 2 and 0, which use 16 seats. Two seats are left over and go to the largest decimal parts, 0.80 and 0.64. So the smallest island receives 0 + 1 = 1 seat.

solve.work: Total 900, SD 50: 10.64, 4, 2.56, 0.8. Lower 16; 2 left to .8 and .64. 40k island gets 1.

questions.stem: Twenty-three seats are shared by the Jefferson method among five states with populations, in thousands, of 437, 248, 131, 54 and 50. How many seats does the state with 437 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 920 thousand, so the standard divisor is 920 / 23 = 40, and its lower quotas give only 21 seats. A smaller divisor is needed, and 36 works: with 36 the modified quotas are 12.14, 6.89, 3.64, 1.50 and 1.39, and the Jefferson method rounds down: 12, 6, 3, 1 and 1, which is 23 seats. The state with 437 thousand people receives 12 seats.

questions.stem: Fifteen seats are shared by the Jefferson method among four states with populations, in thousands, of 253, 119, 46 and 32. Several whole numbers work as the modified divisor. What is the largest whole number that gives exactly 15 seats?
questions.solution: Try 28: the modified quotas are 9.04, 4.25, 1.64 and 1.14, which round down to 9, 4, 1 and 1: 15 seats. Try 29: the quotas are 8.72, 4.10, 1.59 and 1.10, which round down to 8, 4, 1 and 1: only 14 seats. Larger divisors give no more than 14, so the largest whole number that works is 28.

questions.stem: Twenty-six seats are shared by the Jefferson method among five counties with populations, in thousands, of 416, 237, 191, 163 and 33. How many seats does the county with 33 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 1,040 thousand, so the standard divisor is 40, and its lower quotas (10, 5, 4, 4 and 0) give only 23 seats. A smaller divisor is needed, and 36 works: the modified quotas are 11.56, 6.58, 5.31, 4.53 and 0.92, and the Jefferson method rounds down: 11, 6, 5, 4 and 0, which is 26 seats. So the smallest county receives no seat at all.

questions.stem: Twenty-one seats are shared by the Adams method among five districts with populations, in thousands, of 379, 213, 173, 51 and 24. How many seats does the district with 379 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 840 thousand, so the standard divisor is 40. Rounding the standard quotas up gives 24 seats, which is too many, so a larger divisor is needed. With 45 the modified quotas are 8.42, 4.73, 3.84, 1.13 and 0.53, and the Adams method rounds up: 9, 5, 4, 2 and 1, which is 21 seats. The district with 379 thousand people receives 9 seats.

questions.stem: Sixteen seats are shared by the Adams method among four towns with populations, in thousands, of 170, 120, 115 and 75. Which modified divisor gives exactly 16 seats?
questions.solution: With 36 the modified quotas are 4.72, 3.33, 3.19 and 2.08, which round up to 5, 4, 4 and 3: 16 seats. With 31 they are 5.48, 3.87, 3.71 and 2.42, giving 6 + 4 + 4 + 3 = 17. With 38 they are 4.47, 3.16, 3.03 and 1.97, giving 5 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 15. With 41 they are 4.15, 2.93, 2.80 and 1.83, giving 5 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 13.

questions.stem: Seventeen seats are shared by the Adams method among four states with populations, in thousands, of 267, 151, 50 and 42. Several whole numbers work as the modified divisor. What is the smallest whole number that gives exactly 17 seats?
questions.solution: Try 34: the modified quotas are 7.85, 4.44, 1.47 and 1.24, which round up to 8, 5, 2 and 2: 17 seats. Try 33: the quotas are 8.09, 4.58, 1.52 and 1.27, which round up to 9, 5, 2 and 2: 18 seats, too many. Smaller divisors give even more seats, so the smallest whole number that works is 34.

questions.stem: Twenty-two seats are shared by the Webster method among five towns with populations, in thousands, of 367, 255, 97, 96 and 65. How many seats does the town with 255 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 880 thousand, so the standard divisor is 880 / 22 = 40, and rounding its quotas to the nearest whole number gives 21 seats, one too few. A slightly smaller divisor is needed, and 39 works: with 39 the modified quotas are 9.41, 6.54, 2.49, 2.46 and 1.67, and the Webster method rounds to the nearest whole number: 9, 7, 2, 2 and 2, which is 22 seats. The town with 255 thousand people receives 7 seats.

questions.stem: Fifteen seats are shared by the Webster method among four counties with populations, in thousands, of 429, 274, 158 and 39. Which modified divisor gives exactly 15 seats?
questions.solution: With 62 the modified quotas are 6.92, 4.42, 2.55 and 0.63, which round to 7, 4, 3 and 1: 15 seats. With 58 they are 7.40, 4.72, 2.72 and 0.67, giving 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 16. With 60 they are 7.15, 4.57, 2.63 and 0.65, giving 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 16. With 64 they are 6.70, 4.28, 2.47 and 0.61, giving 7 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 14.

questions.stem: Sixteen seats are shared by the Webster method among four states with populations, in thousands, of 578, 95, 87 and 40. Several whole numbers work as the modified divisor. What is the largest whole number that gives exactly 16 seats?
questions.solution: Try 55: the modified quotas are 10.51, 1.73, 1.58 and 0.73, which round to 11, 2, 2 and 1: 16 seats. Try 56: the quotas are 10.32, 1.70, 1.55 and 0.71, which round to 10, 2, 2 and 1: only 15 seats. Larger divisors give no more than 15, so the largest whole number that works is 55.

questions.stem: Twenty-four seats are shared by the Huntington-Hill method among five towns with populations, in thousands, of 546, 299, 139, 131 and 85. How many seats does the town with 131 thousand people receive?
questions.solution: The total is 1,200 thousand, so the standard divisor is 50, but its quotas give 25 seats with the Huntington-Hill rounding, one too many. The divisor 53 works. The modified quotas are 10.30, 5.64, 2.62, 2.47 and 1.60. The cutoffs are $\sqrt{110}$ = 10.49, $\sqrt{30}$ = 5.48, $\sqrt{6}$ = 2.45 and $\sqrt{2}$ = 1.41. So the seats are 10, 6, 3, 3 and 2: 24 in all. The town with 131 thousand people has quota 2.47, which is above 2.45, so it receives 3 seats.

questions.stem: Seventeen seats are shared by the Huntington-Hill method among four counties with populations, in thousands, of 402, 224, 134 and 90. Which modified divisor gives exactly 17 seats?
questions.solution: With 52 the modified quotas are 7.73, 4.31, 2.58 and 1.73. The cutoffs are $\sqrt{56}$ = 7.48, $\sqrt{20}$ = 4.47, $\sqrt{6}$ = 2.45 and $\sqrt{2}$ = 1.41, so the seats are 8, 4, 3 and 2: 17. The divisors 50, 54 and 58 give 18, 16 and 15 seats.

questions.stem: Eighteen seats are shared among four states with populations, in thousands, of 407, 291, 128 and 74. The Webster method gives them 8, 6, 3 and 1 seats, and the Huntington-Hill method gives them 8, 6, 2 and 2 seats. Which state receives more seats from the Huntington-Hill method than from the Webster method?
questions.answer: The state with 74 thousand people
questions.solution: Comparing the lists state by state, the first two states get the same seats in both methods. The third state gets 3 from Webster but 2 from Huntington-Hill, and the fourth, with 74 thousand people, gets 1 from Webster but 2 from Huntington-Hill.

solve.answer: The state with 74 thousand people
solve.work: 74k state: 1 by Webster, 2 by HH. (Checked: d=50 Webster gives 8,6,3,1; d about 52.3 HH gives 8,6,2,2.)

questions.stem: Twenty-six seats are shared among five states with populations, in thousands, of 666, 210, 74, 68 and 22. The Hamilton method gives them 17, 5, 2, 2 and 0 seats, and the Jefferson method gives them 18, 5, 2, 1 and 0 seats. Which state receives fewer seats from the Jefferson method than from the Hamilton method?
questions.answer: The state with 68 thousand people
questions.solution: Comparing the lists state by state: the largest state gets 17 from Hamilton and 18 from Jefferson (more, not fewer), the next two states get the same in both methods, and the state with 68 thousand people gets 2 from Hamilton but 1 from Jefferson.

solve.answer: The state with 68 thousand people
solve.work: 68k state: 2 by Hamilton, 1 by Jefferson. (Results checked.)

questions.stem: The average constituency of a state is its number of people per seat, and the absolute unfairness between two states is the difference of their average constituencies. State X has 48,000 people and 6 seats, and State Y has 15,000 people and 3 seats. One seat is moved from X to Y, so X has 5 seats and Y has 4. What is the absolute unfairness between X and Y afterward?
questions.solution: Afterward X has 48,000 / 5 = 9,600 people per seat and Y has 15,000 / 4 = 3,750 people per seat. The difference is 9,600 - 3,750 = 5,850. (Before the move it was 8,000 - 5,000 = 3,000, so the move made things less fair.)

questions.stem: The average constituency of a state is its number of people per seat. The absolute unfairness between two states is the difference of their average constituencies, and the relative unfairness is the absolute unfairness divided by the smaller average constituency. State A has 36,000 people and 6 seats, and State B has 20,000 people and 4 seats. What is the relative unfairness between A and B?
questions.solution: A has 36,000 / 6 = 6,000 people per seat and B has 20,000 / 4 = 5,000. The absolute unfairness is 6,000 - 5,000 = 1,000. Dividing by the smaller average constituency, 5,000, gives 1,000 / 5,000 = 0.2.

questions.stem: Nineteen seats are shared among four states with populations, in thousands, of 654, 113, 110 and 73, so the standard divisor is 50. The Adams method gives them 12, 3, 2 and 2 seats. Which statement is true?
choices: Every state gets its lower quota or its upper quota, so Adams keeps the quota rule here
The largest state gets more than its upper quota of 14, so Adams breaks the quota rule
The smallest state gets more than its upper quota of 2, so Adams breaks the quota rule
The largest state gets 12 seats, below its lower quota 13, so Adams breaks the quota rule
questions.answer: The largest state gets 12 seats, below its lower quota 13, so Adams breaks the quota rule
questions.solution: The standard quotas are 13.08, 2.26, 2.20 and 1.46. The lower quota of the largest state is 13, but the Adams method gives it only 12, which breaks the quota rule. It is not above its upper quota of 14, and the smallest state's 2 seats equal its upper quota of 2.

solve.answer: The largest state gets 12 seats, below its lower quota 13, so Adams breaks the quota rule
solve.work: SD 50: quotas 13.08, 2.26, 2.2, 1.46. Largest gets 12 < lower quota 13, so Adams breaks the quota rule. Option A.

questions.stem: Fourteen seats are shared among four states with populations, in thousands, of 349, 138, 48 and 25. The Jefferson method gives them 10, 3, 1 and 0 seats, and the Adams method gives them 8, 3, 2 and 1 seats. What do these results suggest?
choices: The Adams method favors larger states, and the Jefferson method favors smaller states
The Jefferson method favors larger states, and the Adams method favors smaller states
Both methods favor larger states, but the Adams method does so more strongly
Neither method leans either way, because both give out exactly 14 seats
questions.answer: The Jefferson method favors larger states, and the Adams method favors smaller states
questions.solution: The largest state receives 10 seats from Jefferson and only 8 from Adams, and the two smallest states receive 1 and 0 seats from Jefferson but 2 and 1 from Adams. That fits Jefferson leaning toward large states and Adams toward small ones. Giving out exactly 14 seats says nothing about bias.

solve.answer: The Jefferson method favors larger states, and the Adams method favors smaller states
solve.work: Jefferson gives the largest state more (10 vs 8), Adams gives the small ones more. Option A.

questions.stem: The Hamilton method shares 10 seats, and then 11 seats, among three counties with populations, in thousands, of 420, 420 and 140. How many seats does the county with 140 thousand people lose when the number of seats goes from 10 to 11?
questions.solution: With 10 seats the standard divisor is 98 and the quotas are 4.29, 4.29 and 1.43. The lower quotas use 9 seats, and the one leftover seat goes to the largest decimal part, 0.43, so the seats are 4, 4 and 2. With 11 seats the divisor is 980 / 11, about 89.1, and the quotas are 4.71, 4.71 and 1.57. The lower quotas 4, 4 and 1 use 9 seats and the two leftover seats go to the largest decimal parts, 0.71 and 0.71, so the seats are 5, 5 and 1. The small county drops from 2 seats to 1, losing 1 seat.

questions.stem: Which of these methods can produce the Alabama paradox?
questions.answer: Hamilton
questions.solution: The Hamilton method can take a seat away from a state when the total number of seats grows. The Jefferson, Adams, Webster and Huntington-Hill methods use a divisor, and a smaller divisor gives every state at least as many seats as before, so they cannot produce the Alabama paradox.

solve.answer: Hamilton
solve.work: Only Hamilton (a quota method) can; divisor methods cannot.
